### lsblk [options] [iodevice]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lsblk</samp> provides a hierarchical list of all block devices or all devices located on a data medium. The command is ideal for quickly obtaining a good overview of all partitions and logical volumes.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-a</samp>
    Also includes empty devices in the result.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-b</samp>
    Specifies sizes in bytes.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-f</samp>
    Also shows the file system type, the label, and the UUID for each device.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-p</samp>
    Specifies complete device names, such as <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">dev/mapper/fedora-swap</samp> for logical volumes.

#### Example

The following <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lsblk</samp> result was created on a server with two hard disks and RAID configuration:

```
root# lsblk
NAME    MAJ:MIN RM   SIZE RO TYPE  MOUNTPOINT
sda       8:0    1   3.7T  0 disk
  sda1    8:1    1    16G  0 part
    md0   9:0    0    16G  0 raid1 [SWAP]
  sda2    8:2    1   512M  0 part
    md1   9:1    0 511.4M  0 raid1 /boot
  sda3    8:3    1     2T  0 part
    md2   9:2    0     2T  0 raid1 /
sdb       8:16   1   3.7T  0 disk
  sdb1    8:17   1    16G  0 part
    md0   9:0    0    16G  0 raid1 [SWAP]
  sdb2    8:18   1   512M  0 part
    md1   9:1    0 511.4M  0 raid1 /boot
  sdb3    8:19   1     2T  0 part
    md2   9:2    0     2T  0 raid1 / 
```

### lsb_release [options]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lsb_release</samp> determines distribution-specific information, such as the name and version number of the running Linux system. LSB stands for Linux Standard Base. If no option is passed, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-v</samp> applies.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-a</samp>
    Displays all available information: the distribution name, the full description, the version number, and the code name (see the example later in this entry).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-v</samp>
    Displays the LSB version number, but only if the LSB modules are installed in addition to the command (<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lsb-core</samp> package). This is often not the case—the command then returns the error message no LSB modules are available. In practice, however, the LSB version number is rarely of interest. If you only want to know the version of the installed Linux system, you should use the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-a</samp> option.

#### Example

In the following example, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lsb_release</samp> was run on an installation of Ubuntu 24.04:

```
root# lsb_release -a
Distributor ID: Ubuntu
Description:    Ubuntu Noble Numbat (development branch)
Release:        24.04
Codename:       noble 
```

### lscpu [options]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lscpu</samp> displays detailed information about the CPU, its cores and cache, and—if applicable—the virtualization system.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-e</samp>
    Displays only a summary of the key data in an easy-to-read format.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-p</samp>
    Like <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-e</samp>, but provides the data in a format that can be easily processed in scripts.

### lshw [options]

The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lshw</samp> command from the package of the same name creates a hierarchical list of all hardware components on the computer.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-businfo</samp>
    Lists the components line by line and specifies an ID for the SCSI, USB, or PCI bus used for each component.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-html</samp>
    Formats the output as an HTML document.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-short</samp>
    Provides only a compact summary.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-xml</samp>
    Formats the output as an XML document.

#### Example

The following hardware overview was created on a Raspberry Pi 4B:

```
root# lshw -businfo
Bus info          Device  Class      Description
================================================
                          system     Raspberry Pi 4 Model B Rev 1.1
                          bus        Motherboard
cpu@0                     processor  cpu
cpu@1                     processor  cpu
cpu@2                     processor  cpu
cpu@3                     processor  cpu
                          memory     855MiB System memory
pci@0000:00:00.0          bridge     Broadcom Limited
pci@0000:01:00.0          bus        VL805 USB 3.0 Host Controller
usb@1             usb1    bus        xHCI Host Controller
usb@1:1                   bus        USB2.0 Hub
usb@1:1.4                 bus        Keyboard Hub
usb@1:1.4.2               input      Apple Keyboard
usb@1:1.4.3               input      USB-PS/2 Optical Mouse
usb@2             usb2    bus        xHCI Host Controller
                  eth0    network    Ethernet interface
                  wlan0   network    Wireless interface 
```

### lsmod

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lsmod</samp> provides a list of all modules that are currently loaded into the kernel.

### lsof [options] [file/interface]

Without any additional parameters, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lsof</samp> provides a usually very long list of all currently open files or interfaces and the processes assigned to them. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lsof file</samp> provides information on the process that keeps this file open.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-i</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">address</samp>
    Provides information on processes that use the specified network address. The address is composed in the following format: <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">[46][protocol][@hostname|hostaddr] [:service|port]</samp>. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-i 4tcp</samp> provides information on all processes that use TCP in IPv4.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-n</samp>
    Doesn’t resolve network names.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-N</samp>
    Takes NFS files into account as well.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-u</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">user</samp>
    Provides only information on files/interfaces that are used by the specified user. Multiple users can also be specified (name or UID, separated by commas).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-X</samp>
    Ignores all open TCP and UDP files.

#### Examples

The following two commands show all processes that use UDP or port 22:

```
root# lsof -i udp
ntpd      3696     ntp   16u  IPv4   9026       UDP *:ntp
portmap   4745  daemon    3u  IPv4  12931       UDP *:sunrpc
rpc.statd 4764   statd    5u  IPv4  12962       UDP *:700
...
root# lsof -i :22
COMMAND  PID USER   FD   TYPE DEVICE SIZE NODE NAME
sshd    5559 root    3u  IPv6  14097       TCP *:ssh (LISTEN)
sshd    7729 root    3r  IPv6  33146       TCP mars.sol:ssh->merkur.sol:45368
                                                                (ESTABLISHED) 
```

### lspci [options]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lspci</samp> provides information about the PCI bus and all devices connected to it.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-k</samp>
    Shows which kernel module is responsible for each PCI device.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-tv</samp>
    Provides a tree-shaped device list that clearly shows how the devices are connected to each other.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-v</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-vv</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-vvv</samp>
    Provides even more details.

### lsscsi [options]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lsscsi</samp> provides information about all connected SCSI and SATA devices.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-c</samp>
    Displays the data in the same format as <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/proc/scsi/scsi</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-H</samp>
    Provides a list of SCSI hosts (instead of SCSI devices).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-l</samp>
    Provides detailed information on each device.

#### Example

The following result was created on a computer with two PCIe SSDs and an external USB hard disk:

```
root# lsscsi
[0:0:0:0]    disk    WD Elements 25A2  1026         /dev/sda
[N:0:4:1]    disk    PM981 NVMe Samsung 2048GB__1   /dev/nvme0n1
[N:1:4:1]    disk    SAMSUNG MZVLB256HAHQ-000L7__1  /dev/nvme1n1 
```

### lsusb [options]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lsusb</samp> provides information about all connected USB devices.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-t</samp>
    Indents the output like a tree and thus makes it clear which device is connected to which bus.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-v</samp>
    Provides detailed information on each device.

#### Example

The following command shows that an Apple keyboard is connected to the computer:

```
user$ lsusb
Bus 004 Device 001: ID 1d6b:0003 Linux Foundation 3.0 root hub
Bus 003 Device 001: ID 1d6b:0002 Linux Foundation 2.0 root hub
Bus 002 Device 004: ID 1058:25a2 Western Digital Technologies, Inc. Elements 25A2
Bus 002 Device 001: ID 1d6b:0003 Linux Foundation 3.0 root hub
Bus 001 Device 007: ID 06cb:009a Synaptics, Inc.
Bus 001 Device 019: ID 05ac:021e Apple, Inc. Aluminum Mini Keyboard (ISO) ... 
```

### lvcreate [options] name

The LVM command <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lvcreate</samp> creates a new logical volume (LV) within the volume group (VG) that has been specified by <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-i</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Distributes the LV evenly over the specified number of physical volumes (PVs). This assumes that the VG consists of at least as many PVs. If the PVs are located on different hard disks, you’ll achieve a similar effect as with RAID-0 (striping).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-L</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">size</samp>
    Indicates the desired size. By default, the size is specified in MiB, but with the corresponding suffix also in bytes, KiB, GiB, or TiB (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-L 2G</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-n</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">lvname</samp>
    Indicates the LV name. If this option is missing, the command uses the name <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">lvoln</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-s</samp>
    Creates a snapshot, that is, a static copy of an existing LV. In this case, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp> doesn’t specify the VG, but the underlying LV. The size specification <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-L</samp> indicates the memory required for copied sectors if the underlying LV changes. Once this memory is exhausted, the life of the snapshot ends.

#### Example

The following command creates a new logical volume in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">myvg1</samp> VG named <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">myvol1</samp> with a size of 50 GiB:

```
root# lvcreate -L 50G -n myvol1 myvg1
  Logical volume "myvol1" created 
```

The command simultaneously creates the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dev/myvg1/myvol2</samp> file. This is a link to the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dev/mapper/myvg1-myvol2</samp> file. The LV can then be used under one of these two device names like an ordinary hard disk partition. The following command sets up a file system there:

```
root# mkfs.ext4 /dev/myvg1/myvol1 
```

### lvdisplay [options] lvname

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lvdisplay</samp> shows detailed information on an LV.

### lvextend [options] lvname [pvname]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lvextend</samp> increases the memory for the specified LV device. You can specify the new total amount of memory via the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-L</samp> option (see [lvcreate](#L_001.xhtml_lvcreate)). Alternatively, you can use the notation <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-L +size</samp> to specify the desired change.

The required memory is reserved within the same VG in which the LV is located. If the VG is composed of multiple physical volumes (PVs), you can use the optional specification of <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">pvname</samp> to select which PV provides the storage.

An example of the use of <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lvextend</samp> can be found in the description of the [resize2fs](#R_001.xhtml_resize2fs) command, which enables you to change the size of ext file systems.

### lvm [command]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lvm</samp> is the central administration command for the Logical Volume Manager (LVM). <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lvm</samp> is usually located in the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lvm2</samp> package and must be installed separately for many distributions if an LVM system hasn’t already been set up during installation.

If you run <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lvm</samp> without any other commands, you’ll be taken to a shell in which you can execute LVM commands interactively. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">help</samp> provides a list of all commands available for selection. Alternatively, you can pass a command to <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lvm</samp>, which is then executed immediately.

All LVM commands can be run either via <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lvm</samp> or directly. The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lvm lvcreate xxx</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lvcreate xxx</samp> commands are therefore equivalent.

For reasons of clarity, I’ve decided to describe the most important LVM commands separately in this book. Commands for editing logical volumes start with the initial letters <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lv</samp>, those for administrating physical volumes start with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pv</samp>, and commands for managing volume groups start with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">vg</samp>.

### lvreduce [options] lvname

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lvreduce</samp> reduces the memory space of the specified LV device. If the LV contains a file system, this must first be reduced in size, or data will be lost! You can either enter the new total size in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-L size</samp> format or the desired change in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-L -size</samp> format.

### lvremove [options] lvname

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lvremove</samp> deletes the specified LV.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-f</samp>
    Suppresses system queries.

### lvrename oldlvname newlvname

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lvrename</samp> gives the LV a new name.

### lvscan [options]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lvscan</samp> lists all LVs.

### lz4 [options] [filename]
lzop [options] [filename]

The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lz4</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lzop</samp> commands from the packages of the same name compress files. Although they achieve lower compression rates than [gzip](#G_001.xhtml_gzip), [](#B_001.xhtml_bzip2), or [](#X_001.xhtml_xz), they are much faster (although <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lz4</samp> is still a little faster than <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lzop</samp>). The syntax of <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lz4</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lzop</samp> is based on the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">gzip</samp> command.

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lz4</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lzop</samp> are perfect if you want to save files in a space-saving way (e.g., for a backup) but don’t want to invest too much CPU power. You’ll mostly use the commands in pipe mode, as shown in the two <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tar</samp> examples later in this entry.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-c</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--stdout</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--to-stdout</samp>
    Redirects the result to the standard output.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-d</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--decompress</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--uncompress</samp>
    Decompresses the specified file instead of compressing it.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Controls the speed and quality of the compression. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-1</samp> is the fastest, and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-9</samp> delivers the smallest files with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">lzop</samp>. With <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lz4</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-12</samp> provides the best compression.

#### Examples

The first command compresses the file and returns <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file.lzo</samp>; the second command decompresses the file again:

```
user$ lzop file
user$ lzop -d file.lzw 
```

The following two examples show the use of <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lzop</samp> in combination with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tar</samp>:

```
user$ tar cf -c verz | lzop -c > backup.tar.lzo   
(create archive)
user$ lzop -d < backup.tar.lzo | tar xf -         
(unpack archive) 
```

## M

### magick [options] imageold imagenew

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">magick</samp> from the ImageMagick package converts image files from one format to another. In this book, the most important commands and options are described in [convert](#C_001.xhtml_convert), which is the command name that’s valid up to version 6\. As of version 7, it’s recommended to call the syntactically equivalent <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">magick</samp> command instead of <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">convert</samp> although <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">convert</samp> still works with most distributions.

### mail [options] mail@hostname [< message text]

You can use the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mail</samp> command from the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mailx</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mailutils</samp> package (Debian, Ubuntu) to read local emails stored in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/var/mail/name</samp>. However, the operation takes some getting used to, to say the least. If you’re looking for a mail client for text mode, it’s better to install <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mutt</samp>.

The strength of <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mail</samp> lies in the fact that you can easily transfer emails to a local mail server, either interactively or in scripts. You can simply run <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mail recipient@site</samp> interactively. You can now enter additional recipients (CC addresses), the subject and finally the message text, which you conclude by pressing Ctrl+D. This transfers the email to the local mail server, using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">loginname@hostname</samp> as the sender.

For a script-controlled mail dispatch, you’ll need to familiarize yourself with the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mail</samp> options, of which I’ll only present the three most important ones here:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-a</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">"header"</samp>
    Specifies an additional header line. This can be used to add a BCC address or to set the character set of the message (see the example next).

    <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mail</samp> doesn’t recognize the correct mail host name in many configurations and then composes the sender address incorrectly. This even applies to Debian and Ubuntu systems, where <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/mailname</samp> would be very easy to evaluate. This issue can be solved by explicitly specifying the sender address with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-a "From:name@myhost.com"</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-A</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file</samp>
    Adds a file to the email.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-s "</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">subject</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">"</samp>
    Specifies the text for the subject line.

#### Example

In its simplest form, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mail</samp> is completely uncomplicated to use:

```
user$ echo "message" | mail -s "subject" name@a-company.com 
```

The following command sends the UTF-8 text from <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">message.txt</samp> to the specified recipients:

```
user$ mail name1@company-abc.com,name1@company-abc.com \
        -s "Subject 1 2 3 äöü" \
        -a "BCC: blindcopy@company-abc.com" \
        -a "Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8" < message.txt 
```

### makepasswd [options]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">makepasswd</samp> from the package of the same name generates a new, random password. The command is well suited if you need a password for a new account but don’t want to stretch your own imagination.

On CentOS, Fedora, and RHEL, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">makepasswd</samp> isn’t available. Instead, you can install the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">expect</samp> package that contains the [mkpasswd](#M_001.xhtml_mkpasswd) command. On (open)SUSE, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mkpasswd</samp> also isn’t available. There, you can switch to [pwgen](#P_001.xhtml_pwgen).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--chars</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Specifies the desired password length (10 characters by default).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--count</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Returns <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> passwords (the default setting is only one).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--strings</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">string</samp>
    Uses the characters contained in the string to compose the password. By default, the command only uses uppercase and lowercase letters (ASCII) and numbers, but no special characters.

#### Example

The following command returns a password with 12 characters:

```
user$ makepasswd --chars 12
TaQKD1VGYmax 
```

### man [group] [options] name

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man</samp> displays online information on the specified command or file. The search can be restricted by specifying a group. Important groups are <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">1</samp> (user commands), <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">5</samp> (configuration files), and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">8</samp> (commands for system administration). In most distributions, the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">man</samp> texts are displayed by <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">less</samp>; that is, the keyboard shortcuts apply for scrolling or searching in the help text, as summarized in the [less](#L_001.xhtml_less) command in [Table 5.11](#05_001.xhtml_t5.11).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-a</samp>
    Displays all <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man</samp> pages of the same name in sequence. Without this option, only the first of several files with the same name from different subject areas is usually displayed. Some Linux distributions use <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-a</samp> as the default setting.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-f</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">keyword</samp>
    Displays the meaning of a keyword (a single-line text). With this option, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man</samp> corresponds to the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">whatis</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">theme</samp> command.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-k</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">keyword</samp>
    Displays a list of all existing <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man</samp> texts in which the keyword occurs. However, no full text search is performed. Instead, only the keywords of each <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man</samp> text are analyzed. With this option, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man</samp> corresponds to the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">apropos</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">thema</samp> command.

### md5sum files

<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">md5sum</samp> calculates checksums for all specified files. Message-Digest Algorithm 5 (MD5) checksums are often used to ensure that a file is unchanged after it has been transferred. Note that the MD5 algorithm is no longer considered secure. The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">sha</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">sum</samp> commands are cryptographically better.

### mdadm [options]

The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mdadm</samp> command from the package of the same name helps with the management of software RAID connections. The command is controlled by countless options. An option usually specifies the mode (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--create</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-C</samp> to set up a new RAID array). The other options control the details of the desired operation.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mddevice</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--add</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">device</samp>
    Adds a partition to the network.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--assemble</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mddevice device1 device2 ... device</samp>m
    Reassembles the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mddevice</samp> network from the hard disk partitions <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">device1</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">devicem</samp>. This only works if <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">device1</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">devicem</samp> were previously initialized using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">--create</samp> as components of a RAID array.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--assemble --scan</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mddevice</samp>
    Composes the RAID partition <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mddevice</samp> from the hard disk partitions specified in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mdadm.conf</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--create</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mddevice</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--level=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--raid-devices=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">m device1 device2 ... device</samp>m
    Creates the new <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mddevice</samp> array for RAID level <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>, which consists of the m hard disk partitions <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">device1</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">devicem</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--detail</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mddevice</samp>
    Provides detailed information about the RAID partition.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--examine</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">device</samp>
    Provides detailed information about the specified hard disk partition, which must be part of a RAID array.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--examine --scan</samp>
    Provides a summary of all available RAID partitions in the syntax of <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mdadm.conf</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mddevice</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--fail</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">device</samp>
    Marks the hard disk partition <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">device</samp> as faulty and deactivates it.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--grow</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mddevice</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--size=max</samp>
    Enlarges the network so that the underlying hard disk partitions are used in an optimal way. The command only makes sense in this form after enlarging the hard disk partitions.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--grow</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mddevice</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--raid-devices=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Increases the number of hard disk partitions integrated into the array (only for RAID levels 1, 5, and 6).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--monitor</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">device</samp>
    Monitors the active RAID arrays. The command is usually started when the computer is booted and sends an email to the administrator (<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-m</samp> option) in the event of problems.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--query</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">device</samp>
    Tests whether the partition is a RAID partition or part of a RAID array.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mddevice</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--remove</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">device</samp>
    Removes the hard disk partition <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">device</samp> from the RAID array. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">device</samp> must not be active, so it may have to be deactivated beforehand by using <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--fail</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--stop</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mddevice</samp>
    Deactivates the specified network. The array can now be reassembled using <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--assemble</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--zero-superblock</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">device</samp>
    Deletes the RAID metadata of a hard disk partition.

#### Examples

The following two commands create a RAID-0 array from the two partitions <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dev/sda3</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dev/sdb3</samp> and set up an ext4 file system there. The partitions must first be marked as RAID partitions. If you use [fdisk](#F_001.xhtml_fdisk) for partitioning, you need to set the partition ID to the hexadecimal value <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">fd</samp> using the T command. In [parted](#P_001.xhtml_parted), you must run <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">set</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">partition number</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">raid on</samp>.

```
root# mdadm --create /dev/md0 --level=0 --raid-devices=2 /dev/sda3 /dev/sdb3
mdadm: array /dev/md0 started.
root# mkfs.ext4 /dev/md0 
```

The procedure for setting up a RAID-1 array is exactly the same as for RAID-0\. Only the command for setting up the RAID system looks a little different and now contains <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--level=1</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--level=0</samp>:

```
root# mdadm --create /dev/md0 --level=1 --raid-devices=2 /dev/sda3 /dev/sdb3
mdadm: array /dev/md0 started.
root# mkfs.ext4 /dev/md0 
```

To test the functionality of a RAID-1 array, you should mark a partition as defective:

```
root# mdadm /dev/md0 --fail /dev/sdb3 
```

You can continue to use the network; however, all changes are now only saved on the remaining hard disk partition. To add <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dev/sdb3</samp> back to <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dev/md0</samp>, you must first explicitly remove the partition marked as defective:

```
root# mdadm --remove /dev/md0 /dev/sdb3
root# mdadm --add    /dev/md0 /dev/sdb3 
```

Now the automatic resynchronization of the two partitions starts, which takes some time depending on the size of the network (approximately 20 minutes per 100 GiB for conventional SATA hard drives). After all, you can continue to work during this time. However, the file system will respond more slowly than usual. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">cat /proc/mdstat</samp> provides information on how far the synchronization process has progressed.

To save all changes made in the RAID configuration file [etc/mdadm/mdadm.conf](#04_001.xhtml_mdadm.conf), you need to run the following command. You must then use an editor to remove any previously entered RAID arrays from the configuration file so that the file is free of duplicates.

```
root# mdadm --examine --scan >> /etc/mdadm/mdadm.conf 
```

### mkdir directory

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mkdir</samp> creates a new directory. The most important options are listed here:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-m</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mode</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--mode=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mode</samp>
    Sets the access rights of the new directory as specified by mode (see [chmod](#C_001.xhtml_chmod)).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-p</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--parents</samp>
    Also creates intermediate directories. If you run <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mkdir -p a/b/c</samp> and the directories <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">a</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">a/b</samp> don’t yet exist, these directories will be created.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-Z</samp>
    Activates the default context of SELinux for the new directory.

### mkfifo file

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mkfifo</samp> sets up a First In, First Out (FIFO) file. Basically, FIFO files work like pipes and enable data to be exchanged between two programs.

#### Example

In the following example, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mkfifo</samp> sets up a FIFO file. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ls</samp> redirects the table of contents to this file. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">more</samp> reads it from there. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ls</samp> must be started with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">&</samp> as a background process because the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ls</samp> process isn’t finished until <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">more</samp> has read all the data from <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">fifo</samp>.

```
user$ mkfifo fifo
user$ ls -l > fifo &
user$ more < fifo 
```

Displaying the table of contents via <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">more</samp> could of course be done much more easily without a FIFO file, namely by using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ls -l | more</samp>.

### mkfs [options] device [blocks]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mkfs</samp> sets up a file system on a previously partitioned hard disk. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mkfs</samp> can only be run by <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">root</samp>. Depending on the specified file system, the program branches to the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mkfs.</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file system type</samp> command.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-t</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file system type</samp>
    Specifies the type of file system. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ext4</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">xfs</samp> are possible. The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-t</samp> option must be specified as the first option! All other options are transferred to the command that actually sets up the file system. They depend on the type of file system.

The most important file system–specific <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mkfs.xxx</samp> commands are described in the next six entries.

### mkfs.btrfs [options] device1 [device2 device3 ...]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mkfs.btrfs</samp> sets up a Btrfs file system. Depending on the distribution, the command is part of the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">btrfs-tools</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">btrfs-progs</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">btrfsprogs</samp> package, which may have to be installed separately.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-A</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--alloc-start</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Leaves <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> bytes unused at the beginning of the device (by default, n=0).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-d</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--data</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">type</samp>
    Specifies the desired RAID type for the data. Permitted values are <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">raid0</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">raid1</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">raid10</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">raid1c3</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">raid1c4</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">raid5</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">raid6</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">single</samp> (applies by default). If you set up a Btrfs RAID array, you must specify a corresponding number of devices (two for RAID-1, four for RAID-10).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-L</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--label</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp>
    Gives the file system a name.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-m</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--data</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">type</samp>
    Specifies the desired RAID type for the metadata. In addition to the RAID variants specified for the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-d</samp> option, there is also <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">dup</samp>. This variant applies by default for file systems that only include one device. All metadata is therefore stored twice for security reasons. SSDs are an exception, where <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">single</samp> is the default for single-device file systems. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">dup</samp> isn’t useful here because the internal optimization of many SSDs recognizes the redundancy of the data and simply stores it. This means that the security gain intended by the duplication is lost again.

    If you distribute a Btrfs file system across multiple devices without specifying any further options, the RAID type <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">raid1</samp> applies by default. This means that the data is simply saved, but the metadata is saved multiple times!

    When creating a RAID array, you usually specify the same RAID type using <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-m</samp> as with the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-d</samp> option. If you want your file system to be as fast as possible, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-d raid0 -m raid0</samp> to eliminate all redundancies.

#### Example

The following command can be used to set up a RAID 1 file system that uses the two equally sized partitions <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dev/sdb1</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dev/sdc1</samp>:

```
root# mkfs.btrfs -d raid1 -m raid1 /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1 
```

If a device fails, you can continue to use the file system with the additional <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mount</samp> option, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">degraded</samp>:

```
root# mount -o degraded /dev/sdb1 /media/btrfs 
```

To restore the RAID array, you should add a new device to the file system. In the following example, this is again <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dev/sdc1</samp>, but this time, the partition comes from a new hard disk or SSD. To redistribute the file system across both devices and thus restore RAID-1 redundancy, you must also run <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">btrfs filesystem balance</samp>. For large file systems, the execution of this command naturally takes a long time. After all, the file system can be used during this time, albeit at a greatly reduced speed.

```
root# btrfs device add /dev/sdc1 /media/btrfs
root# btrfs filesystem balance /media/btrfs 
```

Only now can the defective device be removed from the file system. You can use the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">missing</samp> keyword to specify the device:

```
root# btrfs device delete missing /media/btrfs 
```

### mkfs.exfat [options] device

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mkfs.exfat</samp> from the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">exfat-utils</samp> package sets up an exFAT file system. This file system is specially optimized for large SD cards. It’s used by default with SDXC memory cards and is supported by SDXC-compatible digital cameras and smartphones.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-i</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">id</samp>
    Determines a 32-bit ID for the file system. The number is given as a hexadecimal code. If the command is executed without the option, a random ID is set.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-n</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp>
    Defines the name (label) for the file system. The name remains empty by default. If necessary, the name can be changed subsequently using [exfatlabel](#E_001.xhtml_exfatlabel).

### mkfs.ext2 [options] device [blocks]
mkfs.ext3 [options] device [blocks]
mkfs.ext4 [options] device [blocks]
mke2fs [options] device [blocks]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mke2fs</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mkfs.ext2</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mkfs.ext3</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mkfs.ext4</samp> set up an ext2, ext3, or ext4 file system. All four commands reference the same program via links, but they use different default options that are stored in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/mk2efs.conf</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-b</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Determines the block size (usually 4,096 bytes). The values <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">1024</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">2048</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">4096</samp>, and up to a maximum of <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">65536</samp> are permitted for <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> (i.e., 2^(10), 2^(11), etc. up to 2^(16)).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-c</samp>
    Tests whether defective blocks exist before setting up the data medium with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">badblocks</samp>. This type of blocks isn’t used for the file system. The test requires that each data block be changed and read again, and therefore considerably extends the time required to set up the file system.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-i</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Specifies the number of bytes after which an I-node is set up. I-nodes are internal management units of a file system. All administrative information of a file is stored in an I-node with the exception of the name, that is, access bits, owner, date of last access, and so on. The number of I-nodes is defined during formatting. For example, with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>=<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">4096</samp>, there are 1,048,576 ÷ 4,096 = 256 I-nodes per MiB; that is, a maximum of 256 files or directories can be stored per MiB, regardless of how small the files are.

    If you want to save a large number of very small files, you should make <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> smaller. The minimum value is <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">1024</samp> (this corresponds to 2,048 files per MiB). It doesn’t make sense to select a value smaller than the block size, as only one file can be saved per block anyway. However, if you want to save only a few very large files, you can also select a larger <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>. This reduces the administrative overhead.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-J</samp>
    Allows you to pass additional parameters, for example, to set the size of the journaling file or to set up the journaling file in another device. This can possibly improve the speed of the file system a little, but at the same time makes administration and restoring the file system after a crash more complicated. The available options are described in detail in the manual page of <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mke2fs</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-m</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Specifies what percentage of the disk should be reserved for <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">root</samp> data (5% by default). This reserve memory enables <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">root</samp> to continue working even if the file system is already completely full for all other users. This is therefore a safety reserve.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-t ext2/ext3/ext4</samp>
    Specifies the desired ext version (only required for <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mke2fs</samp>).

#### Example

The following two commands first set up a new ext4 file system in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dev/sda5</samp> partition and then deactivate the automatic file system check (see also the description of the [tune2fs](#T_001.xhtml_tune2fs) command):

```
root# mkfs.ext4 /dev/sda5
root# tune2fs -i 0 -c 0 /dev/sda5 
```

### mkfs.ntfs [options] device

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mkfs.ntfs</samp> sets up an NTFS file system that is compatible with all current Windows versions. The command is part of the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ntfsprogs</samp> package in many distributions and must be installed separately.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-f</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--fast</samp>
    Doesn’t fill each data block with 0 bytes. This option speeds up formatting many times over and is highly recommended.

### mkfs.vfat [options] device

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mkfs.vfat</samp> sets up a Windows file system that is compatible with all common Windows versions. This format is particularly suitable for USB flash drives and SD cards that are also used on Windows or in cameras.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-F 12/16/32</samp>
    Specifies the type of FAT tables (12-, 16-, or 32-bit). Usually, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mkfs.vfat</samp> automatically selects the 32-bit mode for large data media. If not, this option will help.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-I</samp>
    Allows formatting the entire disk without creating a partition table (<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mkfs.vfat -I /dev/sdg</samp>). This method is sometimes used for USB flash drives.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-n</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp>
    Assigns a name (label) to the file system with a maximum length of 11 characters.

#### Example

The following command sets up a 32-bit VFAT file system named <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">MyPhotos</samp> in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dev/sdd1</samp> partition:

```
root# mkfs.vfat -F 32 -n MyPhotos /dev/sdd1 
```

### mkfs.xfs [options] device

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mkfs.xfs</samp> sets up an XFS file system. This process can be controlled by countless options (<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man mkfs.xfs</samp>), the most important of which are listed here:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-b size=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Specifies the desired block size (4,096 bytes by default).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-l logdev=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">device</samp>
    Saves the journaling data in a separate partition.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-l size=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Specifies the size of the area for the journaling data. Without this option, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mkfs.xfs</samp> chooses a suitable size itself.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-L</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">label</samp>
    Gives the file system the desired name (maximum 12 characters).

### mknod devicefile [b|c] major minor

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mknod</samp> sets up a new device file. Device files are located in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dev</samp> directory and enable access to various hardware components. Device files are characterized by three pieces of information: <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">major</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">minor</samp> use two numbers to indicate the driver that can be used to access the devices (major and minor device number). The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">b</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">c</samp> characters indicate whether the device is buffered or unbuffered.

In all current Linux distributions, device files are set up automatically by the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">udev</samp> system. A manual execution of <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mknod</samp> is therefore not necessary. A list of the most important Linux devices and the corresponding device numbers can be found here:

[www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/admin-guide/devices.txt](http://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/admin-guide/devices.txt)

### mkpasswd [options]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mkpasswd</samp> from the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">expect</samp> package (CentOS, Fedora, RHEL) generates random passwords.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-c</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Specifies the minimum number of lowercase letters that must be contained in the password (default: <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">2</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-C</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Specifies the minimum number of capital letters that must be included (default: <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">2</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-d</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Specifies the minimum number of digits that must be included (default: <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">2</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-l</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Specifies the desired number of characters for the password (default: <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">9</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-s</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Specifies the minimum number of special characters that must be included (default: <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">1</samp>).

#### Example

The following command generates a six-character password without special characters:

```
root# mkpasswd -l 6 -s 0
SX39vz 
```

### mkswap device/file

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mkswap</samp> sets up a device (e.g., a hard disk partition) or a file as a swap area. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mkswap</samp> can only be run by <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">root</samp>. The swap area can then be activated using [swapon](#S_001.xhtml_swapon). The swap area must be entered in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/fstab</samp> file so that it’s used automatically each time the computer is started.

#### Example

The following commands first fill a 512 MiB file with zeros, then make the file a swap file, and finally activate the file:

```
root# dd if=/dev/zero of=swapfile bs=1M count=512
root# chmod 600 swapfile
root# mkswap swapfile
root# swapon swapfile 
```

### modinfo module name

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">modinfo</samp> provides information about the specified module. This includes the full file name, author, license, dependent modules, short description, and list of all parameters the module knows.

### modprobe [options] module name [parameter=value ...]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">modprobe</samp> loads the specified module into the kernel. The command is an extended variant of [insmod](#I_001.xhtml_insmod). It takes into account the module dependencies defined in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/usr/lib/modules/kernel-version/modules.dep</samp> and, if necessary, also loads modules that are required by the desired module. In addition, it includes the module parameters specified in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/modprobe.d/*</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-c</samp>
    Provides an almost endless list of all currently valid module options and module settings. The parameters are derived both from the source code of the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">modutils</samp> package and from the settings in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/modprobe.d/*</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-f</samp>
    Forces the module to be loaded even if it was compiled for a different kernel version. Whether this actually works depends on whether there are any incompatibilities between the kernel version and the module version.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-r</samp>
    Removes the module from the kernel (instead of loading it).

### mogrify [options] image file

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mogrify</samp> changes parameters of an image file, for example, the resolution or the number of colors. It uses the same options as are used for <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">convert</samp>. In contrast to [convert](#C_001.xhtml_convert), which creates a new file, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mogrify</samp> overwrites the original file. The command is part of the ImageMagick package.

#### Example

The following command reduces the resolution of an image to 800 × 600 pixels:

```
user$ mogrify -resize 800x600 photo.jpg 
```

### more file

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">more</samp> displays the contents of a text file page by page. The display is interrupted after each page. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">more</samp> is now waiting for a keyboard input. The most important input options are Enter (one line down), ___ (one page down), B (one page up), and Q (quit). Instead of <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">more</samp>, the more powerful [less](#L_001.xhtml_less) command is usually used.

### mount mount [options] device directory

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mount</samp> without parameters returns a list of all currently mounted file systems, including the file system type and the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mount</samp> options. In the second syntax variant, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mount</samp> integrates a data medium (partition of a hard disk, USB flash drive, etc.) into the Linux file system. You must specify the device name of the data medium (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dev/nvme0n1p3</samp>) and the target directory in the directory tree. Instead of the device, you can also specify the UUID of the file system (i.e., <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mount UIID=1234 directory</samp>).

The mounting of file systems when Linux is started is controlled by the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/fstab</samp> file. For all devices listed in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/fstab</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mount</samp> can be used in a short form in which only the device file or the mount directory is specified. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mount</samp> automatically reads the missing data and options from <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">fstab</samp>.

Data media can be removed from the file system using [umount](#U_001.xhtml_umount). As a rule, both <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mount</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">umount</samp> can only be run by <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">root</samp>. Drives that are marked in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">fstab</samp> with the option <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">user</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">users</samp> are exceptions.

The following description of general and file system–specific <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mount</samp> options extends over several pages and is followed by a few examples.

#### General mount Options

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--move</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">olddir newdir</samp>
    Changes the directory in which a file system is mounted.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-o options</samp>
    Allows you to specify additional options, for example, in the format <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-o acl,user_xattr</samp>. The options specified in this way must not be separated by spaces! See the next subsection for a reference of the file system options.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-r</samp>
    Prevents write operations on the data medium (read-only).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-t</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file system</samp>
    Specifies the file system. Possible options include <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ext2/3/4</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">btrfs</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">xfs</samp> for Linux partitions, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">vfat</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ntfs</samp> for Windows partitions, and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">iso9660</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">udf</samp> for data CDs and DVDs.

#### General File System Options

Using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-o</samp>, you can pass countless options that influence the behavior of the mounted file system. The keywords for general options are summarized in the following list. File system–specific options follow a little further down.

All options for <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mount -o</samp> are also permitted in the fourth column of <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/fstab</samp>. This file is evaluated during the boot process; on Ubuntu systems, this is done by the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mountall</samp> command. For this reason, the following compilation also applies to <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/fstab</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mountall</samp> and has therefore been supplemented by some <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">fstab</samp>-specific and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mountall</samp>-specific keywords that aren’t directly relevant for the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mount</samp> command. These include <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">defaults</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">noauto</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">nobootwait</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">optional</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">owner</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">user</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">users</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">atime</samp> / <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">noatime</samp> / <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">relatime</samp> / <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">strictatime</samp>
    Specifies the circumstances under which the inode access time of a file is updated: with every read access (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">atime</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">strictatime</samp>, POSIX-compliant), at most once a day (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">relatime</samp>), or never (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">noatime</samp>). The inode access time always gets changed for write accesses.

    The option has a relatively large influence on the speed of read operations and on the service life of flash data storage devices. The default setting for current kernel versions is <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">relatime</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">defaults</samp>
    Specifies that the file system is to be included in the directory tree with the default options. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">defaults</samp> is specified in the fourth column of <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/fstab</samp> if no other options are to be used. (The column must not be left blank.)

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">dev</samp> / <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">nodev</samp>
    Causes or prevents device files from being interpreted as such. On Linux, files can be marked as block or character devices. This option is useful for external data media for security reasons.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">discard</samp>
    Activates the trim function for the ext4, Btrfs, and XFS file systems. The kernel now informs the SSD about which data blocks have been deleted, giving the SSD the opportunity to optimize the internal management of the memory cells. The trim function also works in combination with LVM and software RAID (<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mdraid</samp>).

    Whether the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">discard</samp> option should be used is controversial: Although it helps with the long-term optimization of the SSD, it can lead to a significant slowdown in delete operations (e.g., if many files are to be deleted in a short time, see [https://forums. freebsd.org/threads/ssd-trim-maintenance.56951/#post-328912](https://forums.freebsd.org/threads/ssd-trim-maintenance.56951/#post-328912)). A good alternative to the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">discard</samp> option is a cron job that runs the [fstrim](#F_001.xhtml_fstrim) command once a day or once a week and in this way reports all deleted sectors to the SSD.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">exec</samp> / <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">noexec</samp>
    Determines whether programs on the file system may be run on Linux or not. For most file systems, the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">exec</samp> setting applies by default. However, security-conscious administrators will specify the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">noexec</samp> option for CD/DVD drives and external data media. (If you use the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">user</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">users</samp> option, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">noexec</samp> applies. This can be changed again using an <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">exec</samp> option.)

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">noauto</samp>
    Is only useful in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/fstab</samp> and ensures that the data medium named in this line isn’t automatically mounted at system startup. Nevertheless, it makes sense to enter the data medium in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">fstab</samp> because users can then conveniently perform <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mount name</samp> without explicitly specifying all other <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mount</samp> options. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">noauto</samp> is used, for example, for rarely required data partitions.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">nobootwait</samp>
    Doesn’t stop the boot process if the device isn’t available. The keyword is evaluated by <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mountall</samp> on Ubuntu and can’t be used in other distributions. It’s particularly suitable for external data media that aren’t always connected, for example, for a USB hard disk.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">nofail</samp>
    Doesn’t report an error if the device doesn’t exist. This option is useful if you want <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mount</samp> to try to access a USB flash drive or a network directory in a script.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">optional</samp>
    Ignores the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">fstab</samp> entry if the file system type isn’t available during the boot process. The keyword is evaluated by <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mountall</samp> on Ubuntu and can’t be used in other distributions.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">owner</samp>
    Allows each user to mount or unmount the relevant file system themselves. The option is only useful in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/fstab</samp>. The difference from <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">user</samp> is that <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mount</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">umount</samp> may only be run if the user has access rights to the relevant device file (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dev/fd0</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">remount</samp>
    Changes the options of a file system already included in the directory tree. This option can only be specified for a direct call of <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mount</samp> and isn’t permitted in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/fstab</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ro</samp> / <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">rw</samp>
    Specifies that files may only be read or modified. Usually, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">rw</samp> (i.e., read/write) applies to most file system types.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">suid</samp> / <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">nosuid</samp>
    Allows or prevents the evaluation of the SID and GID access bit. These access bits allow ordinary users to execute programs with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">root</samp> permissions, which often is a safety risk. The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">nosuid</samp> option prevents the evaluation of such access bits and should be used for CDs, DVDs and external data media.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">sync</samp>
    Causes changes to be saved immediately instead of temporarily storing them in RAM for a few seconds and only transferring them to the data medium later. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sync</samp> minimizes the risk of data loss if you accidentally remove a data medium (e.g., USB flash drive) without using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">umount</samp> or disconnect the cable connection. However, the disadvantage of <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sync</samp> is that writing data is much less efficient depending on the data medium. The speed of cheap USB flash drives and traditional hard disks in particular is reduced by a factor of 10 or more!

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">user</samp>
    Allows normal users to unmount the relevant file system using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">umount</samp> and mount it again via <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mount</samp>. Otherwise, only <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">root</samp> is able to do this. Data media may only be removed from the file system by the user who initiated <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mount</samp>. This option is only useful in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/fstab</samp> and is primarily intended for external data media. If you use <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">user</samp>, the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">noexec</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">nosuid</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">nodev</samp> options also apply automatically.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">users</samp>
    Has the same meaning as <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">user</samp>, but with one small difference: every user may remove data media marked with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">users</samp> from the file system (<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">umount</samp>). <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">users</samp> therefore allows user A to run <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mount</samp> and user B to call <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">umount</samp> later.

#### btrfs Options

Many <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mount</samp> options depend on the respective file system. The most important file system–specific options are therefore summarized here. We start with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">btrfs</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">compress=zlib|lzo|zstd</samp>
    Compresses all new or modified files. Existing files remain unchanged as long as they are read only. You have a choice of three compression methods:

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">zlib</samp>: Good compression

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">lzo</samp>: Faster than <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">zlib</samp>, but worse compression

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">zstd</samp>: Compression similar to <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">zlib</samp>, but slightly faster

    Fedora uses <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">zstd</samp> by default. This method is currently (in 2025) considered the best compromise between good compression and speed.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">compress-force=zlib|lzo</samp>
    Compresses files even if this doesn’t look promising. Usually, the Btrfs file system recognizes files that have already been compressed and doesn’t compress them again because this doesn’t usually save any space, but costs a lot of CPU time. Using <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">compress-force</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">compress</samp> deactivates this recognition.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">degraded</samp>
    Integrates the file system even if some of the RAID devices are missing. This only works if all data is available due to RAID redundancies; that is, a degraded RAID array exists.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">noacl</samp>
    Deactivates the ACL access management.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">nobarrier</samp>
    Deactivates the write barriers. A write barrier blocks further write operations until all previous write operations have been physically completed. Without barriers, the file system is faster, but at the same time, the risk of data loss in the event of a crash increases, especially with file systems that are distributed across multiple devices (RAID). Barriers only work if the hard disk actually follows the write request, which is often not the case for performance reasons.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ssd</samp>
    Optimizes file operations for solid-state drives (SSDs). The option is automatically active if the Btrfs driver can determine that the data medium is an SSD. However, this option has no influence on the trim behavior, which is controlled separately by the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">discard</samp> option.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">subvolume=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">subvolid=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Uses the specified subvolume (and not the default subvolume). You can determine the volume ID for <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">subvolid</samp> using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">btrfs subvolume list</samp>.

#### CIFS Options

The Common Internet File System (CIFS) allows you to integrate Windows network directories into the file system. CIFS replaces SMBFS. To use CIFS, some distributions require you to install a separate package, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">cifs-utils</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">smbfs</samp>.

Regarding access rights, if the files originate from an ordinary Windows PC, they are assigned to the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">root</samp> user on Linux. All users may read the files, but only <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">root</samp> can change them. To give an ordinary user access to the files, you must correctly set the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">uid</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">gid</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file_mode</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">dir_mode</samp> options.

However, if the files originate from a file server that supports the CIFS Unix extension (this is the case if Samba is running on a Linux computer), then the UIDs, GIDs, and access bits of the files are forwarded unchanged. The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">uid</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">gid</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file_mode</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">dir_mode</samp> options then have no effect unless you deactivate the Unix extensions via the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">nounix</samp> option.

Further details on the CIFS-specific <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mount</samp> options can be found in <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man mount.cifs</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">credentials=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file</samp>
    Specifies a file containing the username and password for logging in to the Windows or Samba server. This avoids having to enter passwords in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/fstab</samp>. The file contains three lines with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">username=xxx</samp> (not <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">user=xxx</samp>!), <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">password=xxx</samp>, and, if required, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">domain=xxx</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">dir_mode=n</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">(dmask</samp> for SMBFS<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">)</samp>
    Specifies which access rights apply for access to directories. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">dir_mode=0770</samp> gives the user specified by <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">uid</samp> and all members of the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">gid</samp> group unrestricted rights (read, open, and change directory).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">domain=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">workgroup</samp>
    Specifies the domain or workgroup.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file_mode=n</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">(fmask</samp> for SMBFS<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">)</samp>
