<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pdfimages</samp> attempts to extract images from PDF files. However, this doesn’t always work perfectly because often countless tiny images are recognized. The best way to recognize the relevant images is by their file size.

You pass a PDF file and an image name to the command. The command then creates images, which it names using the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">imagename-nnn.type</samp> format. By default, the command writes images in the unusual PBM and PPM formats, unless you select a different format by using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-f</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-all</samp>
    Saves embedded images in the specified format if possible. Where this isn’t possible, PNG images will be generated.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-f</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-t</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Specifies from which page to which page the PDF file should be analyzed. Without these options, the command takes the entire document into account.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-j</samp>
    Keeps the format of images that are embedded in the PDF file in JPEG format.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-list</samp>
    Lists the images found, but doesn’t create any image files.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-png</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-tiff</samp>
    Saves all images in PNG or TIFF format.

#### Example

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pdfimages -list</samp> provides comprehensive information on all images found. The output has been shortened here for reasons of space.

```
user$ pdfimages -list book.pdf
page   type   width height color comp bpc  enc interp  object  ...  size ratio
   1  stencil     1     1   -      1   1  image  no   [inline]        1B   -
   4  stencil     1     1  -       1   1  image  no   [inline]        1B   -
   4  stencil     1     1  -       1   1  image  no   [inline]        1B   -
   4  stencil     1     1  -       1   1  image  no   [inline]        1B   -
   4  image     415   324  rgb     3   8  image  no        71      11.5K 2.9%
   5  image     626   441  rgb     3   8  image  no        81      19.3K 2.4%
   7  image    1173   635  rgb     3   8  jpeg   no       134      59.6K 2.7%  ... 
```

In the following example, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pdfimages</samp> extracts 11 bitmaps from the PDF file:

```
user$ pdfimages -all book.pdf tst
user$ ls tst*
tst-000.png  tst-001.png  tst-002.png  tst-003.png  tst-004.png  tst-005.png
tst-006.jpg  tst-007.png  tst-008.png  tst-009.png  tst-010.png 
```

### pdftk file1.pdf file2.pdf . . . command

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pdftk</samp> manipulates PDF files. You can use it to extract pages, merge multiple PDF documents, encrypt PDF documents or remove the encryption (if you know the password), and more. For reasons of space, the syntax is simplified here. The complete syntax is provided by <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pdftk</samp>. You can combine multiple commands, but you must adhere to the order in which the commands are described here:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">input_pw</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">password</samp>
    Specifies the password for <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file1.pdf</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">cat</samp>
    Merges all PDF files.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">cat</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">page list</samp>
    Extracts the specified pages. Multiple page ranges are separated by spaces, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">1-5 7-10</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">end</samp> denotes the last page. To merge the pages from multiple PDF files, you must give each input file an abbreviation and refer to it in the page details (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pdftk A=file1.pdf B=file2.pdf cat A2-4 B5 B7</samp>). If you only want pages with even or odd page numbers, you need to add <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">even</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">odd</samp> to the page number, such as <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">1-10odd</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">background</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">watermark.pdf</samp>
    Stores each output page with a page from <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">watermark.pdf</samp>. If <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">watermark.pdf</samp> has fewer pages than the output, the last page from <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">watermark.pdf</samp> will be repeatedly used as the watermark. The source PDF file must be transparent; otherwise, the watermark won’t be visible.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">stamp</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">stamp.pdf</samp>
    Writes a page from <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">stamp.pdf</samp> over each output page. If <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">stamp.pdf</samp> has fewer pages than the output, the last page from <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">stamp.pdf</samp> will be repeated. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">stamp.pdf</samp> must be transparent; otherwise, it will cover the original PDF file.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">burst</samp>
    Creates a separate file for each page of the PDF document and names it page_n<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.pdf</samp>, where n is the page number.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">output</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">result.pdf</samp>
    Saves the resulting PDF file as <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">result.pdf</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">owner_pw</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">password</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">user_pw</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">password</samp>
    Encrypts <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">result.pdf</samp> with the specified password. The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">owner_pw</samp> password applies to printing and other PDF operations, while the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">user_pw</samp> password applies to opening the file.

#### Examples

The following command reads pages 10 to 20 and 30 to 40 from <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">in.pdf</samp> and writes them to the new <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">out.pdf</samp> file:

```
user$ pdftk in.pdf cat 10-20 30-40 output out.pdf 
```

You can also use the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">cat</samp> command to join multiple PDF files together:

```
user$ pdftk in1.pdf in2.pdf in3.pdf cat output out.pdf 
```

The following example creates a separate PDF file named pg_n for each individual page in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">in.pdf</samp>, where n is the page number:

```
user$ pdftk in.pdf burst 
```

The next example creates an encrypted PDF file. The file can be read without the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">xxx</samp> password, but can’t be printed or edited in any other way. If you want to protect the reading of the file yourself, you must use the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">user_pw</samp> command instead of <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">owner_pw</samp>.

```
user$ pdftk in.pdf output encrpyted.pdf owner_pw xxx 
```

Finally, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pdftk</samp> is used to mark a PDF file with a watermark:

```
user$ pdftk in.pdf background watermark.pdf output out.pdf 
```

### pdftops [options] source.pdf [target.ps]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pdftops</samp> from the Poppler library, which is provided in the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">poppler-utils</samp> package on Debian and Ubuntu, generates a PostScript file from a PDF document. Unlike [pdf2ps](#P_001.xhtml_pdf2ps), it supports numerous options for influencing the PostScript file.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-eps</samp>
    Creates an EPS file. For multipage PDF documents, a page must be selected with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-f</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-l</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-f</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-l</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Specifies the first and last page (first and last).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-level</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Specifies the desired PostScript level (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">1</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">3</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-level</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">sep</samp>
    Also performs a color separation. For this purpose, all colors are converted to CMYK format.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-opw</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">password</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-upw</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">password</samp>
    Specifies the owner or user password to process password-protected PDF documents.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-paper</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">format</samp>
    Specifies the desired paper format (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">A3</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">A4</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">letter</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">legal</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-paperw</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-paperh</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Indicates the paper size in dots.

### pdftotext [options] source.pdf [target.txt]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pdftotext</samp> extracts the text from a PDF file and saves it in a plain text file (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">source.txt</samp> by default). The entire formatting and all images will be lost. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pdftotext</samp> is also part of the Poppler library.

The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-f</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-l</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-opw</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-upw</samp> options have the same meaning as in [pdftops](#P_001.xhtml_pdftops) (see there).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-layout</samp>
    Tries to preserve the page layout.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-nopgbrk</samp>
    Doesn’t mark the end of the page with a special character.

### pdfunite in1.pdf in2.pdf . . . out.pdf

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pdfunite</samp> from the Poppler library merges multiple PDF files into a new document (last file name). You can also do this with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pdftk</samp>, but <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pdfunite</samp> is easier to use.

### pg_dump [options] [> backup.sql]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pg_dump</samp> creates a backup of a PostgreSQL database. The options for establishing a connection correspond to those in the [psql](#P_001.xhtml_psql) command (see the “psql” entry). To automate backups, you can save the password in a <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.pgpass</samp> file (see [www.postgresql.org/docs/current/libpq-pgpass.html](http://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/libpq-pgpass.html)).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-a</samp>
    Creates a pure data backup (i.e., without <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">CREATE DATABASE</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-C</samp>
    Includes the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">CREATE DATABASE</samp> command in the backup.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-F plain|directory|tar</samp>
    Defines the database format. Usually, a SQL file is generated (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">plain</samp>), which can be reloaded via <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">psql -f</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">–F directory</samp> creates binary database files that can be restored later using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pg_restore</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-F tar</samp> creates the same files, but packs them into a TAR archive.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-f</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">backupfile/backupdirectory</samp>
    Defines the storage location of the backup. If necessary, the directory will be created.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-s</samp>
    Creates only a backup of the schema. The backup then only contains <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">CREATE</samp> commands, but no data.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-t</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">pattern</samp>
    Takes only those tables into account for the backup that have been specified in the sample. You can specify the option multiple times (<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-T table1 -T table2</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-T</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">pattern</samp>
    Ignores the specified tables.

#### Example

The following command establishes a network connection to the PostgreSQL server running on the local computer and then creates a backup of the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">test</samp> database:

```
user$ pg_dump -h localhost -U name -d test > test.sql
Password: ******** 
```

### pidof program name

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pidof</samp> determines the process numbers of all instances of a named process.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-o %PPID</samp>
    Ignores the parent process, that is, in the case of shell scripts, the shell in which the script is currently being run.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-s</samp>
    Returns only the first matching process (single shot).

#### Example

The following command returns the PIDs of all running <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">bash</samp> shells:

```
root# pidof /bin/bash
32329 21636 21600 3351 1739 922 
```

### pinctrl command

The command determines or changes the state of the GPIO pins of the Raspberry Pi. It replaces the obsolete <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">raspi-gpio</samp> command and is compatible with the RP1-I/O chip of Raspberry Pi 5.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">funcs [</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">nr</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">]</samp>
    Indicates which functions the specified GPIO can perform. If <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">nr</samp> is missing, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">raspi-gpio func</samp> provides this data for all GPIOs.

    <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">nr</samp> refers to the numbering of the GPIOs according to the manufacturer Broadcom’s documentation. These aren’t the pin numbers of the J8 header!

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">get</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[nr</samp>]
    Displays the status of all GPIOs or the GPIO specified by <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">nr</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">help</samp>
    Displays a relatively detailed help text. Unfortunately, there is no <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man</samp> page available in this context.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">set</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">nr state</samp>
    Activates the desired state for the GPIO. Possible values are listed here:

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ip</samp> = input

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">op</samp> = output

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">no</samp> = deactivate (no function)

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">dl</samp> = state 0 (drive low)

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">dh</samp> = state 1 (drive high)

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">pu</samp> = pull-up resistor active

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">pd</samp> = pull-down resistor active

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">pn</samp> = pull-up/down resistor deactivated (no pull)

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">a0</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">a5</samp> = alternative function 0 to 5

    As far as meaningful combinations arise, multiple keywords from the preceding list may be used at once, each separated by spaces. You can use <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pinctrl func</samp> to check which alternative functions a GPIO supports and how they are numbered.

#### Example

The first command determines which functions are supported by the GPIO with the number 23\. On the Raspberry Pi, this GPIO is connected to pin 16 of the J8 header. The second command uses this GPIO as a simple signal output, whereby the level is set to high (3.3 V). An LED connected to pin 16 via a series resistor would now light up. The third command verifies the status of GPIO 23.

```
user$ pinctrl funcs 23
23, GPIO23, SD0_CMD, DPI_D19, I2S0_SDO1, SCL3, I2S1_SDO1,
    SYS_RIO023, PROC_RIO023, PIO23, -
user$ pinctrl set 23 op dh
user$ pinctrl get 23
23: op dh pd | hi // GPIO23 = output 
```

### ping [options] address
ping6 [options] address

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ping</samp> sends a network packet (ECHO_REQUEST according to the Internet Control Message Protocol [ICMP]) to the specified address once per second. If the address is reachable and echo packets aren’t blocked by a firewall, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ping</samp> receives response packets and indicates how long the communication took there and back. By default, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ping</samp> runs indefinitely until it’s terminated by Ctrl+ C.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-4</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-6</samp>
    Uses only IPv4 or IPv6\. In some distributions, you can alternatively call the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ping4</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ping6</samp> commands.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-c</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Sends only <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> packets and terminates afterwards.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-i</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Specifies the interval time between two packets in seconds. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> is a float; that is, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ping -i 0.1</samp> is also possible.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-n</samp>
    Displays only the IP address, but not the host name of the recipient.

### pip or pip3 command

The command from the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">python3-pip</samp> package supports the installation of Python packages from the Python package index (PyPI). In many distributions, the command must be run as <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pip3</samp> to differentiate it from the previously used <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pip</samp> command for Python 2.

In contrast to Linux package management commands, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pip</samp> can usually be run without <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">root</samp> permissions or without <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sudo</samp>. The packages are still available to all users (unless you use the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--user</samp> option described previously).

The local installation of PIP packages sometimes results in conflicts with packages from Linux package management. In current Python versions, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pip</samp> therefore displays an error message. If possible, you should install the desired module as a Linux package (e.g., using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">apt install python3-</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp>). If there is no suitable package in the distribution, you should organize your project in a Python environment (see the following example). Alternatively, you can force the installation using the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">--break-system-packages</samp> option, but this should really only be an emergency solution.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">install [--upgrade] [--user] [--break-system-packages]</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">package name</samp>
    Installs or updates the specified package. With the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--user</samp> option, the package gets installed in such a way that it’s only available to the current user.

    With <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--break-system-packages</samp>, you force the installation of a package, even if the protection mechanism of new Python versions advises against it. The option has a pretty daunting name: problems can occur, but only if there are a lot of packages in play or if an update of the Python version is performed—so ultimately, this happens relatively rarely. Nevertheless, the use of a virtual environment is almost always the better solution.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">list [--outdated]</samp>
    Provides a list of all installed packages or all packages that can be updated.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">search</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">sudor term</samp>
    Searches PyPI for packages with the specified search term.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">show [--files]</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">package name</samp>
    Displays information on an installed package or lists its files.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">uninstall</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">package name</samp>
    Removes the specified package.

#### Example

Using the following commands for Debian/Ubuntu, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pip3</samp> itself is installed first. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">python3 -m venv</samp> sets up a virtual environment in the project directory. The environment is activated via the script provided for this purpose (see also [source](#S_001.xhtml_source)). This will change the prompt. Finally, the Python module for the OpenAI API gets installed in the environment.

```
user$ sudo apt install python3-pip python3-venv
user$ mkdir my-project
user$ cd my-project
user$ python3  -m venv .
user$ source bin/activate
(my-project) user$ pip3 install openai 
```

### pkcon command

PackageKit is a general interface to the various Linux package management systems. PackageKit is mainly used by graphical user interfaces such as Gnome Software, but it can also be controlled via the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pkcon</samp> command. Depending on the backend used by PackageKit (APT, DNF, YUM, etc.), some of the following commands may not be available.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">get-groups</samp>
    Determines package groups.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">get-updates</samp>
    Provides a list of all packages that can be updated.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">install</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">package name</samp>
    Installs a package.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">install-local</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file</samp>
    Installs a local file.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">refresh [force] [options]</samp>
    Updates the cache with the package information. If you use <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pkcon refresh force -c -1</samp>, the permitted age for the cache files will be set to less than zero. This causes the entire cache to be deleted, which can save a lot of space.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">remove</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">package name</samp>
    Uninstalls a package.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">search [name|details|group|file]</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">search term</samp>
    Searches for packages.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">update [</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">package name</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">]</samp>
    Updates the specified package or all installed packages.

### popd

The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">bash</samp> command <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">popd</samp> returns to a directory that was previously saved using [pushd](#P_001.xhtml_pushd). The directory is removed from the directory list. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">popd</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pushd</samp> are usually only used in shell scripts.

### postconf [options] [parameter[=value]]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">postconf</samp> helps to read the configuration of the Postfix mail server and to change it during operation. If the command is called without options, it simply displays the currently valid setting of the approximately 1,000 Postfix parameters.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">parametername</samp>
    Shows the current status of the parameter.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">parametername=new value</samp>
    Sets the parameter again and also makes the change in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/postfix/main.cf</samp> configuration file.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-d</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-df</samp>
    Displays the default value of all parameters (even if the parameters are currently set differently). The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-df</samp> option (fold) instead of <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-d</samp> causes long entries to be wrapped over several lines.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-d</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">parametername</samp>
    Displays the default state of the parameter (possibly different from the current setting).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-n</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-nf</samp>
    Lists all parameters that don’t have the default value. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-nf</samp> wraps long lines.

### postqueue [options]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">postqueue</samp> provides information about emails from the Postfix mail server that haven’t yet been delivered or initiates a new transmission attempt.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-f</samp>
    Attempts to resend all emails in the queue immediately (flush). Postfix takes care of this automatically but maintains wait times between multiple transmission attempts.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-i</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">id</samp>
    Tries to resend the specified email immediately.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-p</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-j</samp>
    Shows all emails in the queue. With <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-j</samp>, the output is in JSON format.

### powertop

The interactive <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">powertop</samp> program from the package of the same name analyzes which processes consume the most energy or wake up the CPU or hard disk most frequently from sleep mode. While the program is running, you can use the Tab key to switch between different result pages.

The most interesting page from the point of view of energy-saving functions is called Tunables. There, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">powertop</samp> shows a list of settings whose current state can be Bad or Good. You can then select individual points with the cursor keys and change them by pressing Enter. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">powertop</samp> shows which command it’s executing.

Then, you can try changing individual settings step by step and test what effect this has: Does the energy consumption of the previously charged notebook, recorded with a power meter, actually drop noticeably? Do the disabled functions cause problems? Can USB devices still be used? Does switching the Wi-Fi adapter on and off still work? Does the audio system work without interference, and so on?

The changes made using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">powertop</samp> are only valid until the next restart of the computer. To activate the power saving measures permanently, you enter the commands displayed by <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">powertop</samp> (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">echo '1' > /sys/xxx</samp>) into a file that is executed at every system start. In most distributions, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/rc.d/rc.local</samp> is suitable for this. If necessary, you must create this file and mark it as executable by using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">chmod a+x</samp>. Depending on the distribution, you may also need to run <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">systemctl daemon-reload</samp> so that systemd includes the file.

A radical solution would be to enter <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">powertop --auto-tune</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">rc.local</samp> instead of individual tuning commands. Then, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">powertop</samp> simply performs all known optimization measures. Unfortunately, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">powertop</samp> often overshoots the mark with this: What good is it if the notebook runs for an hour longer than before, but the network connection is unreliable?

You can get a list of all possible tuning commands by running <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">powertop</samp> with the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">--html</samp> option. After a measurement time of approximately 20 seconds, the command then generates the HTML file <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">powertop.html</samp>, which contains various statistical data as well as a summary of all tuning parameters.

### ppa-purge ppa:ppaowner[/ppaname]

The Ubuntu-specific <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ppa-purge</samp> command from the command of the same name deactivates the specified private package repository (PPA, see also the description of the [add-apt-repository](#A_001.xhtml_add-apt-repository) command). If the PPA provides alternative versions of official packages, these packages will be removed and replaced by the original packages.

#### Example

The following command deactivates the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">libreoffice</samp> package source and replaces the packages originating from this package source with standard Ubuntu packages:

```
root# ppa-purge ppa:libreoffice/ppa 
```

### printenv [variable]

Outputs the content of the specified environment variable or all environment variables line by line.

### printf format para1 para2 para3 ...

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">printf</samp> allows you to format output in the syntax of the C command; <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">printf</samp>. You can obtain detailed information on the formatting options via <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man 3 printf</samp>.

#### Example

The following command outputs an integer, a floating-point number with two decimal places, and an end-of-line character.

```
root# printf "%d %.2f\n" 123 3.1415927
123 3.14 
```

### pro command

The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pro</samp> command is available on all current Ubuntu versions. Although it’s primarily used to control the paid Ubuntu Pro offering, some of the functions can also be used without a Pro subscription.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">attach</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">token</samp>
    Activates the Ubuntu Pro functions. You can obtain valid tokens via the Ubuntu Pro dashboard.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">security status</samp>
    Provides an overview of how many packages are being serviced and for how long. The five-year update guarantee for Ubuntu LTS versions only applies to the package sources main and restricted. A typical Ubuntu installation contains a mix of packages from different package sources.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">status</samp>
    Shows the status of the Ubuntu Pro services.

#### Example

The following results were obtained on a server with Ubuntu 22.04, on which the free version (with a maximum of five installations) of Ubuntu Pro was activated:

```
user$ pro status
SERVICE       ENTITLED  STATUS    DESCRIPTION
anbox-cloud   yes       disabled  Scalable Android in the cloud
esm-apps      yes       enabled   Expanded Security Maintenance for Applications
esm-infra     yes       enabled   Expanded Security Maint. for Infrastructure
livepatch     yes       enabled   Canonical Livepatch service
Subscription: Ubuntu Pro - free personal subscription
user$ pro security-status
1186 packages installed:
 938 packages from Ubuntu Main/Restricted repository
 243 packages from Ubuntu Universe/Multiverse repository
   5 packages no longer available for download
 This machine is attached to an Ubuntu Pro subscription.
Main/Restricted packages are receiving security updates from
Ubuntu Pro with 'esm-infra' enabled until 2032.
Universe/Multiverse packages are receiving security updates from
Ubuntu Pro with 'esm-apps' enabled until 2032\. 
```

### ps [options]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ps</samp> displays the list of running processes (programs) and kernel threads. The command is particularly useful in conjunction with [kill](#K_001.xhtml_kill) to forcibly terminate programs that have hung themselves up. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ps</samp> is equipped with countless options, which are described in detail in the online manual (<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man ps</samp>). There, you’ll also find explanations of what the numerous pieces of information output by <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ps</samp> mean. A variant of <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ps</samp> is [pstree](#P_001.xhtml_pstree), which displays the process tree and thus makes the hierarchy of the processes clear at a glance.

In contrast to other commands, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ps</samp> has options with and without a preceding hyphen. Some of these even have different meanings. (<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ps -a</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ps a</samp> aren’t equivalent!) Both option types can be mixed in groups, such as <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ps -A ul</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">a</samp>
    Also displays processes of other users (not just your own).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-A</samp>
    Displays all processes.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">f</samp>
    Displays the process tree.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-f -l</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">l</samp>
    Displays various additional information (memory requirements, priority, and more).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-p</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-p</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n1</samp>,<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n2</samp>,<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n3</samp>
    Displays only processes with the specified process numbers (PIDs).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--ppid</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Displays only processes that have <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> as their parent process ID, that is, that were started by process <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">u</samp>
    Also displays the names of the users of the respective processes. The option can’t be combined with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">l</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">x</samp>
    Also displays processes to which no terminal is assigned. These include internal Linux processes for managing the system (daemons).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Z</samp>
    Also displays the SELinux context of the processes.

#### Examples

The following examples show basic applications of the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ps</samp> command:

```
root# ps ax             
(shows all processes)
root# ps ax | grep ssh  
(shows processes whose description contains ssh)
root# ps axu            
(shows all processes including owner/account) 
```

On Linux, the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">kthreadd</samp> kernel thread daemon always has process number 2\. All other kernel threads are started by <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">kthreadd</samp>. So, if you only want to list the kernel threads, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ps –ppid 2</samp>:

```
root# ps --ppid 2 
(only shows kernel threads) 
```

### ps2pdf [options] source.ps [target.pdf]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ps2pdf</samp> creates a PDF file from any PostScript or EPS file. If you don’t specify <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">target.pdf</samp>, the PDF file will have the same name as the PostScript file (but the identifier <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.pdf</samp>, i.e., <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">source</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.pdf</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-dEncodeColorImages=false</samp>
    Prevents any compression of images. The resulting PDF files are now very large. In combination with the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/prepress</samp> setting, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ps2pdf</samp> now delivers PDFs in optimum print and exposure quality.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-dPDFSETTINGS=/default | /screen | /printer | /prepress</samp>
    Specifies whether the PDF document is to be optimized for any use, for screen display, for a regular printout, or for exposure (e.g., book printing, etc.). The price for the higher quality is the increasing file size. These four default settings save you having to set numerous options individually.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-r</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Specifies the resolution for bitmap fonts (unit DPI, i.e., dots per inch).

Countless other options are described at the following address:

[https://web.mit.edu/ghostscript/www/Ps2pdf.htm](https://web.mit.edu/ghostscript/www/Ps2pdf.htm)

#### Example

The following command creates the PDF document <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">book.pdf</samp> from the PostScript file <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">book.ps</samp>:

```
user$ ps2pdf book.ps 
```

### psql [options]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">psql</samp> enables the execution of SQL commands for PostgreSQL databases. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">psql</samp> is part of the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">postgresql</samp> package. If you only need the client without the associated database server (e.g., because the database is running on another server or in a Docker container), you can install the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">postgresql-client</samp> (Debian, Ubuntu) or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">libpq</samp> (Fedora, RHEL) package for some distributions.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-c 'SQL command'</samp>
    Runs the specified SQL command and then closes the connection.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-d</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">dbname</samp>
    Specifies the database to which the connection is to be established. If a connection already exists, you can change the active database using <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">\c dbname</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-f</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file.sql</samp>
    Runs the SQL commands contained in the specified file.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-h</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">hostname</samp>
    Specifies the host on which the PostgreSQL server is running. The option can be omitted for local installations if communication via a socket file is possible.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-l</samp>
    Lists all databases and other objects (users, roles, etc.). If a connection already exists, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">\l</samp> lists the database objects. In the active database, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">\d</samp> provides a list of all tables.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-U</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">username</samp>
    Defines the username. Without this option, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">psql</samp> uses the currently active Linux account name.

#### Example

The following listing shows the creation of a database connection, the creation of a test database with a simple table, the insertion of two data records, and a simple query:

```
user$ psql -U name -h localhost
Password for user name: ********
postgres~# CREATE DATABASE test;
postgres~# \c test;            
(activate database)
postgres~# CREATE TABLE mytable (id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, data TEXT);
postgres~# INSERT INTO mytable (data) VALUES ('abc'), ('efg');
postgres~# SELECT * FROM mytable;
 id | data
----+------
  1 | abc
  2 | efg 
```

### pssh [options] command
pscp [options] local_file remote_file
pnuke [options] pattern

The Python script <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pssh</samp> from the package of the same name runs a command on multiple servers at the same time. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pscp</samp> copies files from all or to all specified hosts. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pnuke</samp> terminates a program whose name or pattern has been specified on all hosts via <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">kill -9</samp>. All three commands require that authentication with keys is possible or that the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ssh-agent</samp> background program takes care of authentication.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-h hosts.txt</samp>
    Specifies the location of the text file that contains the host names of the computers on which the command is executed line by line.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-o</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">directory</samp>
    Specifies a directory in which <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pssh</samp> saves the output of the commands and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pscp</samp> saves the files to be copied. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pssh</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pscp</samp> set up separate output files for each host, the names of which indicate the host.

#### Example

The example assumes that all hosts are RHEL systems. Then, a software update is performed on these computers using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">yum</samp>.

```
root# pssh -h hosts.txt yum update 
```

### pstree [options] [pid]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pstree</samp> from the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">psmisc</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pstree</samp> package displays a tree with all processes on the screen. The tree makes it clear which process was started by which other process. If a process number is specified, the tree starts at this point; otherwise, it starts with the first process that is run at system startup (usually systemd).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-h</samp>
    Identifies the current process and all its parent processes.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-p</samp>
    Also shows the process number (PID) for each process.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-u</samp>
    Shows the username or account name for all processes whose UID (user ID) differs from the UID of the parent process.

### pushd directory

The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">bash</samp> command <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pushd</samp> saves the current directory and then changes to the specified directory. [popd](#P_001.xhtml_popd) takes you back to the original directory. [dirs](#D_001.xhtml_dirs) displays the list of saved directories. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pushd</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">popd</samp> are mainly used in shell scripts.

### pvcreate [options] device

The LVM command <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pvcreate</samp> declares a partition or a device as a physical volume (PV) for later use in a volume group (VG; see also [vgcreate](#V_001.xhtml_vgcreate) and [vgextend](#V_001.xhtml_vgextend)).

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pvcreate</samp> requires that the partition or device has previously been marked as an LVM partition. In [fdisk](#F_001.xhtml_fdisk), you must use the T shortcut command and code <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">8e</samp> for this purpose. In [parted](#P_001.xhtml_parted), the required command is <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">set</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">partition number</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lvm on</samp>.

#### Example

The following command turns the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dev/sdc1</samp> partition into a physical volume for LVM:

```
root# pvcreate /dev/sdc1
  Physical volume "/dev/sdc1" successfully created 
```

### pvdisplay device

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pvdisplay</samp> shows detailed information on the specified PV.

### pvremove device

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pvremove</samp> removes the PV label of an unused PV.

### pvscan

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pvscan</samp> lists all PVs.

### pw-cat audio file
pw-cli [command]
pw-mon [options]
pw-top [options]

Most current Linux distributions use PipeWire as an audio and video server. There are various commands for controlling PipeWire, each with a name beginning with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pw-</samp>. Here, I’ll focus on the most frequently used commands:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pw-cat</samp> transfers raw files from or to the audio system. The command can also be run as <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pw-play</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pw-record</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pw-midiplayrecord</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pw-midirecord</samp>.

*   You can change the audio setup using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pw-cli</samp>. There are countless subcommands, of which only the most important are mentioned here:

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">connect</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">disconnect</samp> establishes or terminates a connection to an external PipeWire server.

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">create-link</samp> connects two PipeWire nodes.

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">create-node</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">export-node</samp> manage PipeWire nodes, that is, objects for signal management or forwarding.

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">info</samp> id displays detailed information on a specific object.

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">list-objects</samp> lists all PipeWire objects.

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">list-remotes</samp> lists all external PipeWire instances.

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">load-</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">unload-module</samp> loads or removes PipeWire modules.

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">send-command</samp> sends a command to a PipeWire object.

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">switch-remote</samp> defines the active remote instance.

    <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pw-cli</samp> is a low-level command. Its use is extremely cumbersome. Because PipeWire has a compatibility layer with PulseAudio, in many cases, it’s easier to control the setup via [pactl](#P_001.xhtml_pactl).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pw-mon</samp> lists all audio and video objects known to the PipeWire system, including countless properties.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pw-top</samp> provides an overview of the currently active PipeWire components, including the latencies occurring during audio processing.

### pwd

The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">bash</samp> command <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pwd</samp> specifies the current directory.

In addition to the version included in the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">bash</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pwd</samp> is also available as an independent command, often under the file name of <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">/bin/pwd</samp>. Note that there may be cases in which the two variants of <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pwd</samp> don’t produce the same result. This is because the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">bash</samp> version of <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pwd</samp> works on a relative basis, whereas the external command works with absolute values. Symbolic links to directories can trick the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">bash</samp> version of <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pwd</samp> to a certain extent.

#### Example

In the following example, [ln](#L_001.xhtml_ln) creates a symbolic link to the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/tmp</samp> directory. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">cd</samp> changes to this directory. The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">bash</samp> believes that this directory is the current directory, while <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">/bin/pwd</samp> recognizes that <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/tmp</samp> is actually the current directory.

```
user$ ln -s /tmp symlink
user$ cd symlink
user$ pwd         
(bash version of pwd)
/home/kofler/symlink
user$ /bin/pwd    
(standalone pwd command)
/tmp 
```

### pwgen [options] [n]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pwgen</samp> from the package of the same name generates an entire list of random but easy-to-remember passwords. The idea is that the user selects one of the passwords and then clears the screen using Ctrl+L before anyone can look over their shoulder and read the password. Compared to the passwords generated by [makepasswd](#M_001.xhtml_makepasswd), the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">pwgen</samp> passwords are less random and therefore less secure, but they are still good enough for many use cases.

By default, passwords are eight characters long. You can generate longer passwords by specifying the optional parameter <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-0</samp>
    Doesn’t use numbers in the passwords.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-1</samp>
    Provides only 1 password and not 100.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-B</samp>
    Avoids letters or numbers that are easy to confuse depending on the font, that is, O and 0 as well as l and 1\. This makes passwords less secure.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-y</samp>
    Also includes special characters in the passwords.

#### Example

As the example shows, even the passwords generated in the default settings are by no means trivial:

```
user pwgen
Ohshu3yo Ea1wedoe OhCh2Zua Aili8ooc Xu4iiyix eug3Chee Gaesh2pu Eeth6mah
eMee0jio xieL6oob ob8uYah9 shaif0Ed uep8Eive lang3Eho thaiS7xa Sah3See4
... 
```

The following command generates an 80-character password that also contains special characters:

```
root# pwgen -1 -y 80
AhB9eiv]oo~s0go2ievaF7eePe6ooyoo7Cim%oh8eishiloosaeSeex+eeza9Iem7Ahchuhi6ahch[i1 
```

## Q

### qalc [expression]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">qalc</samp> from the package of the same name calculates the transferred mathematical expression and returns the result. To avoid special characters being processed by the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">bash</samp>, you must enclose most expressions in quotation marks:

```
user$ qalc "(2+3)*4^5"
(2 + 3) * (4^5) = 5120 
```

If no expression is transferred, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">qalc</samp> activates an interactive mode. It then performs calculations until the command is ended via Ctrl+D.

```
user$ qalc
>2^64
 2^64 = approx. 1.8446744E19
>sin(0.2)
 sin(0.2 * radian) = approx. 0.19866933
>sin(pi)
 sin(pi * radian) = 0
>sqrt(2)
 sqrt(2) = approx. 1.4142136
>10 EUR to USD
 10 * euro = $10.651 
```

### qemu [options] [imagefile]

Quick Emulator (QEMU) emulates various CPUs. There is a special variant of the command for each important CPU architecture: <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">qemu-aarch64</samp> for 64-bit ARM systems, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">qemu-mips64</samp> for 64-bit MIPS systems, and more. For x86 systems, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">qemu-x86_64</samp> is the most important command. In some distributions, the names are <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">qemu-system-aarch64</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">qemu-system-x86</samp>, and more. In the following, I’ll simply stick to <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">qemu</samp> for the sake of brevity. Depending on the distribution and CPU architecture, you must call the appropriate variant of the command.

If possible, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">qemu</samp> is combined with Kernel-Based Virtual Machines (KVM), a Linux kernel extension. This means that virtual machines with the same architecture as the host system can be run much faster. KVM is activated with the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-enable-kvm</samp> option or with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-accel kvm</samp>. Depending on the distribution, there are tiny scripts such as <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">kvm</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">qemu-kvm</samp> that start <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">qemu</samp> with the KVM option. On RHEL systems, the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">qemu-kvm</samp> command is located in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/usr/libexec</samp> directory.

In the simplest case, you only transfer the name of an image file to <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">qemu</samp>. QEMU then runs the virtual machine with default settings, including an IDE hard disk. If you want to use other settings or multiple data media, you can add the options <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-drive</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-hda</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-hdb</samp>, and so on. In this case, the direct specification of the image file in the KVM command can be omitted.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-accel kvm</samp>
    Activates KVM. QEMU can also cope with other acceleration systems, which is why the option also supports the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">xen</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">hax</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tcg</samp> settings.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-boot order=xxx,once=xxx,menu=on/off</samp>
    Specifies the order in which the data media are to be considered for the boot process. Here, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">xxx</samp> is a sequence of letters that expresses the order of the data media (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">adc</samp>: first the floppy disk drive, then the CD/DVD drive, then the first hard disk). The letters <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">a</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">d</samp> correspond to the Windows drive letters.

    <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">once=xxx</samp> specifies the boot sequence for the first boot process only. For example, if the virtual machine is supposed to boot from the CD/DVD drive on the first attempt, but from the hard disk on subsequent restarts, you enter <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-boot order=c,once=d</samp> or simply <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-boot once=d</samp>. (The virtual DVD drive is usually connected to the ISO image for the installation system.)

    <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">menu=on</samp> displays the message Press F12 for boot menu at the start of the boot menu. The boot disk can then be selected interactively by pressing the F12 key.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-cdrom</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">iso file</samp>
    Uses the specified ISO file as the data source for the virtual CD/DVD drive. The option corresponds to <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">–drive file=iso-file,index=2,media=cdrom</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-cpu</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">host</samp>
    Transfers all properties of the host CPU to the guest. This isn’t the case by default: only one subset is passed on to maximize the compatibility of virtual machines between different CPUs.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-device</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">cup</samp>
    Adds an additional device to the virtual machine. A list of all supported devices is provided by <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">qemu -device ?</samp> The device name is case-sensitive! You can determine the options available for a specific device using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">qemu –device</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">cup</samp><samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">,?</samp>, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">qemu -device isa-serial,?</samp>.

    Note that you can define most components of a virtual machine in two ways: with the very universal <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-device</samp> option described here or with device-specific options (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-drive</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-soundhw</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-usb-device</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-vga</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-drive</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">details</samp>
    Defines the properties of a virtual hard disk. The detailed parameters are separated from each other by commas only (without spaces!). The option can be used multiple times if the virtual machine is to be equipped with multiple data media.

    <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">boot=on/off</samp> specifies whether the data medium should be taken into account when booting.

    <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">cache=writethrough/writeback/none</samp> specifies whether and how write accesses are cached. By default, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">writethrough</samp> is used: in the guest system, a write access doesn’t appear as completed until the host system has acknowledged the save operation.

    <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">file=fname</samp> specifies the file name of the image, ISO file, or the device name of a logical volume.

    <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">if=ide/scsi/virtio</samp> specifies which interface the virtual machine should use to access the data medium (the default value is <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ide</samp>). <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">virtio</samp> is more efficient with Linux guests.

    <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">index=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> determines the numbering of the data media of an interface. The parameter is only required if the data media aren’t specified in sequence.

    <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">media=disk/cdrom</samp> specifies whether it should be a hard disk (default setting) or a CD/DVD drive.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-enable-kvm</samp>
    Corresponds to <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-accel kvm</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-hda/-hdb/-hdc/-hdd</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">details</samp>
    Specifies a virtual IDE hard disk.
    <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-hda fname</samp> corresponds to <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-drive file=fname,index=0,media=disk</samp>.
    <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-hdb fname</samp> corresponds to <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-drive file=fname,index=1,media=disk</samp>, and more.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-k</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">language identifier</samp>
    Uses the specified keyboard layout. Permitted language identifiers include <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">de</samp> (German) and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">en-us</samp> (US English). This option is only required if the virtual machine is operated by an external VNC client. The VNC clients of the virtual machine manager or the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">virt-viewer</samp> command automatically recognize the keyboard setting.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-localtime</samp>
    Initializes the virtual CMOS clock of the guest system with the local time (instead of the default UTC time).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-m</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Sets the memory size of the virtual machine (in MiB). The default setting varies depending on the distribution.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-machine</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[,</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">para1=value1,para2=value2</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">...]</samp>
    Specifies which hardware is supposed to be emulated. A list of permitted type names is provided by <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-machine help</samp>. The parameters can be used to activate or deactivate additional properties that differ from the basic settings of the respective type.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-monitor</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">device</samp>
    Redirects the input and output of the QEMU monitor to the specified device. If you want to operate the monitor via the current console, you must enter <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">stdio</samp> as the device. With <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">pty</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">qemu</samp> creates a new pseudo TTY device at startup and uses it for communication.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-net nic,</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">details</samp>
    Configures a virtual network adapter. If this option isn’t specified, QEMU emulates an RTL8139-compatible network card by default.

    <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">model=ne2k_pci/i82551/i82557b/i82559er/rtl8139/e1000/pcnet/virtio</samp> defines the network adapter QEMU is supposed to emulate. For Linux guests, you’ll achieve the best results with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">model=virtio</samp>. You use <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">macaddr=52:54:00:nn:nn:nn</samp> to specify the desired MAC address.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-net user,</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">details</samp>
    Uses user mode networking (this is the default setting). Although the guest system can use the internet connection of the host system thanks to NAT and masquerading, a direct network connection between guest and host isn’t possible.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-rtc base=utc/localtime</samp>
    Specifies which start time the virtual machine clock should have. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">utc</samp> is the correct setting for Linux guests, while <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">localtime</samp> is suitable for Windows guests. By default, the clock is always synchronized with that of the host computer. If you don’t want this to happen, you can specify the additional <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">clock=vm</samp> parameter.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-smp</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-smp cores=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">c</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">threads=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">t</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">sockets=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">s</samp>
    Short notation to specify how many CPUs or cores are to be assigned to the virtual machine (only one core by default). For host systems with multiple CPUs, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">c</samp> specifies how many cores are to be used per CPU. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">t</samp> specifies the desired number of threads per core; the value <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">2</samp> is usually useful here for Intel CPUs that support hyperthreading. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">s</samp> finally specifies how many CPUs (sockets) are to be used. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">c*t*s</samp> provides the number of CPUs the virtual machine is able to see.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-soundhw ac97/es1370/hda/sb16/all</samp>
    Adds one of the specified audio devices to the virtual machine (or all if you use <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">all</samp>). <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ac97</samp> stands for Intel 82801AA AC97, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">es1370</samp> for Ensoniq AudioPCI ES1370, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">hda</samp> for Intel High Definition Audio, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">sb16</samp> for Creative Sound Blaster 16.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-spice port=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[,options]</samp>
    Activates the Spice graphics system. For this purpose, you must specify at least the desired port.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-usb</samp>
    Activates the USB driver.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-usbdevice mouse/tablet/disk/host...</samp>
    Adds a USB device to the virtual machine. Most of the time you’ll need the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-usbdevice tablet</samp> option. It replaces the standard emulated PS/2 mouse with a virtual USB pointing device that understands absolute coordinates and thus enables synchronization of the guest’s mouse position with the VNC or Spice client.

    <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-usbdevice disk</samp> makes it possible to pass an image file from the host to the guest in such a way that the guest sees a USB data medium.

    <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-usbdevice host:bus.addr</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-usbdevice host:vendorid:productid</samp> redirects a USB device from the host to the guest. The USB device must not be used by the host. The easiest way to determine the bus and device number or the vendor and product IDs on the host server is to use <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lsusb</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-vga cirrus/qxl/std/virtio/vmware</samp>
    Specifies the desired type of virtual graphics card. By default, QEMU emulates a Cirrus-compatible graphics card with a resolution of up to 1,024 × 768 pixels. This graphics system is recognized correctly by almost all guest systems and runs at an acceptable speed. The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">qxl</samp> graphics card can only be used in combination with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-spice</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-vnc</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n.n.n.n:n</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[,options]</samp>
    Runs a VNC server via which clients can display the contents of the virtual graphics card. You can use <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n.n.n.n</samp> to specify the IP address from which the connection to the VNC server can be established (e.g., 127.0.0.1 for connections from <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">localhost</samp>). <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">:n</samp> indicates the display number. The port for the VNC server is <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>+5900\. If you only enter the display number without the IP address (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">:0</samp>), the connection can be established by any computer.

Only in exceptional cases is <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">qemu</samp> run directly. It’s more common to use the [virsh](#V_001.xhtml_virsh) command from the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">libvirt</samp> package to set up and start virtual machines, to use an interface such as <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">virt-manager</samp>, or to use a cloud framework such as OpenStack.

#### Example

In the following example, an image file with a maximum size of 20 GiB is first created, which is then used as a virtual hard disk to install a Debian system from an ISO file:

```
user$ qemu-img create -f qcow2 disk.img 20G
user$ kvm -accel kvm -m 2048 -smp 2 -boot once=d -cdrom debian.iso \
        -drive file=disk.img,if=virtio,format=qcow2 \
        -net user -net nic,macaddr=52:54:00:12:e4:4e,model=virtio \
        -vga cirrus -vnc 127.0.0.1:0 -k de -usb -usbdevice tablet 
```

To operate the virtual machine, you must now start a VNC client, such as the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">vncviewer</samp> program:

```
user$ vncviewer localhost:0 
```

### qemu-img command

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">qemu-img</samp> supports the creation and management of image files for virtual hard disks. The first parameter you specify must be a command, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">create</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">convert</samp>. This is followed by further options, the file name of the image file, and more, depending on the command.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">convert [-f</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">source format</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">] -O</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">target format source file target file</samp>
    Converts an image file from one format to another. The original file is retained. However, the image file must not be used by a virtual machine during the conversion. The target file is compressed with the additional option <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-c</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">convert -f qcow2 -s</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">snapshotname</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-O</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">target format source file target file</samp>
    Transfers only the snapshot of a QCOW2 image selected with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-s</samp> to the new image file.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">create [-f raw/qcow2/qed] [-o opt1=val1,opt2=val2,...]</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file size</samp>
    Creates a new image file of the specified type and size. The size is specified in bytes by default. Optionally, the suffixes <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">k</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">K</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">M</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">G</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">T</samp> can be used (for KiB, MiB, GiB, or TiB). Depending on the image format, various additional options can be specified. You can determine the parameters available for selection via <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-o '?'</samp>, whereby this option must be specified in a complete, syntactically correct command:

    <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">qemu-img create -f qcow2 -o '?' test.img 1G</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">create -f qcow2 -o backing_file=basis.img overlay.img</samp>
    Creates an overlay file. When the virtual machine is run, all changes are saved in the overlay file; the base file remains unchanged.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">info</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file</samp>
    Provides information about the specified image file. Information about snapshots in QCOW2 images can be obtained using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">qemu-img snapshot</samp> (see that entry at the end of this list).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">resize</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">+/-</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">size</samp>
    Enlarges or reduces the image file by the specified size. The command is only suitable for raw and QCOW2 images.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">snapshot [options]</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">snapshotname file</samp>
    Edits snapshots. This command is only available for QCOW2 images. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-c</samp> creates a new snapshot, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-a</samp> applies a snapshot to the image (thus revoking all changes that have been made since the snapshot was created), <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-d</samp> deletes the snapshot, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-l</samp> lists all snapshots. However, with the exception of <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-l</samp>, you may not use these commands while the image file is being used by a running virtual machine!

#### Examples

The first command creates a QCOW2 image file. A major advantage of this image format is that the file initially takes up hardly any memory on the data medium and grows only gradually.

```
root# qemu-img create -f qcow2 disk.img 10G 
```

The second command creates an equivalent raw image from a QCOW2 file:

```
user$ qemu-img convert -f qcow2 image.qcow2 -O raw image.raw 
```

## R

### rclone command

The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">rclone</samp> command from the package of the same name synchronizes files or entire directories with a storage location in the cloud. The files can also be encrypted or decrypted when they are transported back. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">rclone</samp> is compatible with more than 70 cloud providers, including AWS S3.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">copy</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">remote name</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">:</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">bucketname localdir</samp>
    Copies files from a remote directory to a local directory. (A bucket is a storage location with the cloud provider.)

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">config</samp>
    Guides you through an interactive setup program in which you select your cloud provider and enter the authentication data. This data is saved under the name you specify in a section in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.config/rclone/</samp><samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">rclone.conf</samp>. Each section of this type describes a remote directory.

    To configure automatic encryption, you first need to configure a normal setup for the cloud provider, and then configure a second setup (a second remote directory) of type <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">crypt</samp> that refers to the original setup.
