*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-M</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">aclrule file</samp>
    Like <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-m</samp>, but reads the rule from a file. Rule files must look like the output of [getfacl](#G_001.xhtml_getfacl).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-x</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">aclrule</samp>
    Deletes the specified ACL rule.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-X</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">aclrule file</samp>
    Like <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-x</samp>, but reads the rule from a file.

The simplified structure of an ACL rule (an ACE) is shown in the following table. The complete syntax is documented in <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man setfacl</samp>.

| <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[u:]uid [:rights]</samp> | Changes rights for a user |
| <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">g:gid [:rights]</samp> | Changes rights for a group |
| <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">o[:] [:rights]</samp> | Changes rights for all other users |
| <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">m[:] [:rights]</samp> | Sets the ACL mask (effective right mask) |

The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">rights</samp> consist of up to three letters: <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">r</samp> for read, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">w</samp> for write, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">x</samp> for execute. To remove all rights from a user or group, you must specify <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-</samp>.

If you prefix the entire rule with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">d:</samp>, it applies to the standard ACLs. Instead of the letters <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">u</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">g</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">o</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">m</samp>, you can also use the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">user</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">group</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">other</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mask</samp> keywords.

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">setfacl</samp> can be controlled by further options:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-B</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--remove-all</samp>
    Removes all ACL rules.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-d</samp>
    Applies the transferred rule to the standard ACL.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-k</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--remove-default</samp>
    Removes the standard ACL rules.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-n</samp>
    Dispenses with the automatic recalculation of the ACL mask for every ACL rule change.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--restore=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file</samp>
    Applies the ACL rules specified in the file to the files in the current directory. You can create an ACL backup file using [getfacl](#G_001.xhtml_getfacl) <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-R</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-R</samp>
    Applies the specified rule recursively to all files and subdirectories.

#### Examples

In a file system with ACLs, the default access rights normally apply, which are often also referred to as the minimum ACL. [getfacl](#G_001.xhtml_getfacl) displays these rights in ACL form:

```
user$ touch file1
user$ getfacl file1
# file: file1
# owner: kofler
# group: kofler
user::rw-
group::r--
other::r--
user$ ls -l file1
-rw-r--r-- 1 kofler kofler ...  file2 
```

Using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">setfacl</samp>, you can now define additional access rules. The following commands give the user <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">grace</samp> and all members of the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">docuteam</samp> group write and read access to the file, but deny the user <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">katherine</samp> any access:

```
user$ setfacl -m grace:rw file1
user$ setfacl -m g:docuteam:rw file1
user$ setfacl -m katherine:- file1 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">getfacl</samp> rights list is now somewhat longer. With <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ls -l</samp>, the usual access letters are followed by the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">+</samp> sign to indicate that there are ACL rules.

```
user$ getfacl file1
# file: file1
# owner: kofler
# group: kofler
user::rw-
user:grace:rw-
user:katherine:---
group::r--
group:docuteam:rw-
mask::rw- other::r--

user$ ls -l file1
-rw-rw-r--+ 1 kofler kofler ... file1 
```

### setfattr [options] file name

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">setfattr</samp> changes the extended attributes of the selected files or directories. This only works if the file system supports extended attributes (EAs). For ext3/ext4 file systems, the [mount](#M_001.xhtml_mount) option <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">user_xattr</samp> must be used.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-n</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">attribute name</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--name=attribute name</samp>
    Specifies the name of the attribute to be changed. The actual name must be preceded by <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">user.</samp> (i.e., <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-n user.myattribute</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-v</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">value</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--value=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">value</samp>
    Specifies the value to be saved in the attribute.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-x</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">attribute name</samp>
    Deletes the specified attribute.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--restore=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file</samp>
    Applies the EA definitions specified in the file to the files in the current directory. You can create an EA backup file via <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">getfattr -R -d</samp>.

#### Examples

The following examples show how you can use <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">setfattr</samp> to store attributes and how to read them using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">getfattr</samp>: the number of attributes per file is limited in ext file systems.

```
user$ touch file2
user$ setfattr -n
user.language -v en file2
user$ setfattr --name=user.charset --value=utf8 file2
user$ getfattr -d file2
 # file: file2
user.charset="utf8"
user.language="en" 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">getfattr</samp> usually returns only attributes whose name starts with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">user.</samp>. If you want to see other attributes, you must specify their names using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-n</samp> or their patterns by using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-m</samp>:

```
user$ getfattr -n security.selinux -d tst
# file: tst security.selinux="user_u:object_r:user_home_t:s0^000" 
```

### setsebool [options] bool1=value1 bool2=value2 ...

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">setsebool</samp> changes Boolean parameters at runtime. Boolean parameters can be used to change the behavior of some SELinux rules. You can determine which Boolean parameters are available via [sestatus](#S_001.xhtml_sestatus) <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-b</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-N</samp>
    Saves the change, but doesn’t activate it. The change will therefore only take effect the next time the computer is restarted.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-P</samp>
    Performs the change and saves the setting permanently. The change applies immediately and will also apply in the future, that is, after the next restart.

#### Example

The following command allows the Squid program to act as a transparent proxy:

```
root# setsebool -P squid_use_tproxy 1 
```

### setterm [option]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">setterm</samp> changes various settings of the terminal. If the command is executed without specifying an option, it displays a list of all possible options. Useful options for shell programming are listed here:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--background</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">color</samp>
    Sets the background color. The colors <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">black</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">red</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">green</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">yellow</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">blue</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">magenta</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">cyan</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">white</samp> are permitted. To ensure that the setting remains valid after color output by <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ls</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">grep</samp>, the option must be combined with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">--store</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--blank</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Activates the screen saver after <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> minutes without input (only for text consoles).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--bold on|off</samp>
    Activates or deactivates the bold font. In text consoles, the text doesn’t appear in bold, but at least in a different color than the other text.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--clear</samp>
    Deletes the contents of the terminal.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--default</samp>
    Restores colors and text attributes to the default setting.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--foreground</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">color</samp>
    Sets the text color.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--half-bright on|off</samp>
    Switches highlighted font on/off.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--inversescreen on|off</samp>
    Inverts the display in the text console (black text on a white background) or restores the normal state.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--reverse on|off</samp>
    Sets inverse font on/off.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--store</samp>
    Remembers the color settings (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--foreground</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--background</samp> options) so that they are retained even if commands such as <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ls</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">grep</samp> temporarily use different colors. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">--store</samp> is only valid in the Linux text consoles, but not within terminal windows. The settings aren’t saved in a file there either, but are lost when you log out.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--underline on|off</samp>
    Switches underlined font on/off.

#### Example

If the following line is inserted in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.bashrc</samp>, text consoles use a white background and black font after login:

```
# insert into .bashrc
setterm -background white -foreground black -store 
```

### sfdisk [options]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sfdisk</samp> lists the partitions of a hard disk or repartitions the hard disks. The command is particularly suitable for automated partitioning (e.g., in a script) or for transferring an existing partitioning to a second hard disk, for example, when setting up a RAID array.

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sfdisk</samp> only works with MBR partition tables and is unsuitable for disks with a GUID partition table (GPT)!

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-d [</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">device</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">]</samp>
    Lsts all partitions of all hard disks or the specified hard disk. The output format is suitable for further processing by <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sfdisk</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--force</samp>
    Performs partitioning even if <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">sfdisk</samp> believes that the partition or hard disk is in use, or if partition boundaries don’t match cylinder boundaries.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-l [</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">device</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">]</samp>
    Lists all partitions of all hard disks or the specified hard disk in a readable format. With the additional <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-uS</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-uB</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-uC</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-uM</samp> option, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sfdisk</samp> uses sectors (512 bytes), blocks (1,024 bytes), cylinders, or MiB as the unit of measurement.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-s</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">device</samp>
    Returns the number of blocks (1,024 bytes each) of the specified hard disk or partition.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-uS|-uB|-uC|-uM</samp>
    Uses sectors (512 bytes), blocks (1,024 bytes), cylinders, or MiB as the unit of measurement.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">device</samp> < <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">partitioning table</samp>
    Repartitions the hard disk using the transferred table. The partitioning table must have the same format as the output of <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sfdisk -d</samp>.

#### Example

The following command partitions the second hard disk (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dev/sdb</samp>) exactly like the first hard disk (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dev/sda</samp>). The second hard disk must be at least as large as the first one. All partitions and data on the second hard disk will be lost.

```
root# sfdisk -d /dev/sda | sfdisk /dev/sdb 
```

### sftp [options] sshserver
sftp [optionen] user@sshserver:filename

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sftp</samp> is an alternative to the insecure [ftp](#F_001.xhtml_ftp) command. In the first syntax variant, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sftp</samp> establishes a connection to the specified SSH server. After logging in, you can interactively transfer files between the local computer and the SSH server. In the second syntax variant, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sftp</samp> transfers the specified file directly to the local computer after the password has been entered.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-b</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">batch file</samp>
    Runs the commands specified in the batch file.

### sgdisk [option] device

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sgdisk</samp> helps to edit GUID partition tables on hard disks and SSDs. Unlike [parted](#P_001.xhtml_parted), the command is controlled exclusively by options and isn’t intended for interactive use. Instead, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sgdisk</samp> to create or manipulate partition tables under script control. Despite the similar sounding name, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sgdisk</samp> expects completely different options than [sfdisk](#S_001.xhtml_sfdisk). <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sgdisk</samp> uses MiB and GiB in IEC notation.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-a</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Specifies the multiples of sectors to which new partitions are aligned. By default, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sgdisk</samp> uses the value <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">2048</samp>. This corresponds to 1 MiB.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-b</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file</samp>
    Writes a backup of the partition table to a binary file.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-d</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">nr</samp>
    Deletes the specified partition.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-G</samp>
    Assigns new, random GUIDs to all partitions. This is required after cloning a hard disk.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-l</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file</samp>
    Partitions the data medium according to the partition table stored in the file. The file must first be created using the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-b</samp> option. All existing partitions on the data medium will be deleted. The combination of the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sgdisk -b</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sgdisk -l</samp> commands can be used to transfer the partition layout of a hard disk to a second disk of the same size, for example, when setting up a RAID system.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-n</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">nr</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">:</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">start</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">:</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">end</samp>
    Creates the new partition with the number <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">nr</samp>, which extends from the specified start position to the end position. By default, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">start</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">end</samp> are specified in sectors of 512 bytes. Alternatively, you can also specify the position in MiB and GiB. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sgdisk -n 3:10G:35G</samp> creates a new partition that is 25 GiB in size.

    The start and end positions can be preceded by the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">+</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-</samp> characters. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">+</samp> enables entries that are relative to the default start sector; <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-</samp> enables specifications that are calculated from the end of the hard disk. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sgdisk -n 4:+1M:-20G</samp> creates a partition that starts 1 MiB after the last partition and leaves 20 GiB free at the end of the data medium.

#### Example

The following commands first create a backup of the current partition table on the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dev/sdb</samp> disk and then set up the new partition 3:

```
root# sgdisk -l partbackup /dev/sdb
root# sgdisk -n 3:70G:430G /dev/sdb 
```

### shansum files

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sha1sum</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sha224sum</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sha256sum</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sha384sum</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sha512sum</samp> calculate checksums for all specified files. The number in the command indicates the bit length of the checksum (160 bits for <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">sha1sum</samp>). The checksums are used to ensure that the file is unchanged after it has been transferred.

#### Example

The following command calculates a 256-bit checksum for an ISO file:

```
root# sha256sum image.iso
6ad62fe91eefa4315f852eb1bc8732bc341d95b47f6b4d1f5e362d3629fc981b  image.iso 
```

### shift [n]

The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">bash</samp> command <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">shift</samp> shifts the parameter list passed to the shell script through the predefined variables <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">$1</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">$9</samp>. If <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">shift</samp> is used without parameters, the parameters are shifted by one position; otherwise, they are shifted by n positions.

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">shift</samp> is only used for script programming. The command is a valuable aid if more than nine parameters are to be addressed. Once parameters have been <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">shifted</samp> out of the variables with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">shift</samp>, they can no longer be addressed. They are also removed from the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">$*</samp> variable.

### showmount [options]

Without additional options, the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">showmount</samp> command, when executed on an NFS server, returns a list of all clients using the shared directories via NFS 3\. Note that NFS 4 directories aren’t included in the result and are only taken into account with the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">showmount -e</samp> variant.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-a</samp>
    Also provides the IP address for each NFS 3 client.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-e [hostname]</samp>
    Provides a list of all directories that can be used via NFS, regardless of whether this service is currently in use. If you specify a host name, the list of directories available on this computer will be determined. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">showmount -e</samp> also works for NFS 4.

#### Example

```
root# showmount -e
/nfsexport       *.lan,10.0.0.0/24
/nfsexport/fotos *.lan,10.0.0.0/24
/nfsexport/iso   * 
```

### shutdown [options] time [message]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">shutdown</samp> shuts down the computer. A time (<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">hh:mm</samp>) or the number of minutes (calculated from the current time, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">+m</samp>) or the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">now</samp> keyword (i.e., immediately) must be specified as the time. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">shutdown</samp> can only be executed by <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">root</samp>. Linux is often configured in such a way that users without <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">root</samp> permissions can restart the computer via Alt+Ctrl+ Del.

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">shutdown</samp> informs all other users that the system will be shut down shortly and will no longer allow new logins. All processes are then warned that they will be stopped shortly. Some programs (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">emacs</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">vi</samp>) use this warning and save all open files in backup copies.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-c</samp>
    Attempts to cancel a <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">shutdown</samp> process that has already been initiated. This is possible if the time that precedes the start of the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">shutdown</samp> process hasn’t yet expired.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-f</samp>
    Initiates a restart like <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-r</samp>, but faster.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-F</samp>
    Causes the file systems to be checked at the next reboot. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">shutdown</samp> creates the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/forcefsck</samp> file for this purpose. If this file exists, most distributions trigger a file system check when restarting.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-h</samp>
    Stops the system after shutdown. The computer then no longer responds to inputs, and the system halted message appears on the screen. Then, the computer gets switched off by an ACPI signal.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-n</samp>
    Performs the shutdown particularly quickly, bypassing the init system.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-r</samp>
    Initiates a restart after the system has been shut down.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-t</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">seconds</samp>
    Defines the wait time between the warning message and the kill signal for the processes (usually, 20 seconds).

### sleep time

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sleep</samp> puts the running program into sleep mode for the specified time. During this time, the program consumes virtually no compute time. The time is usually given in seconds. Optionally, the letters <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">m</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">h</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">d</samp> can be added to specify the time in minutes, hours, or days.

### slurp

The command from the package of the same name enables the selection of a rectangle on the screen on Wayland. It then returns the coordinates of the top-left corner and the size of the rectangle as text. The command can be used in combination with [grim](#G_001.xhtml_grim), for example, to select the area for a screenshot.

Unfortunately, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">slurp</samp> isn’t compatible with every Wayland compositor. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">slurp</samp> works excellently on Raspberry Pi OS, but fails with distributions that use Gnome or KDE as the desktop system.

### smartctl options device

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">smartctl</samp> controls the SMART functions of the hard disk. This allows you to detect possible hard disk problems at an early stage.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-a</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--all</samp>
    Provides all available SMART information.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-d ata/scsi/3ware,</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Indicates the hard disk type. This option is only required if <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">smartctl</samp> can’t recognize the type. This applies in particular to SATA hard disks, which <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">smartctl</samp> often believes to be SCSI hard disks. The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">3ware,</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> setting enables the use of SMART functions for hard disks that are connected to a 3ware RAID controller (for details, see <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man smartctl</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-H</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--health</samp>
    Indicates whether the hard disk is currently OK and will probably continue to function for the next 24 hours.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-i</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--info</samp>
    Provides basic information about the hard disk.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-l error/selftest</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--log=error/selftest</samp>
    Provides information on the past five errors or the results of the last 21 self-tests.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-s on/off</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--smart=on/off</samp>
    Activates or deactivates the SMART functions.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-t short/long</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--test=short/long</samp>
    Performs a short or long self-test. You can view the test result later using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-l selftest</samp>.

#### Example

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">smartctl -H</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">smartctl --health</samp> indicates whether the hard disk is currently healthy. If <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">smartctl</samp> doesn’t return PASSED as a result here, you should immediately start performing a full backup!

```
root# smartctl -H /dev/sda
...
SMART overall-health self-assessment test result: PASSED 
```

Three self-tests have been carried out for the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dev/sda</samp> hard disk so far: one immediately after the installation of the disk (after 40 hours of operation), and the other two after approximately 2,600 hours. No problems have occurred.

```
root# smartctl -t short /dev/sda
root# smartctl -t long /dev/sda
...
root# smartctl -l selftest /dev/sda
Num  Test_Description  Status                    Remaining  LifeTime  LBA
# 1  Extended offline  Completed without error         00%      2592    -
# 2  Short offline     Completed without error         00%      2591    -
# 3  Short offline     Completed without error         00%        40    - 
```

### smbclient [options]
smbclient directory [password] [options]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">smbclient</samp> enables interactive access to Windows network directories. In the first syntax variant, you use the program to determine available Windows resources. In the second variant, you enter the desired network directory (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">//mars/data</samp> if you want to use the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">data</samp> directory on the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mars</samp> computer). Once the connection has been established, you’ll be taken to a shell. As with the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ftp</samp> command, you can then view directories via <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ls</samp>, change directories using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">cd</samp>, transfer files to the local computer via <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">get</samp> (download), and save files on the external computer using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">put</samp> (upload). You can get an overview of the most important commands via <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">help</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-L</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">computer name</samp>
    Returns the list of network resources on the specified Windows computer or Samba server.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-m</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">protocol</samp>
    Specifies the maximum protocol version. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-m SMB2</samp> enforces the SMB2 protocol, even if SMB3 would be possible. This option is only necessary in rare cases to avoid compatibility problems.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-N</samp>
    Omits the automatic password prompt. This option is only useful if you know that no password is required to access a particular network resource.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-U</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">username</samp>
    Specifies the username (only necessary if this differs from the current login name).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-W</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">workgroup name</samp>
    Specifies the name of the Windows workgroup (only necessary if it’s not contained in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/samba/smb.conf</samp>).

#### Example

First, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">smbclient</samp> establishes a connection to the NAS hard disk, and then <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ls</samp> returns the list of directories and files stored there:

```
user$ smbclient -U name -W wgname //mynas/myshare
Password: xxxxxx
Domain=[wgname] OS=[Unix] Server=[Samba 3.5.2]
smb: > ls
  data               D        0  Apr  5 18:17:11 2025
  file.xy           AR      226  Sep 14 00:00:00 2024   ... 
```

In the second example, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">smbclient</samp> establishes a connection to the LibreELEC media center on a Raspberry Pi. It then lists the network directories available there, which are accessible without a password by default. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-U none</samp> simply specifies an invalid username here.

```
user$ smbclient -L libreelec -U none -N -m SMB2
Sharename       Type      Comment
---------       ----      -------
Music           Disc
Screenshots     Disk
Videos          Disk
... 
```

### smbpasswd [options] [name]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">smbpasswd</samp> changes the password of the active or specified Samba user.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-a</samp>
    Creates a new Samba account. There must be a Linux account with the same name.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-n</samp>
    Removes the password for the specified account. The network directories are now accessible without a password if the Samba server is configured accordingly (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">null passwords = yes</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-x</samp>
    Deletes the specified Samba account.

### smbstatus [options]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">smbstatus</samp> returns the version number of the Samba server running on the computer as well as a list of all currently active connections.

### snap [options] command

A few years ago, Ubuntu introduced a new system for installing software packages. It works in parallel to the still dominant Debian package system (see [apt](#A_001.xhtml_apt) and [dpkg](#D_001.xhtml_dpkg)), and its objective is similar to that of the Flatpak method supported by Red Hat (see [flatpak](#F_001.xhtml_flatpak)). Like Flatpak, Snap is open to all distributions, but it hasn’t yet found any significant distribution outside of Ubuntu.

Snap packages are usually installed via the Gnome program called Software. The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">snap</samp> command provides the option of administrating Snap packages in the terminal.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">find</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">search term</samp>
    Searches for the specified term in the package descriptions in the standard Snap package source [https://snapcraft.io](https://snapcraft.io).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">install [--classic]</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp>
    Installs the specified package (requires <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">root</samp> permissions or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sudo</samp>). The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">--classic</samp> option needs to be specified only for some packages that require unrestricted access to the file system and are therefore executed with less strict security rules. You can use the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">--edge</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">--beta</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">--candidate</samp> options to install packages from the specified test channels. (Without these options, the release channel is used.)

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">list</samp>
    Lists previously installed Snap packages.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">refresh</samp>
    Displays all installed packages.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">remove</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp>
    Uninstalls the specified package.

#### Example

The following command installs the Atom editor:

```
user$ sudo snap install --classic atom
atom 1.51.0 installed from Snapcrafters 
```

### snapper [options] command

SUSE distributions use a Btrfs file system for the system partition by default. YaST automatically creates a snapshot before and after each administrative operation. These snapshots can be managed either with the YaST module Snapper or with the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">snapper</samp> command briefly presented here. You can prefix the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">snapper</samp> command to be executed with one or more options:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--iso</samp>
    Formats times in ISO format.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--utc</samp>
    Displays UTC times (Universal Time Coordinated).

The actions that will be executed are specified by subcommands:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">cleanup number|timeline|empty-pre-post</samp>
    Deletes old snapshots, using either a maximum number of snapshots, their age, or their content as a criterion (see also the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/snapper/configs/root</samp> configuration file).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">create</samp>
    Creates a new snapshot.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">delete</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n1-n2</samp>
    Deletes the specified snapshots. The numbers to be used can be found in the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">snapper list</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">list</samp>
    Lists all snapshots.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">rollback [</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">]</samp>
    Makes the specified or the most recent available snapshot the active snapshot (strictly speaking: the Btrfs default subvolume). A subsequent <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">reboot</samp> command restores the system to the state it was in at the time the snapshot was created.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">undochange</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n1..n2</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[files]</samp>
    Undoes the changes made between snapshot <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n1</samp> and snapshot <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n2</samp>—either for all affected files or only for the files specified as parameters.

### sort [options] file

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sort</samp> sorts the specified file and displays the result on the screen. The sort order is defined by the language settings and specifically by the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">LC_COLLATE</samp> environment variable.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-c</samp>
    Checks whether the file is sorted or not.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-f</samp>
    Treats lowercase and uppercase letters as equivalent.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-k</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n1</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">,</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n2</samp>
    Takes into account only the characters between the n1 and n2 columns. The column numbering starts with 1\. Usually, columns are separated by spaces or tab characters, but see <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-t</samp>z. If n2 isn’t specified, all characters from n1 to the end of the line will be considered.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-m</samp>
    Merges two or more presorted files into one large sorted file. This is quicker than putting the files together first and then sorting them.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-n</samp>
    Sorts numbers numerically (i.e., 10 after 9 and not after 1).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-o</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">result file</samp>
    Writes the result to the specified file. The file may match the file to be sorted.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-r</samp>
    Sorts in reverse order.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-t</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">z</samp>
    Specifies the separator between two columns. The default setting is white space, that is, any combination of space and tab characters.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-u</samp>
    Eliminates duplicates from the result (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sort | uniq</samp>).

#### Example

The following command sorts the table of contents passed by <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ls</samp> according to usernames and group names. Files with identical usernames and group names are sorted by size.

```
user$ ls -l | sort -k 3 
```

### source file

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">source</samp> runs the specified file in a <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">bash</samp> script as if the commands it contains were in the place of the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">source</samp> command. Once the file has been executed, the running shell program is continued in the subsequent line. No new shell gets started to run the specified file. All variables, including the parameters list, therefore also apply to the specified file. If <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">exit</samp> is executed in this file, there’s no return to the program with the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">source</samp> command, but the program execution ends immediately.

The short form <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.˽</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file</samp> exists for <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">source</samp>, where ˽ represents a space.

### speaker-test [options]

The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">speaker-test</samp> command from the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">alsa-utils</samp> package helps you track down problems with the audio system. To do this, it generates test tones that are output via the audio system.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-c</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Uses <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> audio channels.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-f</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Plays a sine tone at the specified frequency in Hertz. At the same time, the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-t sine</samp> option must be used.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-s</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Tests only the audio channel with the number <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-t pink|sine|wav</samp>
    Outputs pink noise, a sine wave, or a speech pattern from a WAV file.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-w</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file</samp>
    Plays the specified WAV file. The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">–t wav</samp> option must be used at the same time.

#### Example

The following command outputs the words front left or front right respectively via the left and right audio channels. The speech pattern is loaded from a WAV file. The output can be terminated again by pressing Ctrl+C.

```
user$ speaker-test -t wav -c2 
```

### split [options] file [target file]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">split</samp> splits the specified file into multiple individual files. The output file is separated every n bytes or lines (depending on the options). If no target file is specified, the command returns the files <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">xaa</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">xab</samp>, and so on. If a target file is specified, then this file name is used for the result files together with the character combination <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">aa</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ab</samp>, and so on.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-l</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--lines=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Splits the source file into individual files with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> lines each.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-b</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--bytes=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Separates the output file every <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> bytes. The size can also be specified in KiB, MiB, GiB, or multiples of 1,000 bytes: <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">KB</samp> (1,000 bytes), <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">K</samp> (1,024 bytes), <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">MB</samp> (10⁶ bytes), <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">M</samp> (1,024² bytes), <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">GB</samp> (10⁹ bytes), or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">G</samp> (1,024³ bytes).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-C</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--line-bytes=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Like <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-b</samp>, but the files are split at line boundaries and are therefore usually a few bytes smaller than <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>.

#### Example

In the following example, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">split</samp> splits the archive file <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">backup.tgz</samp> into individual files of 4 GiB each and names them <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">dvd.aa</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">dvd.ab</samp>, and so on:

```
user$ split -C 4G backup.tgz dvd. 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">cat</samp> reassembles the individual files into a complete file:

```
user$ cat dvd.* > total.tgz 
```

### sqlite3 [options] database file
sqlite3 [options] database file "sqlcommand1;sql2;..."

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sqlite3</samp> is normally used as a shell for editing SQLite databases. After starting, you can interactively run SQL commands, whereby all commands must be terminated with a semicolon. In addition to the usual SQL commands, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sqlite3</samp> knows some specific commands that begin with a dot, such as <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">.help</samp> to display a help text or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">.tables</samp> to list all tables in the database. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">.quit</samp> or Ctrl+D terminates <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sqlite3</samp>.

In the second syntax variant, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sqlite3</samp> runs the specified SQL commands directly.

#### Example

The following command determines which music albums are stored in an ownCloud database:

```
user$ sqlite owncloud.db
sqlite> select * from oc_media_albums;
1|Nightclub|1|
2|The Monroe Doctrine|2|
3|The Best Of Herbie Mann|3|
...
sqlite> .quit 
```

### ss [options]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ss</samp> (socket statistics) analyzes the network activity of the local computer. If the command is executed without options, it returns a list of all nonlistening TCP sockets with an active connection. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ss</samp> provides similar functionality to <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">netstat</samp>, but is considered the more modern command and in some cases provides more detailed information.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-4</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-6</samp>
    Takes only IPv4 or IPv6 connections into account.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-a</samp>
    Shows all sockets, both listening and nonlistening.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-e</samp>
    Provides even more details (extended).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-n</samp>
    Displays numerical port numbers, not the names of the services.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-p</samp>
    Specifies which processes use which sockets.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-r</samp>
    Replaces port numbers with the names of the services.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-s</samp>
    Displays only summarized information (summary).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-t</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-u</samp>
    Takes only TCP or UDP connections into account.

#### Example

The following command provides a list of all active TCP sockets for IPv6 connections:

```
user$ ss -6 -t -a
State      Recv-Q Send-Q   Local Address:Port             Peer Address:Port
LISTEN     0      100      :::pop3                       :::*
LISTEN     0      100      :::imap2                      :::*
LISTEN     0      128      :::http                       :::*
LISTEN     0      100      :::smtp                       :::*
LISTEN     0      128      :::https                      :::*
LISTEN     0      100      :::imaps                      :::*
LISTEN     0      100      :::pop3s                      :::*
TIME-WAIT  0      0        ::ffff:5.9.22.28:http   ::ffff:188.192.181.195:50045
TIME-WAIT  0      0        ::ffff:5.9.22.28:http   ::ffff:188.192.181.195:50047
ESTAB      0      46200    ::ffff:5.9.22.28:http   ::ffff:46.10.92.30:22893
FIN-WAIT-1 0      1        ::ffff:5.9.22.28:https  ::ffff:203.134.55.243:51106
... 
```

### ssh [options] computer name
ssh [options] computer name command

In the first syntax variant, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ssh</samp> opens a shell on another computer and thus makes it possible to work interactively on this computer. The second syntax variant runs a single command on the second computer. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ssh</samp> only works if an SSH server is running on the second computer.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-l</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">loginname</samp>
    Uses the specified login name on the second computer instead of the current username. The desired login name can also be entered in the following format: <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ssh loginname@computername</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-L</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">localport:host:hostport</samp>
    Forms a tunnel between the local computer (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">localport</samp> port) and the second computer (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">hostport</samp> port).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-o</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">option=value</samp>
    Enables the transfer of additional options in the same syntax as in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/ssh/ssh_config</samp> file (see <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man ssh_config</samp>). For example, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-o StrictHostKeyChecking=no</samp> causes SSH to refrain from checking the host data with entries already saved in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.ssh/know_host</samp>. This can be helpful for the automated administration of many virtual machines.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-t</samp>
    Forces the use of a pseudo-terminal for the execution of commands in the format <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ssh -t hostname "commands"</samp>. This makes it possible to start interactive programs such as <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">top</samp> via SSH. The connection isn’t stopped until the external command ends (with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">top</samp> this happens by entering Q).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-T</samp>
    Prevents the activation of a pseudo-terminal. You can find an application of this option in the following examples.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-v</samp>
    Provides comprehensive debugging information. If you have login problems, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ssh -v</samp> can often help you find the cause. The option can be specified up to three times (i.e., <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-v -v -v</samp>); <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ssh</samp> then provides even more debugging information.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-X</samp>
    Enables the execution of X programs.

#### Examples

The following command shows how you can log in on an external computer, whereby the username remains unchanged. You can then run commands on the external computer (e.g., your root server).

```
kofler@uranus$ ssh kofler.info
kofler@kofler.info's password: ******** 
```

When you use <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ssh</samp> to connect to another computer for the first time, a warning often appears based on the following pattern:

```
The authenticity of host 'kofler.info (1.2.3.4)' can't be established.
RSA1 key fingerprint is 1e:0e:15:ad:6f:64:88:60:ec:21:f1:4b:b7:68:f4:32.
Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no)? yes
Warning: Permanently added 'kofler.info,1.2.3.4' to the list of known hosts. 
```

The following command shows how I copy the entire <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">/var/www</samp> directory tree of my <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">kofler.info</samp> web server to the local <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">~/bak</samp> directory. Here, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ssh</samp> is used to run a single command (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">tar</samp>). This assumes that <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">kofler@kofler.info</samp> can read all files from <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/var/www</samp>. Basically, it’s also possible to run the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">tar</samp> command with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ssh -l root</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">root</samp> permissions. However, for security reasons, most SSH servers are configured in such a way that a direct <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">root</samp> login is impossible.

The results of <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">tar</samp> are transferred securely to the local computer via SSH and processed further by the second <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">tar</samp> command:

```
kofler@uranus$ ssh kofler.info tar -cf - /var/www | tar -xC ~/bak/ -f -
kofler@kofler.info's password: ******** 
```

To run multiple commands in a script via SSH on another server, you can use the HEREDOC syntax of the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">bash</samp> in combination with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ssh</samp> option <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-T</samp>. The following command changes the password of <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">someaccount</samp> on an external host and then runs a few more commands:

```
#!/bin/bash
pw=strictlysecret
...
ssh -T root@host <<ENDSSH
echo someaccount:$pw | chpasswd
rm -f /etc/file1
cp /root/file2 /userxy/file3
ENDSSH 
```

### ssh-copy-id [options] user@host

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ssh-copy-id</samp> inserts the public key of the local computer into the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.ssh/authorized_keys</samp> file of the host computer. If there’s more than one key, the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ssh-add -L</samp> command decides which key will be transferred.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-i [key file]</samp>
    Transfers the specified key file or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.ssh/id_rsa.pub</samp>.

If the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ssh-copy-id</samp> script isn’t available or the key transfer fails due to the security settings of the external SSH server, the public key file (usually <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.ssh/id_rsa.pub</samp>) must be manually transferred to the server and added to the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.ssh/authorized_keys</samp> file there.

If Fedora, RHEL, or a derivative is running on the host system, the use of <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ssh-copy-id</samp> can lead to the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.ssh</samp> directory and the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">authorized_keys</samp> file being created without the SELinux context information. One of the following two commands on the host computer can help:

```
root# /sbin/restorecon -r /root/.ssh
root# /sbin/restorecon -r /home/username/.ssh 
```

### ssh-keygen [options]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ssh-keygen</samp> generates, manages, and converts cryptographic keys that can be used for authentication with SSH. If <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ssh-keygen</samp> is called without additional options, it generates an RSA key pair with a key length of 2,048 bits. The private and public parts of the key are stored in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.ssh/id_rsa</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.ssh/id_rsa.pub</samp> files.

By default, the access to the key is secured by a password; if you simply press Enter instead of entering the password, this security feature will be omitted. If a private key that isn’t protected by a password falls into the hands of a third party, this third party can easily log on to all computers on which you’ve installed the public part of the key!

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-b</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Determines the key length in bits: 3,072 bits are recommended for RSA keys (as of spring 2025). With 4,096 bits, you’re completely on the safe side. For ECDSA keys, only the values 256, 384, or 521 (not 512!) are possible. With the Curve25519 method, the key length is fixed.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-p</samp>
    Allows you to (re)set the password of a key. If the key already had a password, you must enter the old password before you can set a new password. If the new password is empty, the key can be used without a password in future.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-R</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">hostname</samp>
    Removes the entries stored in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.ssh/known_hosts</samp> for the specified host name.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-t ecdsa|ed25519|rsa</samp>
    Defines the key type. The default type depends on the version and configuration of the SSH package. In the past, these were mostly RSA keys (named after the developers; Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman). In current versions, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ssh-keygen</samp> generates cryptographically more secure Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) keys. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ed25519</samp> is a variant of this (Curve25519). Accordingly, the key files are <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">id_rsa*</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">id_ecdsa*</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">id_ed25519*</samp>.

#### Example

The following command generates an ECDSA key:

```
user$ ssh-keygen -t ecdsa
Generating public/private ecdsa key pair.
Enter file in which to save the key (/root/.ssh/id_ecdsa): <Return>
Enter passphrase (empty for no passphrase): ******** <Return>
Enter same passphrase again:  ******** <Return>
Your identification has been saved in /root/.ssh/id_ecdsa
Your public key has been saved in /root/.ssh/id_ecdsa.pub 
```

### stat [options] files

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">stat</samp> provides detailed information about the specified files, including the access rights in <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ls</samp> notation and as an octal number, the number of blocks used, the time of the last change and the last read access, and so on.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-c formatstring</samp>
    Formats the output according to the format string.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-f</samp>
    Provides information about the file system in which the file is located (instead of information about the file). The following codes, among others, can be used in the character string:

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">%a</samp>: Access rights in octal notation

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">%A</samp>: Access rights in <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ls</samp> notation

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">%C</samp>: SELinux context

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">%F</samp>: File type (file, directory, block device, etc.)

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">%g</samp>: GID of the group to which the file is assigned

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">%G</samp>: Name of the group to which the file is assigned

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">%h</samp>: Number of hard links

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">%n</samp>: File name

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">%s</samp>: File size in bytes

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">%u</samp>: UID of the file owner

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">%U</samp>: Name of the file owner

#### Example

Without options, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">stat</samp> provides a clear compilation of various metadata of a file. With <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-c</samp>, the result can be reduced to individual pieces of information, and in the second example, the result is reduced to the octal access rights and the file name.

```
user$ stat print.pdf
   file: print.pdf
   size: 390758         blocks: 768        EA block: 4096   regular file
device    : fd01h/64769d     Inode: 397971      links: 1
access    : (0664/-rw-rw-r--)  Uid: ( 1000/  kofler)   Gid: ( 1000/  kofler)
context   : unconfined_u:object_r:user_home_t:s0
access    : 2013-09-24 11:35:17.316000000 +0200
modified  : 2013-08-06 17:53:16.083000000 +0200
changed   : 2013-08-06 17:53:16.083000000 +0200
birth     : -
user$ stat -c "%a %n" print.pdf
664 print.pdf 
```

### strace [options] command

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">strace</samp> runs the specified command or program and displays all system functions called by the command. Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">strace</samp> is an important tool for debugging compiled programs. Various options can be used to control which (additional) information you want the program to output.

### strings [options] file

The command extracts character strings from a binary file and displays them. This is useful, for example, if you’re looking for a text (e.g., an error message or a file name) in a program file.

#### Examples

The following command determines all strings in the binary file <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/bin/ls</samp> that contain the word <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">error</samp>:

```
root# strings /bin/ls | grep error
error
error initializing month strings
write error 
```

In the following example, I wanted to find out which keyboard configuration file(s) the systemd program <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">systemd-vconsole-setup</samp> accesses on openSUSE Leap:

```
user$ strings /usr/lib/systemd/systemd-vconsole-setup  | grep keyboard
/etc/sysconfig/keyboard
Failed to read /etc/sysconfig/keyboard: %s 
```

### su [options] [user]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">su</samp> (substitute user) without options switches to <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">root</samp> mode when the password is entered. This means that <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">root</samp> is the active user until the next <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">exit</samp> command.

Optionally, another user can be specified for <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">su</samp> instead of the default <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">root</samp> user. If <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">su</samp> is run by <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">root</samp>, you don’t even have to enter a password when changing users.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-c</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">command</samp>
    Runs only the specified command with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">root</samp> permissions.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-l</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--login</samp>
    When the user changes, the new shell is started as the login shell. This means that all login files are also loaded, which is necessary so that environment variables such as <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">PATH</samp> are configured correctly.

### sudo [options] [var1=value1 var2=value2] command

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sudo</samp> runs a command as if it were being executed by different user (usually this is <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">root</samp>). Thanks to <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sudo</samp>, ordinary users can perform administrative tasks or run system-critical commands without knowing the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">root</samp> password.

Before <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sudo</samp> allows the execution of a program, this right must be specified for a specific user and for a specific program in the [etc/sudoers](#04_001.xhtml_sudoers) file.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-b</samp>
    Starts the specified command in the background.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-E</samp>
    Receives the current content of the environment variable. This option is required to start a program with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">root</samp> permissions in graphics mode on Wayland.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-H</samp>
    Enters the home directory of the user for whose account the command is being executed in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">$HOME</samp> environment variable (usually <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/root</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-i</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--login</samp>
    Starts the shell of the target user (<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-u</samp>) or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">root</samp>. The configuration files of the target user are analyzed, that is, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.profile</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.bashrc</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.zshrc</samp>, and so on.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-K</samp>
    Deletes the saved password. The next time <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sudo</samp> is called, the password must be entered again.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-s</samp>
    Starts the shell specified in local environment variable <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">$SHELL</samp>. This makes it possible to run multiple commands in one shell without having to prefix each command with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sudo</samp>. The shell can be exited using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">exit</samp> or Ctrl+D.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-u</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">user</samp>
    Starts the command for the specified user (instead of <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">root</samp>).

Variables defined in the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sudo</samp> command are passed on as environment variables. For this reason, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sudo var1=x var2=y cmd</samp> is a short notation for the following commands:

```
user$ sudo -s
root# export var1=x
root# export var2=y
root# cmd
root# exit 
```

#### Examples

In the following example, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">sudo</samp> is used to run the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">apt install</samp> command with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">root</samp> permissions:

```
user$ sudo apt install gimp
[sudo] password for user: *******
... 
```

The second example allows you to work interactively as user <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">martin</samp> with his shell and with his local shell settings:

```
user$ sudo -u martin -i
martin$ pwd
/home/martin
martin$ exit
user$ 
```

#### Example with Input/Output Redirection

If you try to run a command with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sudo</samp> that uses input or output redirection, an error may occur:

```
user$ cd /etc/samba
user$ sudo grep -Ev '^#|^;|^$' smb.conf > smb.conf.condensed
-bash: smb.conf.condensed: No authorization 
```

The intention was to eliminate all comments from <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">smb.conf</samp> and save the resulting file in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">smb.conf.condensed</samp>. However, the problem is that the output redirection isn’t executed with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sudo</samp> permissions, but runs within <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">bash</samp> with the rights of the current user. Of course, this user isn’t authorized to change any files in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc</samp>. For this type of constructs to work, you must start a shell with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sudo</samp> and pass the command to this shell:

```
user$ sudo sh -c 'grep -Ev "^#|^;|^$" smb.conf > smb.conf.condensed' 
```

### swaks [options]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">swaks</samp> from the package of the same name stands for Swiss Army Knife for SMTP. The command helps you to test or debug mail servers. I’ll limit myself to two examples here. The first command tests the server’s spam detection and sends an email with a sample spam file:

```
user$ swaks --to hawks@a-company.com --server localhost \
       --data /usr/share/doc/spamassassin/examples/sample-spam.txt 
```

The second command tests the plain authentication procedure and adds an additional header line to the mail. The outputs of the failed login have been shortened for reasons of space.

```
user$ swaks --to hawks@a-company.com --from maria@a-company.com \
        --auth LOGIN --auth-user maria@a-company.com \
        --header-X-Test "test email"
Password: **********
=== Connected to efd.a-company.com.
<-  220 efd.a-company.com ESMTP Postfix (Ubuntu) ...
<-  250-STARTTLS ...
-> AUTH LOGIN
<-  334 VXNlcm5hbWU6
-> bWFyaWFAZWluZS1maXJtYS5kZQ==
<-  334 UGFzc3dvcmQ6
-> YXNk
<** 535 5.7.8 Error: authentication failed: UGFzc3dvcmQ6 
```

### swapon [options] device
swapoff device

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">swapon</samp> activates the specified device (usually a hard disk partition) or the file specified instead as a swap area. The partition or file must first be formatted as a swap area using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mkswap</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">swapon</samp> will be automatically run for all swap areas listed in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/fstab</samp> when Linux gets booted.

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">swapon -s</samp> provides a list of all active swap devices, including usage data. An example of <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">swapon</samp> can be found in the description of [mkswap](#M_001.xhtml_mkswap).

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">swapoff</samp> deactivates the specified swap file or hard disk partition.

### sync

Runs all buffered write operations on the hard disks. If for some reason an orderly shutdown of Linux isn’t possible—if the [shutdown](#S_001.xhtml_shutdown), [reboot](#R_001.xhtml_reboot), and [halt](#H_001.xhtml_halt) commands can’t be executed and the computer doesn’t respond to Alt+Ctrl+Del—then <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sync</samp> should be run just before switching off. But this is only an emergency solution!

### sysctl options

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sysctl</samp> reads the status of kernel parameters or changes their value during operation. Permanent changes must be entered in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/sysctl.conf</samp> file.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-a</samp>
    Provides a list of all available kernel parameters, including the current settings.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-n</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">parameter</samp>
    Returns the current value of the specified kernel parameter.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-p [</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">filename</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">]</samp>
    Processes <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/sysctl.conf</samp> or the specified file and activates all settings saved there.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-w</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">parameter=value</samp>
    Changes the specified parameter. The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-w</samp> option can also be omitted.

#### Example

The following two commands first activate the forwarding functions of the kernel and then the masquerading for the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">eth0</samp> network interface:

```
root# sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
root# iptables -A POSTROUTING -t nat -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE 
```

### systemctl command

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">systemctl</samp> is used to administrate the init process for distributions that use systemd as the init system. This is the case with almost all current distributions. You can use <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">systemctl</samp> to determine a list of all processes managed by systemd, stop or restart individual background services, and more.

Among other things, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">systemctl</samp> distinguishes between ordinary services (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">services</samp>), sockets, devices, mount services, and targets (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">targets</samp>, comparable to Init-V runlevels).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">daemon-reload</samp>
    Loads the configuration files. This command must be run for changes to the systemd configuration files and to [etc/fstab](#04_001.xhtml_fstab) to take effect.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">enable/disable</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp>
    Activates the specified service permanently or deactivates it again. When the command is executed, the corresponding links are created or removed again. With current systemd versions, the additional <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">--now</samp> option causes the relevant service to be started or stopped immediately.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">get-default</samp>
    Determines the default target.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">halt/poweroff/reboot</samp>
    Shuts down or restarts the system.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">is-active</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp>
    Tests whether the specified service is active.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">isolate</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.target</samp>
    Activates the specified target and all services that depend on it. Services that aren’t required are stopped. Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">isolate</samp> has a function that’s similar to a runlevel change in an Init-V system.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">list-timers</samp>
    Provides an overview of active timers, that is, jobs to be run periodically by systemd. For each job, the time of the last and planned next run is specified.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">list-units</samp>
    Provides a list of all services, sockets, targets, and so on managed by systemd. Multipage outputs are routed through <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">less</samp> so that they can be read page by page. If you don’t want this, you must specify the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">--no-pager</samp> option. The result can be filtered using <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--type=...</samp> . Permitted unit types are <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">service</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">socket</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">target</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">device</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mount</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">automount</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">snapshot</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">reload/restart</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp>
    Prompts the process to reload the configuration or restarts the service completely.
