*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">set-default</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.target</samp>
    Defines the default target for future boot processes.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">show</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp>
    Provides more detailed data than <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">status</samp>. The result is structured line by line and can be processed relatively easily by a script.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">start/stop</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp>
    Starts or stops the specified init process or service.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">status</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp>
    Provides status information on the specified service in a clearly legible form.

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">systemctl</samp> applies by default to services that are executed at system level. To edit services at user level, you must pass the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">--user</samp> option. This is useful on modern desktop systems, for example, where Gnome uses systemd.

#### Examples

The following lines show typical <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">systemctl commands</samp>:

```
root# systemctl start   cups  
(start CUPS daemon)
root# systemctl stop    cups  
(stop CUPS daemon)
root# systemctl restart cups  
(restart CUPS daemon)
root# systemctl reload  cups  
(reload configuration of CUPS daemon)
root# systemctl status  cups  
(determine status of CUPS daemon)

root# systemctl enable  cups  
(start CUPS daemon automatically in future)
  Created symlink /etc/systemd/system/sockets.target.wants/cups.socket -> 
                  /lib/systemd/system/cups.socket.
  Created symlink /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/cups.path ->  
                  /lib/systemd/system/cups.path.

root# systemctl disable cups  
(no longer start CUPS daemon automatically)
  Removed /etc/systemd/system/sockets.target.wants/cups.socket.
  Removed /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/cups.path.

root# systemctl isolate reboot.target 
(reboot computer) 
```

### systemd-analyze command

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">systemd-analyze</samp> supports troubleshooting in systemd. You can use various commands to analyze aspects of the systemd configuration or the running systemd units. I’ll limit myself to one example here. The following command lists all running units, sorted by the time it took to initialize them.

```
user$ systemd-analyze blame
12.425s plymouth-quit-wait.service
  7.271s dnf-makecache.service
  2.702s NetworkManager-wait-online.service
  2.028s sys-devices-pci0000:00-0000:00:07.0-virtio3-...device
  2.028s dev-virtio ports-org.spice space.webdav.0.device
     ... 
```

## T

### tac file

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tac</samp> displays the specified text file on the screen in reverse order, that is, the last line first. The strange command name is the result of twisting the letters of the [cat](#C_001.xhtml_cat) command, which outputs text files in the correct order.

### tail [options] file

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tail</samp> displays the last 10 lines of a text file on the screen.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-n</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">lines</samp>
    Outputs the specified number of lines.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-n +</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">offset</samp>
    The output starts with the specified line. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tail -n +2 file</samp> thus outputs the entire file with the exception of the first line.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-f</samp>
    Reads the file regularly and outputs all new lines. In this form, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tail</samp> is particularly suitable for monitoring log files.

#### Example

The following command displays the last 10 lines of <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">syslog</samp>. When new lines are added, they are also displayed so that the entire screen is used after a short time—and not just 10 lines. The execution can be terminated via Ctrl+C.

```
root# tail -f /var/log/syslog 
```

### tar action [options] files
tar action [options] directories

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tar</samp> combines multiple files or entire directories in an archive or extracts their components from this archive. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tar</samp> was originally designed as a tool for reading and writing data on a streamer. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tar</samp> therefore accesses the installed streamer (usually <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dev/tape</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dev/rmt0</samp>) by default. If you want to create an archive in a file, you must specify the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-f</samp> file option.

Because <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tar</samp> also compresses the files to be archived depending on the options specified, its function can be compared with the WinZIP program commonly used on Windows. The typical identifier for archive files is <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.tar</samp>. If the archive file is compressed, the identifiers are usually <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.tgz</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.tar.gz</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.tar.bz2</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.tar.xz</samp>.

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tar</samp> is controlled in two stages: First, an action must be specified that <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tar</samp> is supposed to perform, and second, this action can be controlled by one or more options. Even if actions and options formally look the same, there’s a significant difference: exactly one action must be specified before all other options. While I’ll briefly describe all actions in the following lines, I’ll only list the most important options (see <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man tar</samp>).

On many Unix systems, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tar</samp> is controlled with the same commands and options, but the syntax is different: all commands and options are specified as a block without the usual option dashes, such as <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">tar cvf name.tar path</samp>. GNU <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tar</samp> understands both syntax variants; that is, it’s up to you whether you use option dashes or not.

#### Actions

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-A</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--catenate</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--concatenate</samp>
    Attaches another archive to an existing archive. This option is only suitable for streamers (not for archive files).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-c</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--create</samp>
    Creates a new archive; that is, any existing archive is overwritten.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-d</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--diff</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--compare</samp>
    Compares the files in the archive with the files in the current directory and detects any existing differences.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--delete</samp>
    Deletes files from the archive. Only suitable for archive files (not for streamers).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-r</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--append</samp>
    Adds additional files to the archive.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-t</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--list</samp>
    Displays the table of contents of the archive.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-u</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--update</samp>
    Adds new or modified files to the archive. The option can’t be used for compressed archives. Caution: The archive will always be larger because existing files aren’t overwritten! The new files are simply appended to the end of the archive.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-x</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--extract</samp>
    Extracts the specified files from the archive and copies them to the current directory. The files aren’t deleted from the archive.

#### Options

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-C</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">directory</samp>
    Extracts the files to the specified directory (instead of the current one).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-f</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file</samp>
    Uses the specified file as an archive (instead of accessing the streamer). If a simple hyphen is specified instead of a file name (<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-f -</samp>), the data is forwarded to the standard output channel or read from the standard input. This is particularly useful if two <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tar</samp> commands are to be linked by | (typically for transporting entire file trees).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-g timestamp-file</samp>
    Saves metadata about the files saved with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tar</samp> in the binary timestamp file and only takes into account the files that have changed since then when <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tar</samp> is called again. This option provides an easy way to create incremental backups (see also the last of the following examples).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-j</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--bzip2</samp>
    Compresses or decompresses the entire archive via [](#B_001.xhtml_bzip2)(see also <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-z</samp>!).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-J</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--xz</samp>
    Compresses or decompresses the entire archive via [xz](#X_001.xhtml_xz). This assumes that the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">xz</samp> command is available. Many distributions require the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">xz-utils</samp> package to be installed.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-L</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--tape-length</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Specifies the capacity of the streamer in KiB. If the capacity is exceeded by the size of the archive, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tar</samp> prompts you to change the magnetic tape.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-N</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">date</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--after-date</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">date</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--newer</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">date</samp>
    Archives only files that are more recent than the specified date. This facilitates the creation of incremental backups.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-p</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--preserve-permissions</samp>
    Leaves the access rights unchanged when extracting the files. The option applies by default when <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tar</samp> is executed by <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">root</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-T</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--files-from</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file</samp>
    Archives or extracts the file names specified in the file.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-v</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--verbose</samp>
    Displays all file names on the screen while you’re working. If <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-v</samp> is used in combination with the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">t</samp> command, additional information about the files will be displayed (file size and more). If the option is specified twice, the information will be even more detailed.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-W</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--verify</samp>
    Checks the correctness of the files just archived after writing. These can’t be used for compressed archives.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-z</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--gzip</samp>
    Compresses or decompresses the entire archive using [gzip](#G_001.xhtml_gzip). This option is very useful when it comes to creating <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">*.tgz</samp> files. However, if data is actually stored on a streamer, the option can be dangerous: A single error on the magnetic tape can render the entire archive unusable! Without compression, files are also destroyed, but the damage is usually significantly less. DAT streamers are capable of compressing the data to be processed themselves. This is faster but isn’t as efficient as <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">gzip</samp>.

#### Examples

In the following example, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tar</samp> archives all files from the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Documents</samp> directory and from all subdirectories in the compressed <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">myarchive.tgz</samp> file:

```
user$ tar -czf myarchive.tgz Documents 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tar -tzf</samp> returns a table of contents of the archive. The files within the archive are arranged arbitrarily.

```
user$ tar -tzf myarchive.tgz | less... 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tar -xzf</samp> unpacks the archive and extracts all contained files:

```
user$ cd different-directory/
user$ tar -xzf myarchive.tgz 
```

The following command copies all files from <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dir1</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dir2</samp>. The advantage over a regular <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">cp</samp> command is that symbolic links are copied as such (and not the data referenced by the links). The preceding two commands are particularly suitable for transferring entire file trees from one partition to another.

```
root# (cd /dir1 ; tar cf - .) | (cd /dir2 ; tar xvf -) 
```

The last example shows the creation of incremental backups for the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">images</samp> directory. During the first backup, any existing timestamp file is deleted to perform a complete backup (e.g., always on Sunday nights). The subsequent backups during the night on the following weekdays, and then only take into account the changes that have been made since then.

```
user$ rm backup.timestamps
user$ tar czvf backup-0.tgz -g backup.timestamps images  
(Sun: compl. backup)
user$ tar czvf backup-1.tgz -g backup.timestamps images  
(Mon: changes only)
user$ tar czvf backup-2.tgz -g backup.timestamps images  
(Tue: changes only) 
```

For example, if you want to suppress all <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tar</samp> output in a cron script, including error messages, you must add the following input/output redirection to the command:

```
user$ tar czf backup.tgz directory >/dev/null 2>&1 
```

### tasksel

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tasksel</samp> installs or uninstalls predefined package groups. The command is only available on Debian and Ubuntu distributions.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">install</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">group name</samp>
    Installs all packages of the specified package group.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--list-tasks</samp>
    Determines a list of all defined package groups.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">remove</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">group name</samp>
    Removes all packages in the specified package group. Caution: With older <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tasksel</samp> versions, the packages are removed regardless of dependencies on other packages. This often results in significantly more packages being uninstalled than intended.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--task-packages</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">group name</samp>
    Lists all packages in the specified package group.

#### Example

The following two commands install the Apache web server on Debian or Ubuntu with frequently required extensions and additional programs:

```
root# tasksel install web-server     
(Debian)
root# tasksel install lamp-server    
(Ubuntu) 
```

### tcpdump [options] [filter expression]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tcpdump</samp> from the package of the same name reads the network traffic of an interface, filters it according to criteria, outputs it, or saves it in a file. The command not only handles TCP packets, but also UDP and ICMP packets. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tcpdump</samp> uses the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pcap</samp> library internally to read and filter the network packets.

#### Options

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-a</samp>
    Displays package contents in text format (ASCII).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-c</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Terminates the program after <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> packets.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-i</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">interface</samp>
    Considers only packets that flow via the specified interface. You can obtain a list of possible interfaces using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tcpdump -D</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-n</samp>
    Displays IP addresses instead of host names.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-q</samp>
    Displays less information (quiet).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-r</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file</samp>
    Reads the packages from a file previously saved using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tcpdump -w</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-w</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file</samp>
    Saves the packages in binary format (raw) in the specified file. The file can be read and analyzed again later using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tcpdump -r</samp> or other programs (e.g., Wireshark).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-x</samp>
    Displays package contents in hexadecimal format.

#### Filter Expression

The options can be followed by a filter expression, which can be composed of the following keywords, among others:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">greater</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Considers only packets that are larger than <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> bytes.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">host</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ipadr</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">host</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">hostname</samp>
    Takes into account only packets that use the specified IP address or the corresponding host as the source or target.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">less</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Considers only packets that are smaller than <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> bytes.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">net</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">cidr</samp>
    Considers only packets whose source or destination corresponds to the specified address range in CIDR notation (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">10.0.0.0/24</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">port</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">portrange</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n1-n2</samp>
    Considers only packets that use the specified port numbers as source or target.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">proto ether|fddi|tr|wlan|ip|ip6|arp|rarp|decnet|tcp|udp</samp>
    Takes into account only packets of the specified protocol. The expression can be prefixed with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ip</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ip6</samp> if only IPv4 or IPv6 packets are to be analyzed (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ip6 proto udp</samp>).

The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">host</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">net</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">port</samp> keywords can optionally be prefixed with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">dst</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">src</samp> if the specification refers only to the packet destination or source.

You can link multiple filter conditions via <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">and</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">dust</samp>. You must bracket complex expressions using <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">\(</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">\)</samp>. Alternatively, you can use simple parentheses, but then you have to put the entire filter expression in apostrophes (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">'(port 1 or port 2)'</samp>). Other filter options are described in <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man pcap-filter</samp>.

#### Examples

The following command outputs information about all HTTP packets flowing through the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">wlan0</samp> interface:

```
root# tcpdump -i wlan0 port 80
tcpdump: verbose output suppressed, use -v or -vv for full protocol decode
listening on wlan0, link-type EN10MB (Ethernet)
10:34:33.681218 IP imac.57402 > bpf.tcpdump.org.http:
   Flags [S], seq 755525464, win 65535, options [mss 1460,nop,wscale 5,nop,nop,
   TS val 595975353 ecr 0,sackOK,eol], length 0 10:34:33.681793 IP imac.57403 > bpf.tcpdump.org.http:
   Flags [S], seq 2954861158, win 65535, ... 
```

The second command records the next 100 HTTP packets flowing from or to the IP address 192.139.46.66 in the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">dump.pcap</samp> file:

```
root# tcpdump -i wlan0 -n -c 100 -w dump.pcap port 80 and host 192.139.46.66 
```

The third example determines packets that flow through the bridge <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">br0</samp> and that contain the specified MAC address (as sender or target):

```
root# tcpdump -i br0 -en | grep -i '00:50:56:00:D0:56' 
```

### tee file

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tee</samp> duplicates the standard input, displays one copy, and saves the other in a file. In real life, this is useful if the output of a command is to be observed on the screen but saved in a file at the same time. A simple redirection to a file using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">></samp> would result in nothing being visible on the screen.

#### Example

The following command displays the table of contents of the current directory on the screen and saves it in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">contents</samp> file at the same time:

```
user$ ls -l | tee contents 
```

### telnet [options] host [port]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">telnet</samp> allows interactive communication with a network service via the Telnet protocol. The command is primarily suitable for testing basic network functions. Because the communication is unencrypted, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">telnet</samp> is too insecure to run commands on external servers. For that kind of task, you should use [ssh](#S_001.xhtml_ssh)!

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-4</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-6</samp>
    Accepts only IPv4 or IPv6 addresses.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-l</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">user</samp>
    Uses the specified username (instead of the current username).

#### Example

The following example shows the communication with a mail server running on the local computer:

```
user$ telnet localhost 25
Trying 127.0.0.1...
Connected to localhost.
Escape character is '^]'.
220 kofler.info ESMTP Postfix (Ubuntu)
 helo kofler.info
250 kofler.info
 mail from:<user@kofler.info>
250 2.1.0 Ok
... 
```

Mail servers are often configured in such a way that only the first commands are transmitted unencrypted. The server and client then negotiate the key encryption data (STARTTLS method). At this point, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">telnet</samp> has to opt out; it’s therefore only suitable for testing whether the mail server is active on port 25\. [swaks](#S_001.xhtml_swaks) is more suitable for testing authentication procedures.

### test expression

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">test</samp> is used in <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">bash</samp> scripts to formulate conditions and is mostly used in if queries and loops. Depending on whether the condition is fulfilled, it returns the truth value <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">0</samp> (true) or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">1</samp> (false). Instead of <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">test</samp>, you can also use short notation <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">expression</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">]</samp>. It’s important that you enter spaces before and after the expression!

If you use <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">test</samp> or short notation <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">expression</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">]</samp> as a condition in a branch or loop, you must end the condition with a semicolon, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">if [ " $1" = "abc" ]; then ...</samp>

<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">if</samp> queries can sometimes be replaced by the following formulation: <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[ "$1" = "abc" ] && cmd</samp>. In this case, no semicolon is required. The command won’t be run until the preceding condition has been fulfilled.

#### Character Strings

| <samp class="listingcharacter programmierelement">[ cs ]</samp> | True if the string isn’t empty |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmierelement">[ -n cs ]</samp> | True if the string isn’t empty (like [ cs ]) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmierelement">[ -z cs ]</samp> | True if the string is empty (0 characters) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmierelement">[ cs1 = cs2 ]</samp> | True if the strings match |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmierelement">[ cs1 != cs2 ]</samp> | True if the character strings differ from each other |

The character strings or variables should be placed in quotation marks (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">[ "$1" = "abc" ]</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[ "$a" = "$b" ]</samp>). Otherwise, errors may occur with character strings containing multiple words.

#### Numbers

| <samp class="listingcharacter programmierelement">[ n1 -eq n2 ]</samp> | True if the numbers are equal (equal) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmierelement">[ n1 -ne n2 ]</samp> | True if the numbers aren’t equal (not equal) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmierelement">[ n1 -gt n2 ]</samp> | True if n1 is greater than n2 (greater than) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmierelement">[ n1 -ge n2 ]</samp> | True if n1 is greater than or equal to n2 (greater equal) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmierelement">[ n1 -lt n2 ]</samp> | True if n1 is less than n2 (less than) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmierelement">[ n1 -le n2 ]</samp> | true if n1 is less than or equal to n2 (less equal) |

#### Files (Excerpts)

| <samp class="listingcharacter programmierelement">[ -d file ]</samp> | True if it’s a directory (directory) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmierelement">[ -e file ]</samp> | True if the file exists (exist) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmierelement">[ -f file ]</samp> | True if it’s a simple file (and not a device, directory, etc.) (file) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmierelement">[ -L file ]</samp> | True if it’s a symbolic link |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmierelement">[ -r file ]</samp> | True if the file may be read (read) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmierelement">[ -s file ]</samp> | True if the file is at least 1 byte long (size) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmierelement">[ -w file ]</samp> | True if the file may be changed (write) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmierelement">[ -x file ]</samp> | True if the file may be executed (execute) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmierelement">[ file1 -ef file2 ]</samp> | true if both files have the same I-node (equal file) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmierelement">[ file1 -nt file2 ]</samp> | True if file 1 is newer than file 2 (newer than) |

#### Linked Conditions

| <samp class="listingcharacter programmierelement">[ ! cond ]</samp> | True if the condition isn’t fulfilled |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmierelement">[ cond1 -a cond2 ]</samp> | True if both conditions are fulfilled (and) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter programmierelement">[ cond1 -o cond2 ]</samp> | True if at least one of the conditions is fulfilled (or) |

#### bash Variant [[ expression ]]

While <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">test</samp> and the short notation <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[ expression ]</samp> work in this way in most shells, a variant with two square brackets is also available in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">bash</samp>. Among other things, the following additional comparisons or notations are permitted there:

| <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">[[</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">cs</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">=</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">pattern</samp><samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">* ]]</samp> | True if the string starts with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">pattern</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">[[</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">cs</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">==</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">pattern</samp><samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">*]]</samp> | Same as the preceding entry |
| <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">[[</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">cs</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">=~</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">regex</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">]]</samp> | True if the string matches the regular pattern |
| <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">[[</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">bed1</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">&&</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">bed2</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">]]</samp> | True if both conditions are fulfilled (and) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">[[</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">bed1</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">&#124;&#124;</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">bed2</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">]]</samp> | True if at least one of the conditions is fulfilled (or) |

Another difference is that variables aren’t evaluated in the evaluation in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[[ ]]</samp> (no consideration of wildcard characters such as <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">*</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">?</samp>, correct handling of file names with spaces). This is why <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">[[ -f $filename ]]</samp> works even if the variable contains spaces or special characters.

#### Example

The following mini-script doesn’t fulfill any meaningful task, it only demonstrates the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">test</samp> syntax in notation <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[ condition ] && command</samp>. In the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">for</samp> loop, the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">i</samp> variable is supposed to run through the values from 1 to 10\. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">rest</samp> contains the remainder of the integer division by 2\. With <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[ $rest -eq 1 ]</samp>, the script tests whether the remainder is 1, that is, whether <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">i</samp> is an odd number. In this case, the following commands are skipped via <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">continue</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">echo</samp> outputs the contents of <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">i</samp>. When <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">i</samp> reaches the value 6, the loop gets terminated using <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">break</samp>. Thus, the program outputs the numbers 2, 4, and 6.

```
#!/bin/bash
for i in {1..10}; do
   rest=$[$i%2]
   [ $rest -eq 1 ] && continue
   echo $i
   [ $i -eq 6 ] && break
done 
```

### time command

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">time</samp> runs the specified command and then indicates how much time the execution has taken. The output takes place via the standard error channel and can be changed via the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">TIMEFORMAT</samp> environment variable.

Not only does <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">time</samp> replace the stopwatch, it also breaks down the execution time into three components:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">real</samp>
    Displays the actual execution time.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">user</samp>
    Indicates the CPU time used during the execution of the program outside the kernel.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">sys</samp>
    Indicates the CPU time used during the execution of the program within the kernel.

The total of <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">user</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">sys</samp> indicates how much CPU overhead the execution of the command has caused. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">real</samp> is often (much) greater than the total of <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">user</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">sys</samp>. There can be two reasons for this: First, a lot of other processes usually run in parallel to the command started by <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">time</samp>, which of course also cost computing time. Second, there may be wait times when executing the command, for example, when reading or writing files or when transferring data in the network.

<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">user</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">sys</samp> each refer to a CPU core. If the executed command fully utilizes multiple cores, for example, the total of <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">user</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">sys</samp> can be greater than <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">real</samp>.

#### Example

The following command reads the contents of a logical volume and compresses it using the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">7zr</samp> command (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">p7zip</samp> package). The process takes 24 minutes in idle mode on a multi-core system. If only one core were available, the backup creation would take even longer (approximately 40 minutes).

```
root# time dd if=/dev/vg830/lv3 bs=4M | 7zr a -si lv3.img.7z
real  24m53.424s
user  38m37.841s
sys    0m30.446s 
```

#### Alternatives

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">time</samp> is a command integrated into the shell. The earlier description refers to the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">bash</samp> variant. If you work in <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">zsh</samp>, the output of <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">time</samp> looks a little different.

### timedatectl [options] [command]

The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">timedatectl</samp> command changes the time and the active time zone for distributions with the systemd init system. The changed settings take effect immediately; they are also saved permanently in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/localtime</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">list-timezones</samp>
    Provides a list of all known time zones.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">set-local-rtc 0|1</samp>
    Indicates whether the computer’s clock contains the local time or GMT time.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">settime datetime</samp>
    Resets the date and time. The hardware clock of the computer is also changed accordingly. The time must be entered in the format <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">2025-12-31 23:59:59</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">set-timezone</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp>
    Sets the desired time zone.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">status</samp>
    Displays the time, time zone, and various other time data, such as the next change between daylight savings time and winter time.

#### Example

The following commands first show the current time data and then change the time zone:

```
root# timedatectl status
      Local time: 2025-05-18 09:08:37 CEST
  Universal time: 2025-05-18 07:08:37 UTC
        RTC time: 2025-05-17 18:51:42
       Time zone: Europe/Vienna (CEST, +0200)
  ...
root# timedatectl set-timezone Europe/Paris 
```

### timeout [options] time span command

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">timeout</samp> runs the specified command and ends it automatically if it runs for longer than the specified time. The time span is specified as a floating-point number with the trailing letter <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">s</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">m</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">h</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">t</samp> in seconds, minutes, hours, or days (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">0.5h</samp> for half an hour).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-k</samp>
    Terminates the program that has been running for too long via a <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">KILL</samp> signal. By default, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">timeout</samp> uses a <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">TERM</samp> signal, but this can be ignored.

#### Example

In the following command, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">scp</samp> has 30 seconds to transfer a file to another computer. After that, the process gets canceled.

```
user$ timeout 30s scp localfile myserver:destinationdir/ 
```

### tldr command

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tldr</samp> stands for too long, didn't read and is a subtle criticism of the often enormously long <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man</samp> pages. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tldr</samp> tries to do better and provides a few instructive examples of popular commands. The command is therefore a great addition to this book. The outputs are highlighted in color in the terminal.

```
user tldr rsync
Transfer files either to or from a remote host (but not between two remote hosts), by default using SSH.  To specify a remote path, use user@host:path/to/file_or_directory.  More information: https://download.samba.org/pub/rsync/rsync.1.
- Transfer a file:
  rsync path/to/source path/to/destination

- Use archive mode (recursively copy directories, copy symlinks without
  resolving, and preserve permissions, ownership and modification times):
  rsync --archive path/to/source path/to/destination

- Compress the data as it is sent to the destination, display verbose
  and human-readable progress, and keep partially transferred files if
  interrupted:
  rsync --compress --verbose --human-readable --partial --progress \
    path/to/source path/to/destination

- (five more examples of use) 
```

### top [q]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">top</samp> displays the list of all running processes every five seconds, whereby the processes are sorted according to their share of the computing time. If the optional <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">q</samp> parameter is specified during the call, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">top</samp> constantly updates the list and takes up the entire free computing time. Pressing Q terminates the program.

#### Alternatives

More convenient and visually appealing alternatives to <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">top</samp> are the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">btop</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">htop</samp> commands, which must be installed separately for most distributions. The commands provide various additional functions, color the output, and allow horizontal and vertical scrolling through the running processes.

If you’re not interested in the memory consumption and CPU usage, but in the I/O activity or the energy efficiency of the running processes, you should take a look at the description of [iotop](#I_001.xhtml_iotop) or [powertop](#P_001.xhtml_powertop).

### touch [options] files

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">touch</samp> changes the time of the last change saved with the file. If the command is used without options, the current time is saved as the change time. If the file doesn’t yet exist, a new file that’s 0 bytes long will be created.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-r</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file</samp>
    Uses the saved modification time of the specified file.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-t</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">time</samp>
    Saves the specified time. You must use the format <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[[CC]YY]MMDDhhmm[.ss]</samp> for the time specification, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">202512311730</samp> for 12/31/2025 at 5.30 pm. Alternatively, you can also specify the time as a character string with the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-d</samp> option. More readable formats are permitted, which you can find out about via <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">info touch</samp>.

#### Example

In this example, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">touch</samp> is used to compare the modification times of all files in a directory with the files in a second directory. This is useful, for example, if you’ve forgotten the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-a</samp> option for a larger <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">cp</samp> command and the copied files now all have the current date.

```
user$ cd target directory
user$ find . -type f  -exec touch -r /source directory/{} {} \; 
```

### tr [options] zk1 [zk2] [ < source > target]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tr</samp> replaces all characters of string 1 in the specified source file with the corresponding characters of string 2\. The two-character strings should be the same length. Characters that don’t appear in the first string remain unchanged. It’s not possible to replace a single character with multiple characters (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ö</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">"o</samp>)—for this you must use commands such as [recode](#R_001.xhtml_recode) or [sed](#S_001.xhtml_sed).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-d</samp>
    Deletes the characters specified in string 1\. String 2 doesn’t need to be specified.

#### Example

In the following example, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tr</samp> replaces all lowercase letters with uppercase letters and displays the result in the terminal (in the standard output):

```
user$ tr a-zäöü A-ZÄÖÜ < text file 
```

### traceroute[6] [options] target address

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">traceroute</samp> provides a list of all stations on the path of a TCP/IP packet from the local computer to the target address. The total runtime is specified for each station (by default for three attempts). <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">traceroute</samp> only works if UDP port 33434 isn’t blocked by a firewall on the way to the target address. In this case, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">traceroute</samp> only returns three stars instead of the stopover details.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-4</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-6</samp>
    Uses the IPv4 or IPv6 protocol only. By default, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">traceroute</samp> automatically uses the appropriate protocol. If a host name is associated with both an IPv4 and an IPv6 address, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">traceroute</samp> prefers IPv4. For <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">traceroute6</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-6</samp> automatically applies.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-m</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Determines the maximum number of intermediate stations (30 by default).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-n</samp>
    Shows only the IP number of the intermediate stations (not the host name).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-p</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Uses the specified UDP port (33434 by default).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-q</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Sends <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> packets and measures the response times for each packet (3 by default).

#### Example

The following command shows the stations between my local computer and my web server. At some stations, the IP packets are routed via different routers, which indicates a redundant network connection.

```
root# traceroute kofler.info
traceroute to kofler.info (213.239.211.2), 30 hops max, 60 byte packets
 1  dsldevice.lan (10.0.0.138)  14.116 ms  13.376 ms  13.112 ms
 2  62.47.95.239 (62.47.95.239)  25.650 ms  27.489 ms  29.245 ms
...
 9  hos-tr3.ex3k16.rz6.hetzner.de (213.239.252.8)  48.315 ms
    hos-tr4.ex3k16.rz6.hetzner.de (213.239.252.136)  49.034 ms
    hos-tr2.ex3k16.rz6.hetzner.de (213.239.229.136)  51.231 ms
10  kofler.info (213.239.211.2)  52.069 ms  54.640 ms  55.757 ms 
```

### trap [command] signal

The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">bash</samp> command <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">trap</samp> runs the specified command when the shell receives the specified signal. If no command is specified, the program or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">bash</samp> ignores the signal in question. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">trap -l</samp> returns a list of all possible signals and the identification numbers assigned to them. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">trap</samp> is usually used for error protection in shell scripts.

#### Example

The following mini-script runs in an endless loop that can’t be interrupted by pressing Ctrl+C. However, you can end the script using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">kill</samp>, for example.

```
#!/bin/bash
trap 'echo "Ctrl+C will be ignored!"' SIGINT
while true
do
  sleep 1
done 
```

### tree [options] [start directory]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tree</samp> from the package of the same name displays the hierarchy of the directory tree starting from the current or specified start directory.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-a</samp>
    By default, outputs files too instead of directories only.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-L</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Considers only the first <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> hierarchy levels.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-x</samp>
    Remains in the current file system and doesn’t consider <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mount</samp> directories or links to other file systems.

### truncate [options] files

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">truncate</samp> reduces or enlarges files. The file is simply cut off when it’s reduced in size. Caution: you’ll lose data in this process! When the file is enlarged, a corresponding number of 0 bytes are added to the file. With most file systems, this doesn’t change the space required on the data medium because the file will be recognized as a sparse file. If you want to physically fill a file with zeros, you must use the [dd](#D_001.xhtml_dd) command. If the name of a file that doesn’t yet exist is passed to <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">truncate</samp>, the command creates the file in the desired size.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-s</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Specifies the desired size in bytes. If the number is followed by the letters <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">K</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">M</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">G</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">T</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">truncate</samp> multiplies the number by 1,024; 1,048,576; and so on. Alternatively, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">KB</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">MB</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">GB</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">TB</samp> stand for 1,000; 1,000,000; and so on. Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">10K</samp> corresponds to 10,240 bytes, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">10KB</samp> corresponds to 10,000 bytes.

#### Example

In the following example, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file</samp> is first filled with 1 MiB of random data. The file is then enlarged to 2 MiB by using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">truncate</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ls -l</samp> actually shows a size of 2 MiB, but <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">dd</samp> proves that the file only takes up 1 MiB of space on the hard disk or SSD. The space requirement only increases if data other than zeros is written to the file later.

```
user$ dd if=/dev/urandom of=file bs=1024 count=1024
user$ truncate -s 2M file
user$ ls -l file
-rw-r--r-- 1 kofler users 2097152 19\. Nov 14:30 file
user$ du -h file
1,0M    file 
```

### tty

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tty</samp> displays the device name of the active terminal (for the text consoles: <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dev/tty1</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">tty6</samp>, for shell windows under X <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dev/pts/</samp>n).

### tune2fs [options] device

You can use <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tune2fs</samp> to change various system parameters of an ext2/ext3/ext4 file system.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-c</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Specifies after how many <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mount</samp> operations the partition should be checked for errors when booting. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">0</samp> means that a check should never be carried out.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-i</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Specifies how often (in terms of days) the partition should be checked for errors during booting. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">0</samp> means that a check should never be carried out.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-l</samp>
    Displays information on the specified file system, but doesn’t change anything.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-m</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Specifies what percentage of the disk should be reserved for <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">root</samp> data (usually 5% for <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mke2fs</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-U</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">new-uuid</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-U random</samp>
    Gives the file system a new UUID.

#### Example

The following command causes the file system in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dev/sda1</samp> partition to be checked only once a year or after 200 <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mount</samp> operations:

```
root# tune2fs -i 365 -c 200 /dev/sda1
Set the maximum number of mounts to 200
Set the interval between checks to 31536000 seconds 
```

### type command

The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">bash</samp> command <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">type</samp> determines whether the specified command is a shell command (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">cd</samp>), a self-defined function, or an <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">alias</samp> abbreviation. The command is hashed message means that this is a Linux command that has already been executed in this session and whose path name has been memorized by the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">bash</samp> in a hashed directory.

#### Example

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">cd</samp> is a command integrated into the shell:

```
root# type cd
cd is a shell builtin 
```

## U

### ubuntu-security-status [options]

In the past, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ubuntu-security-status</samp> displayed information on the maintenance status of the installed packages. The command has been replaced by [pro](#P_001.xhtml_pro) <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">security-status</samp> (see that entry).

### ufw [options] command

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ufw</samp> is an Ubuntu-specific command for firewall configuration. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ufw</samp> is installed by default on Ubuntu and its derivatives, but it isn’t activated. If you want to use <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ufw</samp> for firewall configuration, you must first activate the firewall using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ufw enable</samp>.

The following subcommands are available for configuring the firewall. They can be combined with the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">--dry-run</samp> option. In this case, no changes are made. The option is useful for testing the syntax of complex commands.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">allow|deny [on</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">interface</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">]</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">port</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">protocol</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/"</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">app name</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">"</samp>
    Allows or blocks a port (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">22</samp>), a protocol (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ssh</samp>), or a program for which there are separate rule files (see <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ufw app list</samp>).

    The rule can optionally be formulated only for a specific network interface, such as <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">on eth0</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man ufw</samp> lists various other options for formulating rules that only apply to incoming or outgoing packets or only for specific protocols or IP versions (e.g., for <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">tcp</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">udp</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ipv6</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">app info "</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">app name</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">"</samp>
    Provides detailed information on a <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ufw</samp> rule file.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">app list</samp>
    Provides a list of all programs for which there are ufw <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">rule</samp> files in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/uf2/applications.d</samp> directory.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">default allow|deny|reject [incoming|outgoing|routed]</samp>
    Defines the default behavior of the firewall. If <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">incoming|outgoing|routed</samp> isn’t specified, the behavior of the input filter will get changed. By default—if the firewall is activated at all—the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">deny</samp> behavior applies for the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">incoming</samp> filter and the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">allow</samp> behavior for the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">outgoing</samp> filter.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">disable</samp>
    Deactivates the firewall. All network traffic can flow unhindered.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">enable</samp>
    Activates the firewall.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">reload/reset</samp>
    Reloads all firewall rules or performs a complete restart of the firewall.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">status [verbose]</samp>
    Displays the status of the firewall.

#### Example

The following commands first allow the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ssh</samp> service and then activate the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ufw</samp> firewall. An existing SSH connection shouldn’t be interrupted by this. However, all other server services will be blocked from now on.

```
root# ufw allow ssh
root# ufw enable
root# ufw status verbose
Status: Active
Logging: on (low)
Default setting:  deny (incoming), allow (outgoing), disabled (sent)
For                        Action      From
-–                         ------      ---
22                         ALLOW IN    Anywhere
22 (v6)                    ALLOW IN    Anywhere (v6) 
```

### ulimit option limit

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ulimit</samp> limits the system resources used by the shell and the processes utilized by it.

Sizes are generally given in KiB. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ulimit</samp> is often preset in [etc/profile](#04_001.xhtml_profile).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-c</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">memory</samp>
    Limits the size of coredumps, that is, the memory image that is automatically saved on the hard disk in the event of a program crash.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-d</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">memory</samp>
    Limits the memory for the data segment of processes.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-f</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">file size</samp>
    Prevents the creation of files that are larger than the specified limit. Doesn’t work with all file systems.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-s</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">memory</samp>
    Limits the stack memory.

### umask [mask]

The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">umask bash</samp> command controls the access rights used to create new files. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">umask</samp> memorizes an octal numerical value for this purpose, which is subtracted from the default access rights of new files or directories.

Linux actually requires that new files be assigned access bits <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">rw-rw-rw</samp> (octal 666). New directories and program files created by a compiler are automatically assigned access bits <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">rwxrwxrwx</samp> (777). These basic settings are too permissive for practical work. That’s why all Linux shells provide for the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">umask</samp> setting. This is a numerical value that specifies the access bits that are subtracted from the standard access bits.

The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">umask</samp> setting is predefined across the entire system and is set in [etc/profile](#04_001.xhtml_profile) or in [etc/bashrc](#04_001.xhtml_bashrc), depending on the distribution. Different values often apply for <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">root</samp> and for all other users. In Ubuntu, the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">umask</samp> value is defined by the PAM system; the default value is stored in [etc/login/defs](#04_001.xhtml_login.defs).

#### Examples

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">umask</samp> without additional parameters shows the current setting:

```
user$  umask  
(Debian, openSUSE, Ubuntu)
0022
user$  umask  
(Fedora, RHEL)
0002 
```

The second example shows the effects on new files and directories if you change the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">umask</samp> value to <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">027</samp>. New files thus receive the access rights 666 - 026 = 640 = <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">rw-r-----</samp>, and new directories have 777 - 027 = 750 = <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">rwxr-x---</samp>.

```
user$ umask 27
user$ touch new-file
user$ mkdir new-directory
user$ ls -ld new*
-rw-r----- ... user user ... new-file
drwxr-x--- ... user user ... new-directory 
```

### umount device
umount directory

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">umount</samp> removes a file system from the Linux directory tree. The file system is specified either by the device name of the data medium or by specifying the directory in which the file system is integrated into the directory tree. The command can only be run by <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">root</samp>. It results in an error message if there are still open files on the file system.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-f</samp>
    Forces the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">umount</samp> process (useful for NFS directories that are no longer accessible).

### unalias abbreviation

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">unalias</samp> deletes the specified abbreviation. If the command is called with the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-a</samp> option, it deletes all known abbreviations. The handling of abbreviations is explained in the description of [alias](#A_001.xhtml_alias).

### uname [options]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">uname</samp> displays the name of the operating system (i.e., Linux). Other information can also be displayed by specifying options.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-a</samp>
    Displays all available information, namely the operating system, version number, date and time, and processor.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-m</samp>
    Provides only the CPU platform (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">i686</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">x86_64</samp> for 64-bit systems).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-r</samp>
    Returns only the kernel version.

#### Example

This computer is running a 64-bit kernel that was compiled in March 2025:

```
root# uname -a
Linux utmf39 6.7.9-200.fc39.aarch64 #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC
Wed Mar  6 20:03:23 UTC 2025 aarch64 GNU/Linux 
```

### uncompress file

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">uncompress</samp> decompresses a file compressed via [compress](#C_001.xhtml_compress). The file identifier <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.Z</samp> is automatically removed. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">uncompress</samp> is a link to <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">compress</samp>, whereby the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-d</samp> option is automatically activated.

### unexpand text file > result

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">unexpand</samp> replaces multiple spaces in the specified text file with tab characters and writes the result to the standard output. The command is the counterpart to [expand](#E_001.xhtml_expand), which replaces tab characters with spaces.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-a</samp>
    Replaces all spaces, not just those at the beginning of a line.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-t</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Specifies the number of characters per tab position (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">8</samp> by default).

### uniq [options] file

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">uniq</samp> outputs the lines of a text file to the standard output, eliminating consecutive lines with the same name. For presorted files, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">uniq</samp> eliminates all lines that occur more than once.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-c</samp>
    Indicates for each line how often it was found.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-d</samp>
    Outputs the duplicates only (but not lines that only occur once).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-u</samp>
    Outputs only lines that have no duplicates (i.e., are unique).

#### Example

[sort](#S_001.xhtml_sort) sorts the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">test</samp> file, and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">uniq</samp> eliminates duplicate lines and saves the result in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">test1</samp>:

```
user$ sort test | uniq > test1 
```

### unset variable

The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">bash</samp> command <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">unset</samp> deletes the specified variable.

### until condition; do
commands done

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">until</samp> creates loops in <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">bash</samp> scripts. The loop keeps running until the specified condition is met. The loop criterion is the return value of the command that is specified as a condition. Comparisons and tests are performed using the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">test</samp> command or its short form in square brackets.

#### Example

The example shows the formulation of a simple loop with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">until</samp>:

```
user$ i=1; until [ $i -gt 3 ]; do echo $i; i=$[$i+1]; done
1
2
3 
```

### unxz [options] files

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">unxz</samp> from the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">xz-utils</samp> package decompresses the files previously compressed using [xz](#X_001.xhtml_xz). The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.xz</samp> file extension gets removed.

### unzip [options] archive.zip [file1 file2]

The command extracts files from ZIP archives, which are particularly common in the Windows world. If the files to be extracted aren’t explicitly listed, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">unzip</samp> unpacks all files in the archive. If you want to create your own ZIP archives on Linux, you must use [zip](#Z_001.xhtml_zip).

#### Example

The following command extracts the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">print.pdf</samp> file from <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">archive.zip</samp>. If there are other files in this archive, they won’t be affected.

```
user$ zipinfo archive.zip
Archive:  archive.zip
Zip file size: 5870439 bytes, number of entries: 4
-rw-r--r--  3.0 unx  3594936 bx defN 24-Mar-24 19:06 ebook.pdf
-rw-r--r--  3.0 unx  3245639 bx defN 26-Mar-24 12:54 print.pdf
...
user$ unzip archive.zip print.pdf
Archive:  ../archive.zip
  inflating: print.pdf 
```

### update-alternatives [options] command

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">update-alternatives</samp> manages the links in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/alternatives</samp> directory. These links determine the active version of multiple programs installed in parallel with the same function (e.g., editors or Java environments). The command is usually executed by the (de)installation scripts of the relevant packages, but can of course also be used interactively. On Red Hat or Fedora systems, the command is also available as [alternatives](#A_001.xhtml_alternatives).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--auto</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp>
    Activates the automatic mode for the command. This means the command with the highest priority value is automatically active.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--config</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp>
    Shows the available alternatives to the specified command. You then interactively specify which alternative should be active in future. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">update-alternatives</samp> then adjusts the links accordingly and switches to manual mode for the command.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--display</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp>
    Provides a list of all installed alternatives to the specified command.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--install ...</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--remove ...</samp>
    Installs or removes an alternative for a command. These commands are usually only used in the (de)installation script of a package.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">--set</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name command path</samp>
    Sets the command specified via <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">command path</samp> as the default program for <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp>.

#### Example

The following command defines <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/usr/bin/jmacs</samp> as the default editor:

```
root# update-alternatives --set editor /usr/bin/jmacs 
```

This example only works on Debian and Ubuntu systems. On Fedora and RHEL, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">update-alternatives</samp> is also available, but the standard editor can’t be changed (whereas the Java version, the mail client, and others can). To configure the default editor, you must add the line <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">export EDITOR=/usr/bin/jmacs</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.bashrc</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.zshrc</samp>, replacing <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">jmacs</samp> with your favorite program.

### update-grub

This script is only available on Ubuntu and Debian. It runs the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/grub.d/*</samp> configuration scripts and creates the new GRUB menu file; <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/boot/grub/grub.cfg</samp>. On other distributions, you need to run the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg</samp> command instead of <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">update-grub</samp>.

### update-initramfs [options]

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">update-initramfs</samp> is responsible for creating, updating, or deleting initrd files in Debian and Ubuntu. The initrd files contain kernel modules that are loaded by GRUB during system startup. These files are configured using the files in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/initramfs-tools</samp> directory. For Fedora, RHEL, and SUSE, you can use the [dracut](#D_001.xhtml_dracut) command instead of <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">update-initramfs</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-c</samp>
    Creates a new initrd file for the kernel version that is specified with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-k</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-d</samp>
    Deletes the initrd file for the kernel version specified with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-k</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-k</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">version name</samp>
    Specifies the kernel version to be processed. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-k all</samp> causes <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">update-initramfs</samp> to process the initrd files of all installed kernel versions.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-u</samp>
    Updates the initrd file of the latest kernel version or the kernel version specified with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-k</samp>.

#### Example

The following command creates a new initrd file for kernel version 6.6.7\. The kernel file has the file name <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/boot/vmlinuz-6.6.7-generic</samp>, and the name of the resulting initrd file is <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/boot/initrd.img 6.6.7-generic</samp>.

```
root# update-initramfs -c -k 6.6.7-generic 
```

### updatedb

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">updatedb</samp> creates an index directory for the [locate](#L_001.xhtml_locate) command. The index contains a list of all files contained in the entire file system. The command is usually executed automatically once a day by a cron job. Its execution requires <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">root</samp> permissions. Depending on the distribution, the file database is saved in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/var/lib</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/var/lib/slocate</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/var/lib/mlocate</samp> directory.

### uptime [options]

Without further options, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">uptime</samp> indicates how long the computer has been running, how many people are currently logged in, and what the average load was in the last minute, in the last 5 minutes, or in the last 15 minutes (load average).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-p</samp>
    Displays the uptime period in a clearly legible format (pretty).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-s</samp>
    Reveals when the computer was started (since).

#### Example

The server on which the following command was executed has been running for more than three months. Such long uptimes are only reasonable if there were no security-relevant kernel patches during this time or if these patches were integrated into the kernel with a live patch system. On Ubuntu servers, you can determine this via [canonical-livepatch](#C_001.xhtml_canonical-livepatch).

```
user$ uptime
 15:48:11 up 104 days, 23 min,  1 user,  load average: 0.15, 0.12, 0.05 
```

### useradd [options] name

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">useradd</samp> sets up a new user. On Debian and Ubuntu, it’s better to use [adduser](#A_001.xhtml_adduser).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-b "</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">basedir</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">"</samp>
    Defines the basis for the user directories (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/home</samp> by default).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-c "</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">full name</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">"</samp>
    Specifies the full name of the new user.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-g</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">group</samp>
    Indicates the main group (primary group) of the user.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-G</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">groupA,groupB,groupC</samp>
    Determines all supplementary groups of the user.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-m</samp>
    If a home directory doesn’t yet exist (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/home/name</samp>), it will be created. All files from <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/skel</samp> will be copied there. On Fedora and RHEL, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-m</samp> applies by default due to the default settings in [etc/login/defs](#04_001.xhtml_login.defs) and doesn’t need to be specified. In such cases, the creation of the home directory can be prevented by <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-M</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-u</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Assigns the specified UID (user identifier) to the user if it’s still available.

#### Example
