    Specifies whether the resolver library returns all entries for each host (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">on</samp>) or only the first matching entry (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">off</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">order a,b,c...</samp>
    Specifies in which order which procedures are to be used for host name determination. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">bind</samp> means that the resolver library falls back on the nameserver set in [etc/resolv.conf](#04_001.xhtml_resolv.conf). <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">hosts</samp> allows the evaluation of [etc/hosts](#04_001.xhtml_hosts) . <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">nis</samp> causes the obsolete Network Information Service to be used.

#### Example

The standard configuration for <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">host.conf</samp> looks like the following listing for most distributions. The resolver library first analyzes the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/hosts</samp> file and then contacts the nameserver set in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">resolv.conf</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">multi</samp> line allows multiple IP addresses to be assigned to a host name specified in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/hosts</samp>.

```
order hosts, bind
multi on 
```

### /etc/hostname

The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/hostname</samp> file contains the full name of the computer, which consists of the host name and the domain name, for almost all common Linux distributions. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/hostname</samp> on the Ubuntu server installation for my web server therefore contains the following text:

```
kofler.info 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/hostname</samp> is evaluated when the computer is started. Changes can be made using the [hostname](#H_001.xhtml_hostname) command. With systemd-compatible distributions, the host name can also be set permanently using the [hostnamectl](#H_001.xhtml_hostnamectl) command.

### /etc/hosts

<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/hosts</samp> assigns IP addresses to their host names. The file normally only contains entries for <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">localhost</samp> and, in the case of statically configured servers, for the host name. In the past, the file was used to list other computers within the local network. Today, however, even in small networks, this function is performed by a router or a local nameserver, such as Bind or dnsmasq.

The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/hosts</samp> file contains line-by-line entries based on the following pattern:

```
ip-addr  hostname1 hostname2 hostname3 ... 
```

The minimal variant looks like this:

```
127.0.0.1   localhost 
```

In most Linux distributions, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">localhost</samp> is also defined for IPv6\. The following lines show the default settings on Fedora and RHEL:

```
127.0.0.1   localhost localhost.localdomain localhost4 localhost4.localdomain4
::1         localhost localhost.localdomain localhost6 localhost6.localdomain6 
```

In the case of a static network configuration, for example, on a root server, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">hosts</samp> can also contain an entry with the IP address and the host name of the computer:

```
211.212.213.214  abc-company.com abc-company 
```

### /etc/network/interfaces

The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/network/interfaces</samp> file (ENI for short) contains the network configuration for Debian distributions. With Ubuntu, the NetworkManager and Netplan take care of the network configuration. In current versions of the Raspberry Pi OS, the NetworkManager has sole control over the network.

#### Interaction with the NetworkManager

For desktop installations, the file is normally almost empty and only contains the settings for the loopback interface:

```
# loopback interface
auto lo
  iface lo inet loopback 
```

The NetworkManager is responsible for all other interfaces.

#### IPv4 Configuration

The situation is completely different for server installations or on computers with a static network configuration. In this case, the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">auto name</samp> line initiates a configuration block for each network interface that will be activated when the computer is started. The subsequent <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">iface</samp> name options line describes the basic configuration of the interface. The other parameters then follow depending on the configuration type.

If the interface obtains the IP data from a DHCP server, the configuration is very brief:

```
# IPv4 network interface with DHCP
auto eth0
iface eth0 inet dhcp 
```

In a static configuration, the network parameters are specified line by line using multiple keywords, the meaning of which is self-explanatory. The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">dns-nameservers</samp> keyword is only used on Ubuntu to configure the nameservers. The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">resolvconf</samp> package is responsible for the evaluation. On Debian, however, you must set the nameserver yourself in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/resolv.conf</samp>.

```
# IPv4 network interface, static configuration
auto eth0
iface eth0 inet static
  address         211.212.213.37
  netmask         255.255.255.224
  gateway         211.212.213.1
  dns-nameservers 211.222.233.244 212.232.234.245 
```

You can activate changes to a single interface using [ifup](#I_001.xhtml_ifup) <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">xxx</samp>, replacing <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">xxx</samp> with the interface name.

#### IPv6 Configuration

If you also want to use IPv6, you can simply define the relevant interface a second time in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/network/interfaces</samp> using the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">inet6</samp> keyword. The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">auto</samp> keyword specifies that the IPv6 configuration takes into account the router advertisement of the gateway or IPv6 router.

```
# IPv4 configuration via DHCP, IPv6 configuration via router advertisement
auto eth0
iface eth0 inet dhcp
iface eth0 inet6 auto 
```

If the IPv6 gateway uses a DHCPv6 server, the correct method is <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">dhcp</samp>. If, in addition, the router address is to be configured via router advertisement, the additional <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">accept_ra 1</samp> option is required. This is the case, for example, if you use <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">dnsmasq</samp> with the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">enable-ra</samp> option as the DHCP server.

```
# IPv4 and IPv6 configuration via DHCP
auto eth0
iface eth0 inet dhcp
iface eth0 inet6 dhcp
 accept_ra 1 
```

For a static configuration, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">interfaces</samp> must look as follows:

```
# IPv4 and IPv6 configuration static
auto eth0
iface eth0 inet static
  ... (IPv4 configuration as before)
iface eth0 inet6 static
  address 2a01:4f8:161:107::2
  netmask 64
  gateway fe80::1 
```

#### Wi-Fi and WPA Configuration

NetworkManager normally takes care of Wi-Fi interfaces and WPA authentication on notebooks. However, it’s also possible to make the configuration directly in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/interfaces</samp>. This is particularly common on embedded devices or minicomputers such as the Raspberry Pi.

Wi-Fi interfaces are basically configured in the same way as Ethernet interfaces. You control the interaction with the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">wpa_supplicant</samp> program for authentication using <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">wpa</samp> parameters. In the simplest case, the configuration can look as follows:

```
# File /etc/network/interfaces
...
auto wlan0
iface wlan0 inet dhcp
  wpa-ssid "wlan-name"
  wpa-psk "top secret" 
```

You use <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">wpa-ssid</samp> to specify the name of your Wi-Fi network. (SSID stands for Service Set Identifier.) <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">wpa-psk</samp> specifies the Wi-Fi password, whereby it’s assumed that the encryption is performed using the Wi-Fi Protected Access (WPA) method with preshared keys. This is the rule in the home sector.

If more parameters need to be set, it’s common practice to save the authentication data in an external file. The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">interfaces</samp> parameters then has the following structure:

```
# /etc/network/interfaces (manual WiFi configuration with WPA)
auto wlan0
iface wlan0 inet dhcp
  wpa-conf /etc/wpa_supplicant/wpa_supplicant.conf 
```

Here, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">wpa-conf</samp> specifies the location of a WPA configuration file, which must correspond to the syntax of [etc/wpa/supplicant/wpa_supplicant.conf](#04_001.xhtml_wpa_supplicant.conf).

If there’s a graphical user interface for Wi-Fi configuration to manage the connection data to multiple Wi-Fi networks, as on the Raspberry Pi OS, you must use the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">wpa-roam</samp> keyword:

```
# /etc/network/interfaces (WiFi default configuration on Raspberry Pi OS)
allow-hotplug wlan0
iface wlan0 inet manual
  wpa-roam /etc/wpa_supplicant/wpa_supplicant.conf
iface default inet dhcp 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">allow-hotplug</samp> line allows other programs to control the Wi-Fi interface. The line that starts with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">wpa-roam</samp> specifies the file in which the WPA keys of various Wi-Fi networks are stored. As soon as a suitable network is within range, a connection is automatically established, and the IP data is obtained via DHCP. The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">iface default inet dhcp</samp> statement states that every network defined in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">wpa_supplicant.conf</samp> should use DHCP for IP configuration by default.

#### Network Bridges and Special Settings

To configure virtual bridges or to fulfill special configuration requests, there are a number of other keywords that are documented on the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man</samp> page for <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">interfaces</samp>. In particular, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">pre-up</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">up</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">post-up</samp> keywords as well as <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">pre-down</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">down</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">post-down</samp> keywords to specify commands that are to be executed immediately before, during, or after setting up or stopping a network interface. The following lines show a network bridge that is connected to physical interface <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">eth0</samp> and redirects network packets to four virtual machines:

```
# IPv4 network bridge
auto  br0
iface br0 inet static
  # static configuration
  address     210.211.212.18
  broadcast   210.211.212.31
  netmask     255.255.255.224
  gateway     210.211.212.1
  pointopoint 210.211.212.1

  # Bridge
  bridge_ports   eth0
  bridge_stp     off
  bridge_fd      0
  bridge_maxwait 0

  # additional IPs for KVM
  up route add -host 210.211.212.26 dev br0
  up route add -host 210.211.212.27 dev br0
  up route add -host 210.211.212.28 dev br0
  up route add -host 210.211.212.29 dev br0

  # static routes for IPv6
  up ip -6 addr add 2a01:1234:567:890::2/64     dev br0
  up ip route   add default via fe80::1         dev br0
  down ip route del default via fe80::1         dev br0
  down ip -6    del add 2a01:1234:567:890::2/64 dev br0 
```

### /etc/systemd/journald.conf

The journal log service belonging to systemd is controlled by the following configuration files:

```
/etc/systemd/journald.conf
/etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/*.conf /run/systemd/journald.conf.d/*.conf [/usr]/lib/systemd/journald.conf.d/*.conf 
```

In many distributions, only <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/systemd/journald.conf</samp> exists, and this file also only contains commented-out example lines. In this case, the default settings apply.

To change the configuration, you can use the following keywords within the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[Journal]</samp> configuration group:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ForwardToSyslog</samp>
    Specifies whether messages logged by the journal should also be forwarded to a traditional syslog service.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">MaxFileSec</samp>
    Specifies the latest time after which a new logging file should be started. The default setting is one month. This setting is only relevant if the logging files grow slower than the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">SystemMaxUse</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">SystemMaxFileSize</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">SystemKeepFree</samp> limits specify.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">MaxLevelStore</samp>
    Indicates the priority level up to which messages are saved in the journal. The default setting is <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">debug</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">SystemKeepFree</samp>
    Specifies what percentage of the file system must remain free. The default setting is 15%.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">SystemMaxFileSize</samp>
    Specifies the maximum size of a logging file. The default setting is one eighth of <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">SystemMaxUse</samp>. This results in automatic rotating, creating a maximum of seven older files in addition to the current logging file.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">SystemMaxUse</samp>
    Specifies the maximum percentage of the file system that the logging files can occupy. Before this limit is exceeded, old logging files will be deleted. The default setting is 10%.

You can look up countless other options via <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man journald.conf</samp>.

### /etc/locale.conf

The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/locale.conf</samp> file contains the language and character set settings for distributions that use a current systemd version as the init system. The [localectl](#L_001.xhtml_localectl) command helps you change the settings. The following list describes the most important localization parameters that can be set:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">LANG=xxx</samp>
    Determines the default value for all LC variables that haven’t been set.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">LC_ALL=xxx</samp>
    Overwrites all individual LC settings.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">LC_COLLATE=xxx</samp>
    Determines the sorting order.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">LC_CTYPE=xxx</samp>
    Determines the character set.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">LC_MESSAGES=xxx</samp>
    Determines the display of messages, error messages, and so on.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">LC_MONETARY=xxx</samp>
    Determines the representation of monetary amounts.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">LC_NUMERIC=xxx</samp>
    Determines the representation of numbers.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">LC_PAPER=xxx</samp>
    Determines the paper size.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">LC_TIME=xxx</samp>
    Determines the display of date and time.

A list of all possible settings is provided by <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">locale -a</samp>. The notation <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">spr_land.zs</samp> is usually used, where <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">spr</samp> denotes the language by two letters, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">land</samp> denotes the country by two letters. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">zs</samp> specifies the character set. In German-speaking countries, for example, you would use <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">de_DE.utf8</samp>.

Depending on the distribution, these or other localization settings are saved in other locations:

| Debian, Ubuntu | <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/default/locale</samp> |
| SUSE | <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc:/sysconfig/language</samp> |

#### Example

In the following setting in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">locale.conf</samp>, German is the default language, and UTF-8 is the default character set:

```
LANG="de_DE.utf8" 
```

### /etc/login.defs

<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/login.defs</samp> contains various settings that are taken into account when creating new users and groups. The settings apply to the commands from the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">shadow-utils</samp> package, for example, for [adduser](#A_001.xhtml_adduser) and [useradd](#U_001.xhtml_useradd) as well as for [addgroup](#A_001.xhtml_addgroup) and [groupadd](#G_001.xhtml_groupadd). The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">login.defs</samp> parameters, on the other hand, have no influence on commands that use the pluggable authentication modules (PAM); this includes in particular [passwd](#P_001.xhtml_passwd)!

The settings in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">login.defs</samp> are made line by line. In each line, first a keyword is entered, then one or more blank or tab characters, and finally the desired setting.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">CREATE_HOME</samp>
    Specifies whether a home directory should also be created automatically when new users are created (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">yes</samp>/<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">no</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ENCRYPT_METHOD</samp>
    Specifies which algorithm is to be used to store the hash codes in [etc/shadow](#04_001.xhtml_shadow). Permitted settings are <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">DES</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">MD5</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">SHA256</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">SHA512</samp> (most secure).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ENV_PATH</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ENV_SUPATH</samp>
    Contains a default setting for the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">PATH</samp> environment variable for normal users and for <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">root</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">su</samp>. For most distributions, additional settings for the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">PATH</samp> variable are made in [etc/profile](#04_001.xhtml_profile) or in [etc/bashrc](#04_001.xhtml_bashrc).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">GID_MIN</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">GID_MAX</samp>
    Specifies the minimum and maximum group ID for common groups.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">LOG_OK_LOGINS</samp>
    Records successful logins with syslog (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">yes</samp>/<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">no</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">MAIL_DIR</samp>
    Specifies the location of the directory for storing local emails.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">PASS_MAX_DAYS</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">PASS_MIN_DAYS</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">PASS_WARN_AGE</samp>
    Specifies how long passwords are valid and the earliest period after which they may be changed (see [chage](#C_001.xhtml_chage)).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">PASS_MIN_LEN</samp>
    Defines the minimum password length.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">SYS_GID_MIN</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">SYS_GID_MAX</samp>
    Specifies the minimum and maximum GID for system accounts.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">SYS_UID_MIN</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">SYS_UID_MAX</samp>
    Specifies the minimum and maximum UID for system accounts.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">SYSLOG_SU_ENAB</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">SYSLOG_SG_ENAB</samp>
    Records <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">su</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">newgrp</samp> commands with syslog (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">yes</samp>/<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">no</samp>).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">UID_MIN</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">UID_MAX</samp>
    Specifies the minimum and maximum user ID for normal users.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">USERGROUPS_ENAB</samp>
    Controls whether a separate group should be created for each user (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">yes</samp>/<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">no</samp>).

#### Example

The following lines show the default settings in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">login.defs</samp> on Fedora. You should note, however, that the settings for <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">PASS_MIN_LEN</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">UMASK</samp> aren’t relevant for the operation of Fedora! The minimum requirements for passwords are specified by PAM module <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">pwquality</samp>, while <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">umask</samp> is preset to <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">022</samp> in [etc/profile](#04_001.xhtml_profile).

```
MAIL_DIR     /var/spool/mail
PASS_MAX_DAYS          99999
PASS_MIN_DAYS              0
PASS_MIN_LEN               5
PASS_WARN_AGE              7
UID_MIN                 1000
UID_MAX                60000
SYS_UID_MIN              201
SYS_UID_MAX              999
GID_MIN                 1000
GID_MAX                60000
SYS_GID_MIN              201
SYS_GID_MAX              999
CREATE_HOME              yes
UMASK                    077
USERGROUPS_ENAB          yes
ENCRYPT_METHOD        SHA512 
```

### /etc/mailname

On Debian and Ubuntu systems, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/mailname</samp> contains the host name to be used by the mail server. The setting is analyzed by postfix (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">myorigin = /etc/mailname</samp>) and the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mutt</samp> program, among others. This setting is particularly important for sending email. It completes the mail address of local mails. So, when <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">huber</samp> sends an email, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">huber@mailhostname</samp> is used as the sender, whereby <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mailhostname</samp> is read from <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/mailname</samp>.

In other distributions, the host name is set directly in the configuration files of the mail server; with postfix, this is in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/postfix/main.cf</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">myorigin =</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mailhostname</samp>.

### /etc/mdadm/mdadm.conf

The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/mdadm/mdadm.conf</samp> file summarizes the configuration of the computer’s software RAID system. If the file is missing or lost, it can be partially recreated from the metadata stored in RAID partitions using the following command:

```
root# mdadm --examine --scan > /etc/mdadm/mdadm.conf 
```

The following list shows the most important keywords in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mdadm.conf</samp>:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ARRAY device1 metadata=... UUID=... name=... devices=...</samp>
    Specifies which components make up a RAID array.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">CREATE owner=... group=... mode=... auto=...</samp>
    Specifies which default settings should apply when activating a RAID device. The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">auto</samp> parameter corresponds to the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">--auto</samp> option of the [mdadm](#M_001.xhtml_mdadm) command.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">DEVICE device1 device2 | partitions | containers</samp>
    Specifies which hard disks or partitions can contain RAID components. If the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">DEVICE</samp> specification is missing, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">DEVICE partitions containers</samp> applies. The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mdadm</samp> command scans all SSD and hard disk partitions as well as all logical volumes.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">MAILADDR name</samp>
    Specifies the local email address to which messages, warnings, and error messages are to be sent if <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mdadm</samp> is running in monitor mode.

#### Example

The following lines show the configuration file of a Linux server with two RAID-1 devices:

```
CREATE owner=root group=disk mode=0660 auto=yes
MAILADDR root
ARRAY /dev/md/0 metadata=1.2 UUID=0860...f0a2 name=rescue:0 ARRAY /dev/md/1 metadata=1.2 UUID=2546...e6e2 name=rescue:1 
```

### /etc/modules

The Debian/Ubuntu-specific file <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/modules</samp> contains the names of kernel modules that are to be loaded at computer startup, line by line. Usually, Linux itself recognizes which kernel modules need to be loaded. Only if this doesn’t work do you need to add the relevant module names to the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/modules</samp> file.

#### Alternative Procedures

Kernel modules that are already required during the boot process must be installed in the initrd file. The [dracut](#D_001.xhtml_dracut) (Fedora, CentOS, RHEL) and [update-initramfs](#U_001.xhtml_update-initramfs) (Debian, Ubuntu) commands help with this.

Another option is to load the kernel module at the end of the init process using the [etc/rc.local](#04_001.xhtml_rc.local) script. The Raspberry Pi OS uses device trees to manage the kernel modules that match the hardware. The configuration is performed using [boot/firmware/config.txt](#04_001.xhtml_config.txt). The device tree files with the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">*.dtb</samp> identifier are located in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/boot/firmware</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/boot/firmware/overlays</samp> directories.

### /etc/netplan/netplan.yaml

Netplan ([https://netplan.io](https://netplan.io)) is used in Ubuntu. The framework configures and controls other network backends such as NetworkManager and systemd component networkd. The configuration files for Netplan are located in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/netplan</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/lib/netplan</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/run/netplan</samp>, and they have the extension <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">*.yaml</samp>. For configuration changes to take effect, you must run [netplan](#N_001.xhtml_netplan) <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">apply</samp>. The configuration files are parsed in alphabetical order.

On desktop systems, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/netplan</samp> only contains a minimal configuration file by default, which delegates all further work to NetworkManager:

```
# File /etc/netplan/01-network-manager-all.yaml (desktop systems)
network:
  version: 2
  renderer: NetworkManager 
```

For server installations in local networks that use DHCP, the configuration reads as shown in the following lines. networkd is responsible for the actual implementation of the network connection. (The line <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">renderer: networkd</samp> can be omitted because <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">networkd</samp> is the default backend for Netplan.)

```
# File /etc/netplan/01-netcfg.yaml (server/DHCP)
# Configure interface enp0s3 via DHCP
network:
  version: 2
  renderer: networkd
  ethernets:
   enp0s3:
    dhcp4: true 
```

You can use this template as a guide for static network configuration including nameserver specification:

```
# File /etc/netplan/01-netcfg.yaml (server/static)
# Configure interface ens3 static
network:
  version: 2
  renderer: networkd
  ethernets:
   ens3:
   addresses: [ 138.201.20.182/26 ]
   gateway4:    138.201.20.176
   nameservers:
       search: [ ubuntu-book.info ]
       addresses:
           - "213.133.100.100"
           - "213.133.98.98" 
```

Of course, IPv6 addresses are also permitted in the configuration files. In some cases, you must specify IPv4- and IPv6-specific keywords, such as <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">gateway4</samp> versus <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">gateway6</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">dhcp4</samp> versus <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">dhcp6</samp>. You can find many more examples including routing, bridging, bonding, VLANs, and so on, at the following site:

[https://netplan.io/examples](https://netplan.io/examples)

### /etc/systemd/network/networkd.network

The network backend networkd, which is part of systemd, is currently installed in many distributions, but is rarely active. The main exception is Ubuntu Server, where networkd is controlled by Netplan.

networkd parses configuration files in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/systemd/network</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/lib/systemd/network</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/run/systemd/network</samp> directories. The files must have the extension <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">*.network</samp>.

The following lines show an example of how you can set up an Ethernet interface with a static IP address in a virtual machine:

```
# File /etc/systemd/network/01-mystatic.network
[Match]
Name=ens3

[Network]
Address=138.201.20.182/26
Gateway=138.201.20.176
DNS=213.133.100.100
DNS=213.133.98.98
Domains=ubuntu-book.info 
```

The second example also shows a static configuration, this time for a root server at Hetzner, including routing and IPv6 setup:

```
[Match]
MACAddress=90:1b:0e:8e:48:86

[Network]
Address=2a01:4f8:171:2baf::2/64
Gateway=fe80::1
Address=138.201.20.176/26
Gateway=138.201.20.129

[Route]
Destination=138.201.20.128/26
Gateway=138.201.20.129 
```

If a DHCP server is available, a possible configuration looks as follows:

```
# File /etc/systemd/network/01-dhcpclient.network
[Match]
Name=enp0s3

[Network]
DHCP=ipv4

[DHCP]
UseMTU=true
RouteMetric=100 
```

You can find further details on the syntax of the networkd configuration in <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man systemd.network</samp>. The Arch Linux wiki also contains very useful information:

[https://wiki.archlinux.org/index.php/systemd-networkd](https://wiki.archlinux.org/index.php/systemd-networkd)

### /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/<interface>.nmconnection

Almost all Linux distributions rely on the NetworkManager for Wi-Fi configuration. For other network distribution, distribution-specific procedures are often used in parallel. Exceptions include the current Fedora and RHEL versions (from RHEL 9), which rely entirely on the NetworkManager, even for static configurations on servers. The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ifcfg</samp> files in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/sysconfig/network-scripts</samp> that used to be common in RHEL are obsolete.

With NetworkManager, the configuration of the network interfaces is saved in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/NetworkManager/system-connections</samp> directory in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">keyfile</samp> syntax. The syntax of these files is documented here:

[www.linux.org/docs/man5/nm-settings-keyfile.html](http://www.linux.org/docs/man5/nm-settings-keyfile.html)

[https://people.freedesktop.org/~lkundrak/nm-docs/nm-settings.html](https://people.freedesktop.org/~lkundrak/nm-docs/nm-settings.html)

If possible, you should configure the network using graphical tools. In Gnome, that’s in the network module of the settings. [nmcli](#N_001.xhtml_nmcli) and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">nmtui</samp> work well in the console or terminal. (<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">nmtui</samp> stands for NetworkManager Text User Interface and is a menu-guided and dialog-guided configuration program for text mode.)

It’s of course also possible to change the configuration files directly. For NetworkManager to take your configuration files into account, they must be owned by <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">root</samp> and must be readable only by <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">root</samp>. Make sure to execute <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">chmod 600 filename</samp> and, if necessary, also <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">chown root:root filename</samp>!

When experimenting with your own configuration files, dynamically generated files in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/var/run/NetworkManager</samp> directory often interfere. Perform a reboot! NetworkManager creates dynamic configuration files only for those interfaces for which there’s no explicit configuration in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/NetworkManager</samp>.

For changes to the configuration to take effect, you must ask NetworkManager to reread existing configuration files. Then, you explicitly tell it your wish to actually apply the changes for a specific interface—here, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">enp1s0</samp>:

```
root# nmcli connection reload     
(reload configuration)
root# nmcli dev reapply enp1s0    
(apply new configuration)
root# nmcli connection show       
(interface overview) 
```

#### DHCP Configuration

An Ethernet interface that receives its network configuration via DHCP doesn’t actually need a configuration file. NetworkManager automatically takes care of the configuration. However, you can still write the configuration in a file like in the following sample:

```
# File /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/enp1s0.nmconnection
[connection]
id=myInterfaceName
uuid=27afa607-ee36-43f0-b8c3-9d245cdc4bb3
type=802-3-ethernet
autoconnect=true
interface-name=enp1s0
[ipv4]
method=auto
[802-3-ethernet]
mac-address=52:54:00:64:9b:85 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">method=auto</samp> is responsible for DHCP to be used. You can create the mapping to the interface either via <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">interface-name</samp> or via <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mac-address</samp>. You can determine the required hexadecimal address using [ip](#I_001.xhtml_ip) <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">addr</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">autoconnect=true</samp> causes the network interface to be activated automatically when the computer is booted.

<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">id</samp> is a freely selectable name for the connection. This name must be used in some [nmcli](#N_001.xhtml_nmcli) commands to select the interface. It’s often convenient to simply use the interface name (here, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">enp1s0</samp>) as the ID.

You’re also free to decide on the file name for the configuration file. It’s advisable to follow the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen"><interface name>.nmconnection</samp> method that applies on Fedora and RHEL. NetworkManager takes into account all files that aren’t clearly identifiable as backup files.

#### Static Configuration

For a static IPv4 configuration, you need to change a few lines in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[ipv4]</samp> section:

```
# File /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/enp1s0.nmconnection
...
[ipv4]
address1=192.168.122.244/24,192.168.122.1
dns=192.168.122.1
method=manual 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">method=manual</samp> activates the static configuration. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">address1=...</samp> assigns an IP address, the mask, and (if required) the corresponding gateway address to the interface. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">dns</samp> sets the nameserver you want. If required, you can also specify multiple nameserver addresses separated by commas.

#### IPv6 Configuration

The relevant lines for a static IPv6 configuration looks as follows:

```
# File /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/enp1s0.nmconnection
...
[ipv6]
addr-gen-mode=default
address1=2abc:1234:1234::10/64,2abc:1234:1234::1
dns=2001:4860:4860::8888,2001:4860:4860::8844
method=manual 
```

In the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[ipv6]</samp> section, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">address1</samp> again assigns the IP address including mask as well as the corresponding gateway address. The public Google nameservers are used as nameservers in this example.

#### Firewall Zones

You can include the desired zone for the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">firewalld</samp> program in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[connection]</samp> section of the configuration files:

```
# File /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/enp1s0.nmconnection
[connection]
...
zone=trusted 
```

Without this specification, the firewall system automatically uses the default <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">public</samp> zone. You can determine the currently valid zones for all interfaces using [firewall-cmd](#F_001.xhtml_firewall-cmd) <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">--get-active-zones</samp>.

### /etc/nsswitch.conf

The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/nsswitch.conf</samp> file controls how host names, usernames, and group names are resolved via the name switch functions in the GNU C library. Changes to this file are rarely necessary, unless LDAP or another network service is used in the local network for user administration and authentication.

The file contains entries line by line, with the first column indicating the name of a database. The term “database” refers to a group of information, such as the list of all users, including login name, full name, home directory, default shell, and so on. Permitted keywords for the first column include <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">aliases</samp> (mail aliases), <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">group</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">hosts</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">networks</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">passwd</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">rpc</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">shadow</samp>.

The database name is followed by a colon and then a list of services separated by spaces. The most important services are as follows:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">files</samp> reads the data from local configuration files, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/passwd</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/group</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">compat</samp> has a similar meaning to <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">files</samp>, but allows the interpretation of additional information in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/passwd</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">db</samp> reads the data from database files.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">nis</samp> analyzes the outdated network information service.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">dns</samp> queries the nameserver (for host names).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mdns4_minimal</samp> uses Zeroconf to resolve host names.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ldap</samp> communicates with an LDAP server.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">wins</samp> uses a WINS server.

In addition, commands can be specified in the form <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[STATUS=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ACTION</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">] bzw. [!STATUS=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ACTION</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">]</samp>, which are then to be executed when a certain event occurs or doesn’t occur. Permissible <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">STATUS</samp> values are <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">success</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">notfound</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">unavail</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">tryagain</samp>. Possible actions are <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">return</samp> (return result immediately, don’t fall back on other options) and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">continue</samp> (use the next lookup service).

#### Example

The following lines show an excerpt from the default configuration on Fedora. Only the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/passwd</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/shadow</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/group</samp> files are taken into account for the user accounts. Host names are read from <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/hosts</samp>, requested from the nameserver and determined via Zeroconf (Avahi).

```
passwd:     files
shadow:     files
group:      files
hosts:      files dns mdns4_minimal
... 
```

### /etc/os-release

For current distributions that use systemd as the init system, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/os-release</samp> contains information about the installed distribution. The following lines show the syntax of the file:

```
NAME="AlmaLinux"
VERSION="9.3 (Shamrock Pampas Cat)"
ID="almalinux"
ID_LIKE="rhel centos fedora"
VERSION_ID="9.3"
PLATFORM_ID="platform:el9"
PRETTY_NAME="AlmaLinux 9.3 (Shamrock Pampas Cat)"
... 
```

Strictly speaking, the file isn’t a configuration file, but an information file. It therefore makes no sense to change the file. However, it may be updated from time to time in the course of updates.

### /etc/passwd

The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/passwd</samp> file contains data on all local accounts on the computer, including the login name, the full name, the default shell, and the home directory. However, for security reasons, the hash code of the password isn’t included; it’s stored in the separate [etc/shadow](#04_001.xhtml_shadow) file. If possible, you should use the commands provided for managing the accounts, such as [useradd](#U_001.xhtml_useradd), [usermod](#U_001.xhtml_usermod), or [userdel](#U_001.xhtml_userdel).

The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">passwd</samp> file consists of seven columns, each separated by colons:

*   First column (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Account name</samp>)
    Contains the login name. It must not contain any spaces and should be free of special characters. It’s customary to use only lowercase letters.

*   Second column (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Password</samp>)
    In the past, this contained the hash code of the password. All current Linux distributions now store the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">x</samp> character in this column, the hash codes can be found in [etc/shadow](#04_001.xhtml_shadow).

*   Third column (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">UID</samp>)
    Contains the internal user ID, which is used to manage access rights and processes. In most distributions, UIDs smaller than 1000 are reserved for system accounts, and UIDs from 1000 are intended for regular users.

*   Fourth column (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Primary group</samp>)
    Indicates the number of the user’s primary group. The user can be assigned to other groups; secondary groups are saved in [etc/group](#04_001.xhtml_group).

*   Fifth column (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Comment</samp>)
    Intended for a comment string, which can consist of several parts. In practice, only the full username is usually saved here. If this wasn’t specified when the user was created, the fifth column is the same as the first.

*   Sixth column (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Home directory</samp>)
    Contains the path to the home directory.

*   Seventh column (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Shell</samp>)
    Specifies the shell that is automatically active after login; often this is <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">/bin/bash</samp> for normal users. For system accounts for which no login is provided, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/sbin/nologin</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/bin/false</samp> is often used instead of the shell. The default shell can be changed via the [chsh](#C_001.xhtml_chsh) command.

#### Example

The following lines show some system accounts and a user account on a Fedora system:

```
root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash bin:x:1:1:bin:/bin:/sbin/nologin daemon:x:2:2:daemon:/sbin:/sbin/nologin adm:x:3:4:adm:/var/adm:/sbin/nologin
...
kofler:x:1000:1000:Michael Kofler:/home/kofler:/bin/bash 
```

### /etc/profile

<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/profile</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/profile.d/*.sh</samp> contain system-wide settings for environment variables. Variables such as <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">PATH</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">MAIL</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">HOSTNAME</samp> are preset there. In addition, many distributions use [umask](#U_001.xhtml_umask) to set which access bits are to be set for newly created files.

<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/profile</samp> is a shell script file. Syntactically, therefore, everything is permitted that the common denominator of the most important shells allows. On Ubuntu, in addition to <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/profile</samp>, the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/environment</samp> file is provided for the system-wide setting of environment variables. However, this file usually only contains the settings for the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">PATH</samp> variables.

The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">profile</samp> settings are supplemented by user-specific settings in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.profile</samp> and by shell-specific settings. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">bash</samp> loads the files <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/bashrc</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/bash.bashrc</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.bashrc</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.alias</samp>. Depending on the distribution, there may be additional configuration files. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">PATH</samp> in Debian and Ubuntu is set by <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/environment</samp>. For the environment variables valid in the X graphics system, the files in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/X11/Xsession.d/</samp> directory are also processed if this exists.

### /etc/rc.local /etc/rc.d/rc.local
/etc/init.d/boot.local

Many distributions run the script file <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">rc.local</samp> for compatibility with old Init-V systems. The file has different locations depending on the distribution:

| Debian, Raspberry Pi OS, Ubuntu | <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/rc.local</samp> |
| CentOS, Fedora, RHEL | <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/rc.d/rc.local</samp> |
| openSUSE/SUSE | <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/init.d/boot.local</samp> |

The file must be executable ([chmod](#C_001.xhtml_chmod) <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">+x</samp>)! In addition, with some distributions, you must run <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">daemon-reload</samp> after setting up the [systemctl](#S_001.xhtml_systemctl) file so that the file is taken into account from the next reboot.

<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">rc.local</samp> is a relic of the old Init-V system, which was replaced by systemd many years ago. Depending on the distribution, the file is empty or doesn’t exist by default, but it will be taken into account if you create it correctly. However, it’s conceivable that this will change in the future. Then, you must set up a “real” systemd unit instead of <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">rc.local</samp> (see [systemd.service](#04_001.xhtml_systemd.service)).

#### Example

The following script saves the time of the last boot process in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/var/log/boottime</samp>:

```
#!/bin/bash
# File /etc/rc.local or /etc/rc.d/rc.local or /etc/init.d/boot.local
date > /var/log/boottime 
```

To ensure that the script in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/rc.d</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/init.d</samp> is taken into account by systemd, you must run the following commands:

```
root# chmod +x /etc/rc.local    
(change file name depending on distribution!)
root# systemctl reload-daemon
root# reboot 
```

### /etc/resolv.conf

<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/resolv.conf</samp> controls how the IP addresses for unknown network names (host names) are determined. “Unknown” means that the names aren’t defined in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">hosts</samp>. The file usually consists of only two or three lines with the following keywords:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">nameserver</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ipaddr</samp>
    Specifies the IP address of a nameserver. The keyword can be used multiple times to specify alternative nameservers. A maximum of three IPv4 and three IPv6 nameservers are permitted.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">domain</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mydomain</samp>
    Specifies the local domain name. This enables the shortened specification of host names, that is, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name.mydomain</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">search</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">domain</samp>
    Specifies a domain name that is taken into account for search queries. A total of up to six domain names can be specified, each with its own <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">search</samp> entry. During name resolution, the specified domain names are tested in sequence; that is, for <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ping name</samp>, it’s first <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp>, then <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name.domain1</samp>, then <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name.domain2</samp>, and so on. The default setting for <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">search</samp> is the local domain name.

    <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">domain</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">search</samp> are mutually exclusive. If <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">resolv.conf</samp> contains both keywords, the latter applies.

<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/resolv.conf</samp> is often generated dynamically, especially if the IP configuration is carried out via DHCP.

An increasing number of distributions (Fedora, Ubuntu) are setting up a local nameserver with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">systemd-resolv</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/resolv.conf</samp> then references this server (often 127.0.0.53). If you want to know which external nameserver the local service is accessing, you must run [resolvectl](#R_001.xhtml_resolvectl) or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">systemd-resolv --status</samp>.

#### Example

The following lines show a manual nameserver configuration for IPv4 and IPv6:

```
# /etc/resolv.conf
domain mylan                     # Domain name of the LAN
nameserver 211.212.213.1         # IPv4 DNS
nameserver 211.212.214.1         # Replacement DNS (if the first one fails)
nameserver 2001:4860:4860::8888  # IPv6-DNS 
```

### /etc/rsyslog.conf

Many Linux distributions use the syslog-compatible program <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">rsyslogd</samp> to log messages from the kernel and various network services. This program must be configured using the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/rsyslog.conf</samp> file and the supplementary <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf</samp> files. These configuration files contain rules that consist of two parts:

*   Selector
    The first part of each rule specifies what is supposed to be logged.

*   Action
    The second part controls what should be done with the message.

Rules can be spread across multiple lines using the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">\</samp> character. It’s possible that multiple rules apply to one message. In this case, the message is logged or passed on several times. For changes to the syslog configuration to take effect, the syslog service must be <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">restarted</samp> via <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">service rsyslog restart</samp>!

#### Selectors

Each selector consists of two parts separated by a dot: service.prioritylevel. It’s allowed to specify multiple selectors separated by a semicolon. Furthermore, multiple services can be separated by commas in one selector. All Linux programs that use syslog must assign a service and priority to their messages.

Syslog recognizes the following services (facilities): <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">auth</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">authpriv</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">cron</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">daemon</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ftp</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">kern</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">lpr</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mail</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">news</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">syslog</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">user</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">uucp</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">local0</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">local7</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">*</samp> character comprises all services.

Syslog also knows the following priority levels (in increasing importance): <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">debug</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">info</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">notice</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">warning = warn</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">err = error</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">crit</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">alert</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">emerg = panic</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">warn</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">error</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">panic</samp> keywords are considered obsolete—you should use <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">warning</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">err</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">emerg</samp> instead. The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">*</samp> character comprises all priority levels. The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">none</samp> keyword applies to messages that aren’t assigned a priority.

The specification of a priority level includes all higher (more important) priority levels. Thus, the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mail.err</samp> selector also includes <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">crit</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">alert</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">emerg</samp> messages from the mail system. If you explicitly want only messages of a certain priority, you must prefix the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">=</samp> character (i.e., <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mail.=err</samp>).

#### Actions

The name of a logging file is normally specified as the action. Logging files are usually synchronized after each output. If the file name is preceded by a minus sign, syslog won’t synchronize. This is much more efficient, but messages that haven’t yet been physically saved will be lost in the event of a crash.

Syslog can also forward messages to First In First Out (FIFO) files or pipes. In this case, you need to prefix the file name with the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">|</samp> character. The file <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/dev/xconsole</samp>, which appears in the following listing, is a special FIFO file for passing messages to the X graphics system.

The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">*</samp> character means that the message will be sent to all users logged into consoles or via SSH. As this is very disruptive, it’s only used by default for critical messages.

#### Journal Configuration

Current distributions use the Journal program belonging to the systemd project instead of or in addition to <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">rsyslogd</samp>. It’s configured using [etc/systemd/journald.conf](#04_001.xhtml_journald.conf) and a few other files.

#### Example

The following lines show the standard Ubuntu syslog configuration in a slightly shortened and more clearly formatted form:

```
# File /etc/rsyslog.d/50-default.conf bei Ubuntu
# Selector                      Action
auth,authpriv.*                 /var/log/auth.log
*.*;auth,authpriv.none          -/var/log/syslog
kern.*                          -/var/log/kern.log

mail.*                          -/var/log/mail.log
mail.err                        /var/log/mail.err
*.emerg                         :omusrmsg:*

daemon.*;mail.*; news.err; *.=debug;*.=info; *.=notice;*.=warn  |/dev/xconsole 
```

In plain language, the preceding configuration means:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/var/log/auth.log</samp> contains authentication messages of all priority levels. These include failed and successful login attempts (also via SSH), PAM messages, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sudo</samp> commands, and so on. As the only logging file, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">auth</samp> is synchronized immediately with each message.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/var/log/syslog</samp> contains all messages logged via syslog, including authentication messages that aren’t assigned a priority. The all-encompassing approach is both an advantage and a disadvantage. On one hand, you can extract all conceivable information from a single file; on the other hand, it’s of course particularly difficult to find relevant entries in this hodgepodge.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/var/log/kernel.log</samp> contains all kernel messages.

*   The messages from the mail system (e.g., postfix) are distributed across several files. In <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mail.log</samp> all messages are stored; in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">mail.err</samp> only error messages.

*   Critical system messages, for example, about an imminent shutdown or kernel errors, are forwarded to all users via <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">:omusrmsg:*</samp>, specifically to all terminal windows and consoles. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">omusrmsg</samp> is a <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">rsyslog</samp> module for sending messages to users.

*   Various warnings and error messages are also forwarded to the X system. To track these messages on X, you must start the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">xconsole</samp> program. It looks like a small terminal window, but doesn’t allow any input.

### /etc/services

The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/services</samp> file contains a list of all common network services and the IP ports and protocol types assigned to them. Changes to this file are only necessary in exceptional cases. The syntax of the file is clearly shown in the following sample lines:

```
# service-name  port/protocol  [aliases]   [# comment]
tcpmux          1/tcp                       # TCP port service multiplexer
tcpmux          1/udp                       # TCP port service multiplexer
rje             5/tcp                       # Remote Job Entry
rje             5/udp                       # Remote Job Entry
echo            7/tcp
echo            7/udp
...
ftp             21/tcp
ftp             21/udp          fsp fspd
ssh             22/tcp                      # The Secure Shell (SSH) Protocol
ssh             22/udp                      # The Secure Shell (SSH) Protocol
telnet          23/tcp
telnet          23/udp
... 
```

### /etc/shadow

<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/shadow</samp> adds the password hash to the user information from [passwd](#P_001.xhtml_passwd) as well as data indicating how long the account is valid and when the password should be renewed. To change this data, you usually use the [passwd](#P_001.xhtml_passwd) and [chage](#C_001.xhtml_chage) commands. The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">shadow</samp> file consists of nine columns separated by colons:

*   First column (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Account name</samp>)
    Matches the first column of <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/passwd</samp>.

*   Second column (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Password hash</samp>)
    Allows the password to be checked. However, it’s impossible to reconstruct the password from the hash code. In current Linux distributions, the hash code is generated via [sha](#S_001.xhtml_sha). As a random initialization value is used when generating each hash code (the salt), two users who use the same password will still have different hash codes. This also makes dictionary attacks impossible in which pregenerated hash codes are compared with the content of <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/shadow</samp>.

    For accounts that don’t require a login, the second column simply contains an asterisk. For locked accounts, the hash code is preceded by two exclamation points. The code becomes invalid. To reactivate the account, the exclamation points are removed again.

*   Third column (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Last change</samp>)
    Indicates when the password was last changed. This is calculated in days from January 1, 1970\. The value <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">0</samp> means that the user must change the password immediately at the next login.

*   Fourth column (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Minimum age</samp>)
    Indicates the earliest number of days after which a password may be changed. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">0</samp> allows a change at any time.

*   Fifth column (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Maximum age</samp>)
    Specifies the maximum number of days after which a password must be changed. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">0</samp> allows unlimited use of the password.

*   Sixth column (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Warning time</samp>)
    Specifies how many days before the password expires the user is notified. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">0</samp> deactivates these warnings.

*   Seventh column (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">lockout time</samp>)
    Specifies how many days after the password expires the account will be locked. It can then only be reactivated by the administrator using [passwd](#P_001.xhtml_passwd) <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-u</samp>.

*   Eighth column (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Expiry time</samp>)
    Specifies when the account expires. The date is given in days from January 1, 1970\. If the account is to be valid indefinitely, this column remains empty. The value <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">0</samp> isn’t used!

*   Ninth column
    Reserved for future extensions.

#### Example

The following lines show an excerpt from <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/shadow</samp>, whereby the long hash codes have been shortened:

```
root:$6$.cc11McOB::0:99999:7:::
bin:*:18095:0:99999:7:::
daemon:*:18095:0:99999:7:::
adm:*:18095:0:99999:7:::
...
kofler:$y$j9T$1...:19793:0:99999:7::: 
```

To find out when the password was last changed, you must run [date](#D_001.xhtml_date):

```
user$ date -d "1970-01-01 + 19793 days"

Mon Mar 11 00:00:00 CET 2025 
```

The other <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">chage</samp> entries for the users <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">root</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">kofler</samp> indicate that the password can be changed at any time (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">0</samp>) and is valid almost indefinitely (<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">99999</samp> = approximately 273 years). The user is warned seven days before the password expires when logging in.

### /etc/apt/sources.list

The APT package sources are defined in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/apt/sources.list</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/apt/sources.list.d/*</samp>. The syntax of each line looks as follows:

<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">package type uri distribution [component1] [component2] [component3] ...</samp>

The package type is <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">deb</samp> for ordinary Debian packages or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">deb-src</samp> for source packages. The second column specifies the root directory of the package source. In addition to HTTP and FTP directories, APT also supports ordinary directories as well as RSH or SSH servers.

The third column indicates the distribution. All other columns indicate the components of the distribution that can be taken into account. The component names depend on the distribution and the package source! For example, Ubuntu distinguishes between main, restricted, universe, and multiverse packages, while Debian differentiates between main, contrib, non-free, and similar components.

The package sources mentioned first are preferred: thus, if a particular package is available for download from multiple sources, APT downloads it from the first source.

#### Example

The following listing shows some Ubuntu package sources. For space reasons, each entry was spread across two lines.

```
# File /etc/apt/sources.list
deb http://de.archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/ mantic          \ 
                                     main restricted universe multiverse
deb http://de.archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/ mantic-updates  \ 
                                     main restricted universe multiverse
deb http://security.ubuntu.com/ubuntu    mantic-security \ 
                                     main restricted universe multiverse 
```

### /etc/sudoers

The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/sudoers</samp> file and the additional files in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/sudoers.d</samp> define which users are allowed to run which commands with which rights via [sudo](#S_001.xhtml_sudo). The file also contains various general settings that control the basic behavior of <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sudo</samp>. The settings vary greatly depending on the distribution.

The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sudoers</samp> file should only be changed using the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">visudo</samp> command. It calls the editor defined by the environment variables <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">VISUAL</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">EDITOR</samp> (by default, this is <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">vi</samp>), performs a syntax check before saving, and thus ensures that you don’t exclude yourself from further administration work due to a <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sudoers</samp> file that contains errors. This is especially important for distributions such as Ubuntu, which don’t provide a <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">root</samp> login.

#### Basic Settings

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Defaults always_set_home</samp>
    Changes the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">HOME</samp> environment variable when the user changes, so that it refers to the new user’s home directory. Usually, this happens automatically. This option is only relevant if <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">!env_reset</samp> applies or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">env_keep</samp> contains the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">PATH</samp> variable.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Defaults env_keep="</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">var1 var2 var3</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">"</samp>
    Specifies which environment variables are to be retained when the user changes and are therefore excluded from <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">env_reset</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Defaults env_reset</samp>
    Causes all environment variables to be reset when the user changes. This setting applies by default. To deactivate it, you must enter <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">Defaults !env_reset</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Defaults mail_badpass</samp>
    Causes a warning email to be sent to the administrator after an incorrect login attempt.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Defaults secure_path="</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">pfad1:pfad2:pfad3</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">"</samp>
    Defines the content of the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">PATH</samp> environment variable for <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sudo</samp> commands.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Defaults targetpw</samp>
    Indicates that the password for the account in which the command is to be run must always be entered, that is, usually the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">root</samp> password. Without this setting, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sudo</samp> expects the password of the current user.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Defaults timestamp_timeout=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp>
    Specifies the time after which <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sudo</samp> asks for the password again. The default setting is five minutes.

#### Rights

Three-column entries in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/sudoers</samp> define which users are allowed to run which programs from which computer. The following line indicates that the user <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">katherine</samp> is allowed to run the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">/sbin/fdisk</samp> command on the computer named <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">uranus</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ALL</samp> keyword indicates that <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">katherine</samp> can run the command under any account, that is, as <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">root</samp>, as <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">news</samp>, as <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">lp</samp> and so on.

```
katherine uranus=(ALL) /sbin/fdisk 
```

If the first column of <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">sudoers</samp> is prefixed with the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">%</samp> character, the entry applies to all members of the specified group. The following line means that all users in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">wheel</samp> group can run all commands from any computer as any user:

```
%wheel   ALL=(ALL) ALL 
```

It’s possible to allow a specific user to run <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sudo</samp> without specifying a password. However, the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">NOPASSWD</samp> keyword is only valid if there are no other <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">sudoers</samp> lines that require a password from the same user. This also applies to group entries, such as <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">%admin</samp>.

```
kofler ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL 
```

The following rule, which reads as follows, is extremely liberal: anyone can do anything. This rule only makes sense in combination with the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Defaults targetpw</samp> option, which always requires the password of the user on whose behalf a command is to be run to be entered.

```
ALL ALL=(ALL) ALL 
```

#### Example

The following lines show the default configuration on Ubuntu. In this distribution, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">root</samp> is set up without a valid password. A <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">root</samp> login is therefore impossible! In addition, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">su</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">ssh -l root</samp> don’t work. The only way to run admin commands is thus provided by <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sudo</samp>. All members of the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">admin</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">sudo</samp> groups have this permission, whereby the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">admin</samp> group is only included for reasons of compatibility with older Ubuntu versions. In current Ubuntu versions and in most other distributions, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sudo</samp> is the usual group for users with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sudo</samp> rights.

```
# Default configuration in /etc/sudoers on Ubuntu
Defaults    env_reset
Defaults    mail_badpass
Defaults    use_pty
Defaults    secure_path=\
               "/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin"
root        ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL
%admin      ALL=(ALL) ALL
%sudo       ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL
@includedir /etc/sudoers.d 
```

### /etc/sysctl.conf

<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/sysctl.conf</samp> contains default settings for kernel parameters. The file is analyzed at system startup, and all the parameters listed there are set accordingly. For subsequent changes, you can use [sysctl](#S_001.xhtml_sysctl) <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-p</samp> to ensure that all settings are loaded from <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">sysctl.conf</samp> and set.

The kernel parameters to be set are specified line by line in the form <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">name.name.name=value</samp>. Comment lines start with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">;</samp> or with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">#</samp>.

#### Example

The following setting in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">sysctl.conf</samp> causes forwarding to be activated for IPv4 and IPv6 when the computer is started. This is necessary if the computer is supposed to work as a router.

```
net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1 
```

### systemd.service

The init system systemd is controlled by a whole range of configuration files, which are located in the following three directories:

```
/etc/systemd/system
/run/systemd/system
[/usr]/lib/systemd/system 
```

If systemd is also used to manage user-specific services, there are also <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">*.service</samp> files in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/home/name/.config/systemd/user</samp> and in some other directories.

The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">*.service</samp> files described in this section define how a service—for example an SSH server—is started, monitored, and, if necessary, stopped again by systemd. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">*.service</samp> files consist of several sections that are introduced by lines with the content <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[Unit]</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[Service]</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[Install]</samp>.

#### [Unit] Keywords

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Before/After=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp>
    Names other services or units that are to be started before or after. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Before</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">After</samp> provide systemd with information on the sequence in which the services should be started.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Description=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">description</samp>
    Describes the service using a character string.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">OnFailure=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp>
    Names one or more services that are to be run if the start of the current service fails.
