*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Wants/Requires=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp>
    Names other services that should or must be started beforehand. These keywords define dependencies. systemd attempts to start the relevant services beforehand. With <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Wants</samp>, a possible failure is silently ignored, while with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Requires</samp> it means that the current service isn’t started and an error is triggered instead.

#### [Service] Keywords

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Environment=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">var1='value1' var2='value2' ...</samp>
    Defines several environment variables that are passed on to the process to be started.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">EnvironmentFile=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">filename</samp>
    Loads the file and takes into account the variable assignments contained in it line by line.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ExecReload=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/path/program options</samp>
    Runs the specified command to reload the configuration of the service during operation.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ExecStart=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/path/program options</samp>
    Runs the specified command to start the service. In combination with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Type=oneshot</samp>, multiple <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ExecStart</samp> lines are permitted, which are then executed in sequence.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ExecStop=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/path/program options</samp>
    Runs the specified command to end the service. If you don’t use this keyword, the service will be terminated by a <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">KILL</samp> signal. If required, the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">KillMode</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">KillSignal</samp> keywords, which are listed in the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">systemd.kill man</samp> page, describe which signal is to be sent and how. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ExecStop</samp> is only possible in combination with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Type=oneshot</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">RemainAfterExit</samp>
    Often used in combination with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Type=oneshot</samp>. systemd remembers the currently activated state.

    Without this option, systemd believes that the action has ended with the end of the last <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">StartExec</samp> command after <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">systemctl start name</samp> and immediately sets the status back to <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">stop</samp>. Explicitly executing <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">systemctl stop</samp> would then have no effect.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Type=simple|forking|oneshot|dbus|notify|idle</samp>
    Specifies the type of service or how the program should be started.

    If the type specification is missing, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">simple</samp> applies. systemd then assumes that the command specified with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ExecStart</samp> starts a background service. Not until this command ends does systemd consider the service to be regularly terminated.

    <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Type=notify</samp> works in a similar way, but systemd expects an explicit notification that the start process is complete. The background service must call the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">sd_notify</samp> function or an equivalent function.

    <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Type=forking</samp> also has similarities with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">simple</samp>, but here, the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ExecStart</samp> command is responsible for starting a background process that is detached from the start command. As soon as the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">ExecStart</samp> command is completed, systemd assumes that the service is running in its own background process.

    With the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">oneshot</samp> type, systemd assumes that the command to be executed is completed so quickly that it can be waited for before other actions are performed. The status of the service is reset to <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">stop</samp> at the end, unless the service file contains the keyword <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">RemainAfterExit</samp>.

    Details on the other <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">type</samp> variants are provided by <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">systemd.service</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">User=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">username</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">Group=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">groupname</samp>
    Determines under which account the command is executed. By default, system services run with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">root</samp> rights.

#### [Install] Keywords

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">WantedBy=</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">RequiredBy=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">target</samp>
    Specifies for which target the service is desirable or required, for instance, for <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">multi-user.target</samp> or for <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">reboot.target</samp>. In practice, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">WantedBy</samp> is usually used. This means that the target is reached even if the start of individual services fails. <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">RequiredBy</samp>, on the other hand, results in an error if there are problems. Then, the relevant target can’t be activated.

#### Example

The following lines show the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">httpd.service</samp> file in the default configuration of Fedora. It’s responsible for starting the Apache web server. A prerequisite for the start is the successful activation of the network and any network file systems. The web server is supposed to be started automatically as part of the multiuser target.

```
# File /lib/systemd/system/httpd.service (Fedora)
[Unit]
Description=The Apache HTTP Server
Wants=httpd-init.service
After=network.target remote-fs.target nss-lookup.target httpd-init.service
Documentation=man:httpd.service(8)

[Service]
Type=notify
Environment=LANG=C

ExecStart=/usr/sbin/httpd $OPTIONS -DFOREGROUND
ExecReload=/usr/sbin/httpd $OPTIONS -k graceful
# Send SIGWINCH for graceful stop
KillSignal=SIGWINCH
KillMode=mixed
PrivateTmp=true
OOMPolicy=continue

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target 
```

#### Setting Up Custom systemd Services

To set up your own systemd service, you need to create a <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">*.service</samp> file in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/systemd/system</samp> directory. The best way to do this is to use a service file from another, comparable service. Suitable files can be found in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/lib/systemd/system</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/usr/lib/systemd/system</samp> directories, depending on the distribution.

For efficiency reasons, systemd keeps the contents of important configuration files in a cache. After configuration changes, you must explicitly reload the configuration files using [systemctl](#S_001.xhtml_systemctl):

```
root# systemctl daemon-reload 
```

To start the service immediately and in future every time the multiuser target is reached, the following command is required:

```
root# systemctl enable --now myservice 
```

In case of issues, it’s best to use [journalctl](#J_001.xhtml_journalctl) <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">-u</samp> myservice for debugging.

#### Other systemd Configuration Files

In addition to the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">*.service</samp> files, there are also files for systemd configuration with the identifiers <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">*.mount</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">*.path</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">*.socket</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">*.target</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">*.wants</samp>, which aren’t discussed any further in this book. Their syntax is documented in the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man</samp> pages <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">service.mount</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">service.path</samp>, and so on. All of these files together are considered unit files. The general syntax of those units is explained in <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man systemd.unit</samp>.

If you want to set up jobs that are run periodically by systemd, you must familiarize yourself with the format of the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">*.timer</samp> files (see [systemd/timer](#04_001.xhtml_systemd.timer)).

### systemd.timer

systemd can take care of the regular execution of processes in a way similar to cron. The configuration is performed using a <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name.timer</samp> file that must have a service file with the same name (i.e., <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name.service</samp>). For custom-defined jobs, both files are usually located in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/systemd/system</samp> directory.

The structure of a <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">*.timer</samp> file is similar to that of a <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">*.service</samp> file (see [systemd/service](#04_001.xhtml_systemd.service)). It usually consists of three sections: the familiar <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[Unit]</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[Install]</samp> sections, as well as a <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[Timer]</samp> section, whose settings control when and how often the job is executed.

#### [Timer] Keywords

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">AccuracySec=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">time span</samp>
    Specifies the accuracy within which the jobs are to be run. By default, a time window of one minute is provided for this, within which the start time is determined randomly. Shorter time spans are possible, but should only be used if this is really necessary.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">OnBootSec=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">time span</samp>
    Runs the job for the first time after the specified period of time after the boot process. If the time is given without a unit, seconds are meant. The syntax of the time specifications is documented in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">man systemd.time</samp>. Permissible time spans include, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">2h 15min</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">2weeks</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">4months</samp>.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">OnCalendar=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">time</samp>
    Specifies the time at which the job is to be run. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">12.30</samp> means daily at 12.30 pm. The syntax for absolute time specifications is somewhat complex. The details are documented in detail in the Calendar Events section of <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man systemd.time</samp>. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">OnCalendar=Sun 2025-*-* 17:15</samp> means that a job is executed every Sunday at 5:15 pm in 2025.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">OnUnitActiveSec=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">time span</samp>
    Restarts the job as soon as the specified period of time has passed since the job was last started.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">OnUnitInactiveSec=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">time span</samp>
    Restarts the job as soon as the specified period of time has passed since the job was last completed.

#### Example

The following <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">dnf-automatic.timer</samp> file ensures that the service described in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">dnf-automatic.service</samp> file is run once a day. Both files are part of the Fedora package <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">dnf-automatic</samp>, which automatically performs updates with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">dnf</samp>.

```
# File /usr/lib/systemd/system/dnf-automatic.timer
# (Fedora, if the dnf-automatic package is installed automatically)
[Unit]
Description=dnf-automatic timer
ConditionPathExists=!/run/ostree-booted

[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 6:00
RandomizedDelaySec=60m
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=basic.target 
```

If you want to set up your own timer, you must create both a <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">*.service</samp> and a <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">*.timer</samp> file in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/systemd/system</samp>. Then, ask systemd to reload the configuration and activate the timer:

```
root# systemctl daemon-reload

root# systemctl enable --now mytimer.timer 
```

### /etc/vconsole.conf

The <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/vconsole.conf</samp> file contains the keyboard and font settings for working in text consoles for distributions that use a current systemd version as the init system. The [localectl](#L_001.xhtml_localectl) command helps you change the settings. This command has the advantage over a direct change via <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">vconsole.conf</samp> in that it also saves the desired keyboard layout in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/X11/xorg.conf/00-keyboard.conf</samp> so that the setting also applies to the graphics system.

<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">vconsole.conf</samp> usually consists of just two lines with the following parameters:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">FONT=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp>
    Specifies the font to be used in text consoles. Suitable font files can be found in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/lib/kbd/consolefonts</samp> directory in most distributions.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">KEYMAP=</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">name</samp>
    Specifies the keyboard layout. You can determine the settings available for selection via <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">localectl list-keymaps</samp>.

#### Example

In a German Fedora installation, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">vconsole.conf</samp> contains the following settings:

```
KEYMAP="de-nodeadkeys"
FONT="eurlatgr" 
```

### /etc/wpa_supplicant/wpa_supplicant.conf

The background service <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">wpa_supplicant</samp> is responsible for authentication in wireless networks (Wi-Fi). In desktop distributions, the program is used by NetworkManager as a backend; the configuration is performed via settings dialogs of KDE, Gnome, and so on.

The situation is different if you want to set up a Wi-Fi connection on a Raspberry Pi or another device (embedded device) without a graphical user interface. Then, you must enter the Wi-Fi authentication data in the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/wpa_supplicant/wpa_supplicant.conf</samp> file. The following lines represent an example of this:

```
ctrl_interface=DIR=/var/run/wpa_supplicant GROUP=netdev
update_config=1
country=DE

network={
ssid="wlan-sol3"
  psk="strengGeheim"
  key_mgmt=WPA-PSK
} 
```

The first three lines contain the default settings on the Raspberry Pi OS. The correct <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">country</samp> setting is crucial. It ensures that the Wi-Fi adapter complies with the regulations of the respective country. This is followed by any number of <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">network</samp> groups, one for each wireless network.

When writing <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">wpa_supplicant.conf</samp>, make sure that you don’t enter any spaces before and after the equal signs! You can read a lot of details about the permitted keywords as well as further examples with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man wpa_supplicant.conf</samp> and in the following documentation file and the following website:

<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/usr/share/doc/wpasupplicant/README.modes.gz</samp>

[https://wiki.ubuntuusers.de/WLAN/wpa_supplicant](https://wiki.ubuntuusers.de/WLAN/wpa_supplicant)

In simple cases, you can also create the required configuration lines using [wpa_passphrase](#W_001.xhtml_wpa_passphrase) or perform the configuration directly in [etc/network/interfaces](#04_001.xhtml_interfaces).

# Keyboard Shortcuts

The last section of the Linux Command Reference deals with the keyboard shortcuts of the most important editors and other commands that are usually operated via the keyboard. These include, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">bash</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">info</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">less</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mutt</samp>.

Almost all programs offer the option of defining custom keyboard shortcuts. This section refers to the default configuration, which is the standard configuration for most Linux distributions.

### bash

[Table 1](#05_001.xhtml_t5.1) summarizes which keyboard shortcuts you can use within the Bourne Again Shell (<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">bash</samp>) when entering commands. The keyboard shortcuts actually originate from the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">readline</samp> library. You can change the configuration of this library in <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/etc/inputrc</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.inputrc</samp>.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Ctrl+A | Moves the cursor to the beginning of the line (like Pos1) |
| Ctrl+C | Cancels the current command |
| Ctrl+E | Moves the cursor to the end of the line (like End) |
| Ctrl+K | Deletes the rest of the line from the cursor position |
| Ctrl+Y | Reinserts the most recently deleted text |
| Ctrl+Z | Interrupts the current command (can be continued via <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">fg</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">bg</samp>) |
| Tab | Completes file and command names |
| Arrow Up/Arrow Down | Scrolls through the commands executed so far |

**Table 1**     Keyboard Shortcuts for Entering Commands in bash

### emacs

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">emacs</samp> is one of the most feature-rich and complex editors available on Linux. There are hundreds of keyboard shortcuts and commands, of which only the most important are presented here.

In general, there are three ways to enter <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">emacs</samp> commands: the menu, using keyboard shortcuts (mostly a combination with Ctrl or Alt), or typing the entire command name. The third variant is initiated with Alt+X or Esc, for example, Alt+X <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">delete-char</samp> Enter. The input of commands and other parameters is facilitated by two mechanisms:

*   During input, you can add Tab to the name of an <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">emacs</samp> command. You can also complete file names in the same way.

*   Commands previously specified using Alt+X can be accessed with Alt+P (previous) and Alt+N (next) after the new command has been introduced with Alt+X.

In the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">emacs</samp> documentation, keyboard shortcuts are presented somewhat differently: <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">DEL</samp> refers to Backspace! <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">C</samp> stands for Control (Ctrl) and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">M</samp> for Meta. There is no direct equivalent of the Meta key on a standard PC keyboard. <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">M-x</samp> can be emulated on a PC keyboard in two ways: by Esc and X (in succession) or by Alt+X.

[Table 2](#05_001.xhtml_t5.2) summarizes the basic functions. You can use the cursor keys and various keyboard shortcuts to move the cursor (see [Table 3](#05_001.xhtml_t5.3)).

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Ctrl+X, Ctrl+F | Loads a new file |
| Ctrl+X, Ctrl+S | Saves the current file |
| Ctrl+X, Ctrl+W | Saves the file under a new name |
| Ctrl+G | Cancels the input of a command |
| Ctrl+X, U | Undoes the last change (undo) |
| Ctrl+X, Ctrl+C | Exits <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">emacs</samp> (with prompt to save) |

**Table 2**     Basic Emacs Commands

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Alt+F/Alt+B | Moves the cursor one word forward or backward |
| Ctrl+A/Ctrl+E | Places the cursor at the beginning or end of the line |
| Alt+</Alt+Shift+> | Moves the cursor to the beginning or end of the text |
| Alt+G n Enter | Moves the cursor to line <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> |

**Table 3**     Cursor Movement

[Table 4](#05_001.xhtml_t5.4) specifies how you can select, delete, and reinsert text, and [Table 5](#05_001.xhtml_t5.5) summarizes how to search and replace.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Ctrl+___ | Sets an (invisible) marker point |
| Ctrl+W | Deletes the text between the marker point and the current cursor position |
| Ctrl+Y | Reinserts the most recently deleted text |
| Ctrl+X, Ctrl+X | Swaps cursor position and marker point |
| Alt+D | Deletes the next word or the end of the word from the cursor |
| Alt+Backspace | Deletes the preceding word or the beginning of the word up to the cursor |
| Ctrl+K | Deletes the rest of the line from the cursor position |
| Alt+0, Ctrl+K | Deletes the beginning of the line before the cursor position |
| Alt+M | Deletes the paragraph that follows |
| Alt+Z, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">x</samp> | Deletes all characters until the next occurrence of <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">x</samp>, which is also deleted |
| Ctrl+Y | Inserts the last deleted text at the cursor position |

**Table 4**     Selecting, Deleting, and Reinserting Text

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Ctrl+S | Incremental search forward |
| Ctrl+R | Incremental search backward |
| Alt+P | Selects a previously used search text (previous) |
| Alt+N | Selects a search text to be used later (next) |
| Ctrl+G | Cancels the search |
| Ctrl+X, Ctrl+X | Swaps the marker point (start of the search) and the current cursor position |
| Ctrl+Alt+S | Incremental pattern search forward |
| Ctrl+Alt+R | Incremental pattern search backwards |
| Alt+ % | Search and replace without pattern |
| Alt+X <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">query-replace-r</samp> Enter | Search and replace with pattern |

**Table 5**     Search and Replace

### gnome-terminal

If you run shell commands on Gnome, you’ll most likely use the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">gnome-terminal</samp> program. So that you can use the usual keyboard shortcuts in the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">bash</samp>, you should first deactivate the Menu shortcut letters option to control the menus using Alt shortcuts with Edit • Settings. You can then still use the F10 key for menu control if required—unless you also deactivate the processing of this key in the configuration dialog just mentioned. Some <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">gnome-terminal</samp>–specific keyboard shortcuts remain available in any case; they are summarized in [Table 6](#05_001.xhtml_t5.6).

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Shift+Ctrl+C | Copies the selected text to the clipboard |
| Shift+Ctrl+F | Searches for a text in the terminal outputs |
| Shift+Ctrl+G | Repeats the backward search |
| Shift+Ctrl+H | Repeats the forward search |
| Shift+Ctrl+N | Opens a new terminal window |
| Shift+Ctrl+Q | Closes the window |
| Shift+Ctrl+T | Opens a new terminal tab |
| Shift+Ctrl+V | Pastes the contents of the clipboard |
| Shift+Ctrl+W | Closes the tab |
| Shift+Ctrl++ | Enlarges the font |
| Shift+Ctrl+- | Reduces the font size |
| Shift+Ctrl+Arrow Up/Arrow Down | Goes to the previous/next tab |
| F11 | Activates or deactivates full screen mode |

**Table 6**     Keyboard Shortcuts in gnome-terminal

### grub

In the Linux boot loader GRUB, you can use the cursor keys to select an operating system or a Linux variant and then start it by pressing Enter. GRUB also provides the option of interactively changing the parameters of a menu item or running custom commands. [Table 7](#05_001.xhtml_t5.7) summarizes the most important shortcuts for this. The table refers to the current GRUB version 2.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Esc | Exits graphics mode and activates text mode. |
| C | Starts the command mode for the interactive execution of GRUB commands. When entering commands, file names can be completed with a Tab as in the shell. |
| E | Starts the editor for the selected menu item. |
| P | Enables the interactive GRUB functions by entering a password. This is only necessary if GRUB is protected by a password. |
| Ctrl+X or F10 | Starts the menu item previously changed with E. |

**Table 7**     Keyboard Shortcuts for Interactive Control of GRUB 2

### info

info starts the online help system of the same name. To navigate in the help text, you can use the keyboard shortcuts summarized in [Table 8](#05_001.xhtml_t5.8). You can also read <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">info</samp> texts more conveniently via the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">pinfo</samp> command from the package of the same name, with the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">emacs</samp> editor or in the Gnome and KDE help systems.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Spacebar | Scrolls text down |
| Backspace | Scrolls text up |
| B, E | Jumps to the beginning/end of the info unit (beginning/end) |
| Tab | Moves the cursor to the next cross-reference |
| Enter | Tracks a cross-reference to another info unit |
| N | Displays the next info unit in the same hierarchy level (next) |
| P | Displays the previous info unit in the same hierarchy level (previous) |
| U | Jumps up one hierarchy level |
| L | Jumps back to the last text displayed (last) |
| H | Displays detailed operating instructions (help) |
| ? | Displays an overview of commands |
| Q | Exits <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">info</samp> (quit) |

**Table 8**     info Keyboard Shortcuts

### joe

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">joe</samp> is a simple editor whose keyboard shortcuts are based on the WordStar word processor (see [Table 9](#05_001.xhtml_t5.9)). The editor can also be started under the name <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">jmacs</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">jpico</samp>. Other keyboard shortcuts that are compatible with <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">emacs</samp> or Pico then apply.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Ctrl+K, H | Shows/hides the help window |
| Ctrl+K, E | Loads a new file |
| Ctrl+K, D | Saves the file (optionally under a new name) |
| Ctrl+Y | Deletes a line |
| Ctrl+Shift+- | Undoes the deletion |
| Ctrl+C | Exits <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">joe</samp> (with confirmation prompt to save) |

**Table 9**     Keyboard Shortcuts in joe

### konsole

KDE fans usually run shell commands in the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">konsole</samp> program. Most keyboard shortcuts are passed directly to the shell by this program. However, there are also some <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">konsole</samp>-specific keyboard shortcuts, which are summarized in [Table 10](#05_001.xhtml_t5.10).

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Shift+Ctrl+A | Marks the tab for activity |
| Shift+Ctrl+C | Copies the selected text to the clipboard |
| Shift+Ctrl+F | Searches for a text in the terminal outputs |
| F3 | Repeats the backward search |
| Shift+ F3 | Repeats the forward search |
| Shift+Ctrl+I | Marks the tab for longer periods of inactivity |
| Shift+Ctrl+N | Opens a new terminal window |
| Shift+Ctrl+Q | Closes the window |
| Shift+Ctrl+T | Opens a new terminal tab |
| Shift+Ctrl+V | Pastes the contents of the clipboard |
| Shift+Ctrl+W | Closes the tab |
| Shift+Ctrl++ | Enlarges the font |
| Shift+Ctrl+- | Reduces the font size |
| Shift+Ctrl+Arrow Left/Arrow Right | Goes to the previous/next tab |

### less

The less command displays texts. While the program is running, you can use the cursor keys to scroll through the text, search for texts, start the editor set by the <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">$EDITOR</samp> environment variable, and so on (see [Table 11](#05_001.xhtml_t5.11)). <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">less</samp> is also used to display <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man</samp> help texts.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Cursor keys | Scrolls the text up or down |
| Pos1, End | Jumps to the beginning or end of the text |
| G, Shift+G | Jumps to the beginning or end of the text |
| / pattern Enter | Searches forwards |
| ? pattern Enter | Searches backwards |
| N | Repeats the forward search (next) |
| Shift+N | Repeats the backward search |
| V | Starts the editor set by <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">$EDITOR</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">$VISUAL</samp> |
| Q | Quits <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">less</samp> (quit) |
| H | Displays a help text with additional shortcuts |

**Table 11**     Keyboard Shortcuts for less

### man

The man command displays the documentation for important commands, configuration files, C functions, and so on. To enable simple scrolling through the help text, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">less</samp> command. For this reason, the same shortcuts apply within <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">man</samp> as for <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">less</samp> (see [Table 11](#05_001.xhtml_t5.11)).

### mutt

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mutt</samp> is an email client for text mode. The program is well suited for reading and replying to emails stored locally on the computer. Died-in-the-wool Linux fans even prefer <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">mutt</samp> in graphical user interfaces because the program can be controlled particularly efficiently using the keyboard. [Table 12](#05_001.xhtml_t5.12) only contains the most important shortcuts.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Cursor keys | Moves the cursor through the mail list |
| Enter | Displays the first lines of the selected email |
| Spacebar | Scrolls through the text of an email |
| T | Deletes the email |
| I | Switches from the email view back to the inbox |
| Y | Displays the next email |
| M | Composes a new email using the editor set by <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">$EDITOR</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">$VISUAL</samp> |
| R | Replies to the email |
| ? | Displays a help text with all keyboard shortcuts |

**Table 12**     Keyboard Shortcuts for mutt

### nano

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">nano</samp> is a minimalist editor that is particularly suitable for beginners. The most important keyboard shortcuts (see also [Table 13](#05_001.xhtml_t5.13)) are always displayed in the two bottom text lines.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Ctrl+A | Moves the cursor to the beginning of the line |
| Ctrl+D | Deletes a character |
| Ctrl+E | Moves the cursor to the end of the line |
| Ctrl+H | Deletes one character backward |
| Ctrl+^ | Sets a marker point |
| Ctrl+K | Deletes the current line or the selected text |
| Ctrl+U | Reinserts the most recently deleted text |
| Ctrl+R | Inserts a text file into the text |
| Ctrl+O | Saves the file |
| Ctrl+X | Exits the editor |

**Table 13**     Keyboard Shortcuts for nano

### screen

You can use the screen command to run multiple terminal sessions in parallel (multiplex). <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">screen</samp> is controlled by keyboard shortcuts that all start with Ctrl+A.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Ctrl+A, ? | Displays the online help |
| Ctrl+A, * | Lists all sessions |
| Ctrl+A, 0 through 9 | Switches between the first and tenth session |
| Ctrl+A, C | Creates a new session (create) |
| Ctrl+A, D | Detaches the current session from <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">screen</samp> (detach) |
| Ctrl+A, Shift+H | Activates/deactivates logging |
| Ctrl+A, K | Ends the active session |
| Ctrl+A, N | Switches to the next session |
| Ctrl+A, \ | Ends all sessions and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">screen</samp> |

**Table 14**     Keyboard Shortcuts in screen

### Text console

If you work directly in text consoles, that is, not in KDE, Gnome, or another desktop system, and also not via SSH, then some special keyboard shortcuts apply. [Table 15](#05_001.xhtml_t5.15) summarizes the most important shortcuts.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Ctrl+Alt+Fn | Switches from graphics mode to text console <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> |
| Alt+F1 | Switches back to graphics mode |
| Alt+Fn | Switches from a text console to text console <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> |
| Alt+Arrow Right/+Arrow Left | Switches to the previous/next text console |
| Shift+Arrow Up/Arrow Down | Scrolls forward/backward page by page |
| Ctrl+Alt+Del | Terminates Linux via <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">shutdown</samp> (caution!) |

**Table 15**     Keyboard Shortcuts in Text Consoles

### vi/vim

The <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">vi</samp> editor is a veteran in the history of Unix. Almost all Linux distributions install the <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">vi</samp>-compatible <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">vim</samp> program by default, which you can start via both <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">vi</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">vim</samp>.

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">vi</samp> provides a similar number of functions to <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">emacs</samp> but is even more difficult to learn to use. [Table 16](#05_001.xhtml_t5.16) summarizes the basic commands.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| I | Activates the insert mode. |
| A | Activates the insert mode. The text input starts at the next character. |
| Esc | Activates the standard mode or cancels the command input. |
| Commands in standard mode |
| D, W | Deletes a word. |
| D, D | Deletes the current line. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> D, D | Deletes n lines. |
| P | Inserts the last deleted text after the cursor position. |
| Shift+P | Inserts the most recently deleted text before the cursor position. |
| . | Repeats the last command. |
| U | Undoes the last change (undo). |
| Shift+U | Undoes all changes in the current line. |
| Ctrl+R | Undoes undo (redo, as of Vim 7). |
| : <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">w</samp> | Saves the file. |
| : <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">q</samp> | Exits <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">vim</samp>. |
| : <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">q!</samp> | Exits <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">vim</samp> even if there are unsaved files. |
| Commands in insert mode |
| Ctrl+O <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">command</samp> | Runs the command without leaving the insert mode. |

**Table 16**     Basic Commands

The main fundamental difference from other editors is that <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">vi</samp> distinguishes between different modes.

*   Insert mode
    To enter text, you must switch to insert mode using I (insert) or A (append). <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">vim</samp> then displays the text <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">-- INSERT --</samp> in the bottom line on the far left. In insert mode, you can enter text, move the cursor, and delete individual characters (Del and Backspace). The difference between I and A is that with I, the input starts at the current cursor position, but with A, input starts at the character behind it.

*   Complex command mode
    However, most commands are entered in complex command mode, which can be activated using :. You may have to exit the insert mode beforehand by pressing Esc.

[Table 17](#05_001.xhtml_t5.17) provides an overview of the most important keyboard shortcuts for deleting text. [Table 18](#05_001.xhtml_t5.18) lists useful commands for moving the cursor. [Table 19](#05_001.xhtml_t5.19), [Table 20](#05_001.xhtml_t5.20), and [Table 21](#05_001.xhtml_t5.21) deal with how to copy, select, and edit text.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Keyboard Shortcuts in insert mode |
| Del, Backspace | The usual meaning |
| Commands in standard mode |
| X | Deletes the character at the cursor position or the selected text |
| Shift+X | Deletes the character before the cursor |
| D, D | Deletes the current line |
| D <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">cursor command</samp> | Deletes the text according to the command for cursor movement (see [Table 18](#05_001.xhtml_t5.18)) Examples: D, $ deletes everything to the end of the line.
D, B deletes the previous word
D, W deletes the next word |

**Table 17**     Deleting Text

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Cursor keys | Standard meaning |
| H/L | Moves the cursor to the left/right |
| J/K | Moves the cursor down/up |
| Shift+H/ Shift+L | Moves the cursor to the beginning or end of the current page |
| Shift+M | Moves the cursor to the center of the current page |
| B/W | Moves the cursor one word to the left/right |
| E | Moves the cursor to the end of the word |
| G, E | Moves the cursor to the beginning of the word |
| (,) | Moves the cursor to the beginning of the current/next block |
| {, } | Moves the cursor to the beginning of the current/next paragraph |
| ^, $ | Moves the cursor to the beginning or end of the line |
| Shift+G | Moves the cursor to the end of the line |
| G, G | Moves the cursor to the beginning of the line |
| n Shift+G | Moves the cursor to line <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> |
| n &#124; | Moves the cursor to column <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">n</samp> |
| % | Moves the cursor to the corresponding parenthesis character ()[]{} |

**Table 18**     Keyboard Shortcuts for Cursor Movement in Standard Mode

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| V | (De)activates the character selection mode |
| Shift+V | (De)activates the line selection mode |
| Ctrl+V | (De)activates the block selection mode |
| A, W | Extends the selection by one word |
| A, S | Extends the selection by one block |
| A, P | Extends the selection by one paragraph |
| A, B | Extends the selection by one () level |
| A, Shift+B | Extends the selection by one {} level |
| G, V | Selects the most recently selected text again |
| O | Toggles the cursor position between the start and end of the selection |

**Table 19**     Selecting Text

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Y | Copies the selected text to the copy register |
| Y, Y | Copies the current line to the copy register |
| Y <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">cursor command</samp> | Copies the text captured by the cursor movement Example: Y, } copies text to the end of the paragraph |

**Table 20**     Copying Text to the Copy Register

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| X | Deletes the selected text |
| Y | Copies the selected text to the copy register |
| ~ | Changes between uppercase and lowercase |
| Y | Merges the selected lines into one long line |
| G, Q | Performs a line break (for continuous text) |
| >, < | Indents or outdents the text by one tab position |
| = | Indents the text according to the current <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">indent</samp> mode |
| <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">!sort</samp> | Sorts the lines using the external <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">sort</samp> command |

**Table 21**     Editing Selected Text

#### Searching and Replacing

In the default mode, /<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">searchtext</samp> Enter moves the cursor to the text being searched for. N repeats the search, and Shift+N repeats the search backwards. To search backward from the outset, you must start the search using ? <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">search term</samp>. [Table 22](#05_001.xhtml_t5.22) summarizes the most important special characters for searching for patterns.

| Character | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">.</samp> | Any character. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">^</samp>   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">$</samp> | Start of line/end of line. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">\<</samp>  <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">\></samp> | Start of word/end of word. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">[a-e]</samp> | A character between a and e. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">\s</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">\t</samp> | A space or a tab character. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">\(</samp>   <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">\)</samp> | Summarizes a search pattern as a group. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">\=</samp> | The search term must occur 0 times or once. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">*</samp> | The search term may occur any number of times (even 0 times). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">\+</samp> | The search term must occur at least once. |

**Table 22**     Special Characters in the Search Term

<samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">vim</samp> distinguishes between uppercase and lowercase during the search. If you don't want this, you must initiate the search pattern with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/c</samp> (applies only to this search) or run : <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">set ignorecase</samp> (applies to all subsequent searches).

Use : <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">set incsearch</samp> to activate the incremental search: <samp class="listingcharacter konsolenbefehl">vim</samp> moves the cursor to the first matching location as soon as you enter the search text using /<samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">searchterm</samp>. Enter ends the search, and Esc cancels it. After the search, all matches in the text remain highlighted until you perform a new search or run : <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">nohlsearch</samp>.

To replace all occurrences of the text <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">abc</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">efg</samp> without prompting, you need to run : <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">%s/</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">abc</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">efg</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/g</samp> in standard mode. ’ ’ then takes you back to the start of the search. [Table 23](#05_001.xhtml_t5.23) summarizes some variants of the search-and-replace command.

| Keyboard Shortcut | Function |
| --- | --- |
| : <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">%s/</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">abc</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">efg</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/g</samp> | Replaces all occurrences of abc with efg without query |
| : <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">%s/</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">abc</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">efg</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/gc</samp> | Replaces all occurrences of abc with efg with query |
| : <samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">%s/</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">abc</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">efg</samp><samp class="listingcharacter listingzeichen">/gci</samp> | Replaces without considering uppercase or lowercase |

**Table 23**     Searching and Replacing

# The Author

[![](bilderklein/klein2749_kofler.png)](img-b6.1.xhtml)

Michael Kofler is a programmer and one of the most successful and versatile computing authors in the German-speaking world. His current topics include AI, Linux, Docker, Git, hacking and security, Raspberry Pi, and the programming languages Swift, Java, Python, and Kotlin. Michael also teaches at the Joanneum University of Applied Sciences in Kapfenberg, Austria.

# Service Pages

The following sections contain notes on how you can contact us. In addition, you are provided with further recommendations on the customization of the screen layout for your e-book.

## Praise and Criticism

We hope that you enjoyed reading this book. If it met your expectations, please do recommend it. If you think there is room for improvement, please get in touch with the editor of the book: [Rachel Gibson](mailto:rachelg@rheinwerk-publishing.com). We welcome every suggestion for improvement but, of course, also any praise! You can also share your reading experience via Social Media or email.

## Technical Issues

If you experience technical issues with your e-book or e-book account at Rheinwerk Computing, please feel free to contact our reader service: [support@rheinwerk-publishing.com](mailto:support@rheinwerk-publishing.com).

Please note, however, that issues regarding the screen presentation of the book content are usually not caused by errors in the e-book document. Because nearly every reading device (computer, tablet, smartphone, e-book reader) interprets the EPUB or Mobi file format differently, it is unfortunately impossible to set up the e-book document in such a way that meets the requirements of all use cases.

In addition, not all reading devices provide the same text presentation functions and not all functions work properly. Finally, you as the user also define with your settings how the book content is displayed on the screen.

The EPUB format, as currently provided and handled by the device manufacturers, is actually primarily suitable for the display of mere text documents, such as novels. Difficulties arise as soon as technical text contains figures, tables, footnotes, marginal notes, or programming code. For more information, please refer to the section [Notes on the Screen Presentation](#notes.xhtml_screenpresentation) and the following section.

Should none of the recommended settings satisfy your layout requirements, we recommend that you use the PDF version of the book, which is available for download in your online library.

## Recommendations for Screen Presentation and Navigation

We recommend using a sans-serif font, such as Arial or Seravek, and a low font size of approx. 30–40% in portrait format and 20–30% in landscape format. The background shouldn’t be too bright.

Make use of the hyphenation option. If it doesn't work properly, align the text to the left margin. Otherwise, justify the text.

To perform searches in the e-book, the index of the book will reliably guide you to the really relevant pages of the book. If the index doesn't help, you can use the search function of your reading device.

Since it is available as a double-page spread in landscape format, the table of contents we’ve included probably gives a better overview of the content and the structure of the book than the corresponding function of your reading device. To enable you to easily open the table of contents anytime, it has been included as a separate entry in the device-generated table of contents.

If you want to zoom in on a figure, tap the respective figure once. By tapping once again, you return to the previous screen. If you tap twice (on the iPad), the figure is displayed in the original size and then has to be zoomed in to the desired size. If you tap once, the figure is directly zoomed in and displayed with a higher resolution.

For books that contain programming code, please note that the code lines may be wrapped incorrectly or displayed incompletely as of a certain font size. In case of doubt, please reduce the font size.
